SharePoint administrator grants the one site in Graph Explorer: **GET**
`https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/sites/contoso.sharepoint.com:/sites/team-reports` for its `id`, then **POST**
`https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/sites/<id>/permissions` with:

```json
{
  "roles": ["write"],
  "grantedToIdentities": [{ "application": { "id": "<Application (client) ID>", "displayName": "awa files" } }]
}
```

Set `MS_SITE_URL` to the site's address and run `awa connectors test sharepoint`. The agents can list, search,
download and read Excel sheets; uploads, new folders and Excel edits wait for approval. A workbook is edited as a file:
awa changes a copy and uploads it only if nobody saved it in between, and refuses workbooks with macros, pivot tables
or charts. Search under `Sites.Selected` covers file and folder names only.

### Teams

An app cannot post to a channel on its own, so awa offers two ways. A **Workflows webhook** (in Teams: the channel,
**Workflows**, the template **Send webhook alerts to a channel**; the link goes to `TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL`) posts cards as
"Workflows". A **signed-in user** (`awa connect microsoft --teams`, a device code sign-in) posts, replies and reads in
the one channel named by `TEAMS_TEAM_ID` and `TEAMS_CHANNEL_ID`. Use a separate user for awa, protected with
multi-factor authentication.

### Check the connection

```console
awa check microsoft                      # live, read only: one line per check, red ones with the fix
awa check microsoft --allow-post teams   # also send one test card
```

`awa check microsoft` checks the shape of the values, the sign-in, the mailbox, the site, a workbook and Teams, and
two **negative tests**: the app must be refused on another mailbox (`AWA_CHECK_NEGATIVE_MAILBOX`) and on the root
site. A red line names the fix, for example `ms.secret_id_copied` (the Secret ID was pasted instead of the Value) or
`ms.rbac_not_scoped` (the app can still read other mailboxes).

Use the `outlook` connector, not `imap` or `smtp`, for Microsoft 365 mail: Microsoft is retiring password sign-in
for those protocols.

## Use a process with your own data

1. Copy the process folder, and `examples/microsoft/.env.example` next to it as `.env`. Fill in the values above, the
   mailbox, the site and a model (`AWA_DEFAULT_MODEL`).
2. In `blueprint.yaml` replace `company.example` (the digest's reviewer and `allowed_domains`). Nothing else holds
   company data.
3. Put the documents the process needs (the price list, the list of responsibilities) into the SharePoint folder
   `Approved`. Keep a **test** mailbox and site until the acceptance is done.
4. Check the connections, reading only: `awa validate blueprint.yaml`, then
   `awa connectors test mail --blueprint blueprint.yaml` and `awa connectors test files --blueprint blueprint.yaml`.
5. Run the cases three times: `awa eval blueprint.yaml cases.yaml --repetitions 3`. Then run your own requests with
   `awa run blueprint.yaml "..."` and read the drafts.
6. Only after the acceptance: set `enabled: true` on the trigger and keep `awa serve blueprint.yaml` running; waiting
   approvals are answered in the web app or with `awa runs decide`.

### Run budgets

Every run is bounded by `limits:` in its blueprint, and by `defaults.max_steps` and `automation.run_timeout` as a
second fence. Add `prices:` for your model and a `max_cost:` of your own.

| Process | `max_requests` | `max_total_tokens` | `max_tool_calls` | `max_duration` and `run_timeout` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sharepoint-briefing`, `outlook-briefing` | 25 | 40,000 | 14 | 5 minutes |
| `sales-inbox` | 30 | 50,000 | 16 | 10 minutes |
| `administration-inbox` | 50 | 80,000 | 30 | 10 minutes |
| `approved-digest` | 35 | 60,000 | 20 | 10 minutes |
| `sales-offer-preparation` | 80 | 120,000 | 60 | 15 minutes |

### Acceptance before a schedule

1. **Access is narrow.** `awa connectors test` is green for each connection, and both negative tests of
   `awa check microsoft` pass.
2. **The cases pass** three times each on test data; failures are reproduced, fixed and run again.
3. **Your own cases**: the typical requests of your company and the ones that scare you (a wrong price, another
   language, an order hidden in an email).
4. **A person reads the drafts** of one full run and compares every number with the price list.
5. **Approvals and recovery** (digest): approve, reject and edit a send on a test mailbox; stop the server while a
   send waits and start it again.
6. **Operation**: the owner, the stop procedure, how a rotated secret is replaced, the budgets, and the model, process
   version and test date written down.

Known limits: the briefings list *unread* mail, so a request can appear again on the next run; a re-run on a still
unread request makes a second draft; gross prices and other currencies are stopped, not converted.

## Send by role, not by address

`awa people` finds colleagues in the company directory and pins them to roles in `config/people.yaml` (kept out of
version control, readable by its owner only). A blueprint then names the role, and awa checks every recipient in the
directory when it sends:

```console
awa people search "carla mei"
awa people pin "carla mei" --role finance_recipients
awa people check
```

```yaml
connectors:
  mail: {use: outlook, recipients: [role:finance_recipients]}
```

`recipients` makes the roles the exact list of allowed recipients: any other address is refused, whatever the model
wrote, and a person who left or was disabled is left out. The app needs the application permission `User.Read.All`.
For each pinned person awa keeps only the directory ids, the name, the mail address, the state and the date of the last
check. `awa people check` ends with exit code 1 when a pinned person is gone.

## Hand-over to IT

Before a process runs on company data, the process owner and IT agree on one source, read only, and one output, such
as a reply draft. IT provides, per process: the owners and who may approve, the exact resources (mailbox, site,
folder), a dedicated integration identity (never a personal administrator account), only the read rights needed, the
sign-in method with its expiry, the model provider allowed for the data, and the trigger, time limit, cost limit and
alert target. Then the process is switched on in this order:

1. Define one process with its input, output, rules and stop cases.
2. Work in a copy with sample data and no production credentials.
3. Narrow the access: a test identity, read rights only, one resource.
4. Narrow the tools: `read_only: true`, `include`, single tool references per agent.
5. Check offline (`awa validate`, the project's tests), then make one live read; a forbidden resource must fail.
6. Test your normal, exception and attack cases, three times each. Run write tests only in a sandbox.
7. Allow one output, keep the approval by a person, then switch on the trigger and start a small pilot.

`read_only: true` limits the tools awa offers; it does not replace read-only rights in Microsoft 365, and it does not
stop data from going to the model provider. Dynamics 365, Business Central and other ERP systems are reached through
their OData or REST interfaces with the `odata`, `rest` and `openapi` connectors ([Connect systems](connect.md)), with
`create` and `update` left out at first.

## Common mistakes

| awa says | Meaning | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "the client secret is wrong" or "has expired" | The value (not the Secret ID) or its date | Create a new secret; update `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`. |
| `ms.mail_tenant_wide` (warning) | `Mail.*` is granted for the whole organization | Scope it with RBAC for Applications, then revoke the tenant-wide consent. |
| `ms.site_not_granted` (HTTP 403) | The app has no role on the site | Do the grant above; use `write` to upload. |
| HTTP 404 "requested user is invalid" | The mailbox does not exist or has no Exchange Online license | Check `MS_MAILBOX` (the full address). |
| "changed by someone else" | Someone saved the workbook after awa read it | Read it again and repeat the change. |
| "may or may not have been made" | A send got no clear answer | Do not resend; check the draft id the message names. |
| `ms.webhook_old_host` | The webhook link is on an old host | Copy the workflow's current trigger link. |

<!-- guide:do cd . -->
<!-- guide:do copy awa:examples/microsoft/briefings/outlook-briefing outlook-briefing -->

!!! example "In code"

    A Microsoft 365 process is a blueprint like any other: its connector, its budget and its switched-off schedule
    are plain fields ([Blueprints](../develop/blueprints.md)).

    <!-- guide:python -->
    ```python
    from awa.blueprints import Blueprint

    briefing = Blueprint.from_yaml_file("outlook-briefing/blueprint.yaml")
    print(briefing.name, {name: entry.get("use") for name, entry in briefing.connectors.items()})
    print(briefing.limits.max_requests, [(t.name, t.enabled) for t in briefing.triggers])
    ```

    <!-- guide:expect -->
    ```text
    outlook-briefing {'mail': 'outlook'}
    25 [('weekday-briefing', False)]
    ```

<!-- source: guide/agents-and-teams.md -->

# Agents and teams

Each step of a process is done by an [**agent**](../reference/glossary.md#agent): an AI model with one job, its
tools and its rules. Read this page when your process needs more than one agent and you must decide how they work
together: as a [workflow](../reference/glossary.md#workflow), a [team](../reference/glossary.md#team) or a
[network](../reference/glossary.md#network). Code enforces the limits of every structure; a model only decides
within them.

The shortest form is two agents in a fixed order, written in `blueprint.yaml`:

```yaml
agents:
  - name: drafter
    description: Drafts the reply.
  - name: editor
    description: Improves the draft until it is approved.
workflow:
  sequential: [drafter, editor]
```

More than one agent helps when the jobs differ:

- An agent with one job and short instructions makes fewer mistakes.
- A checker can be allowed to read, while only the clerk may change something.
- Two reviewers can work at the same time.
- Every delegation and handoff shows in the trace.

Every agent makes its own model calls, so use as few agents as the process needs.

## Choose the structure

| Structure | How it works | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **One agent** | A single agent does the whole job. | The job is small and needs one skill. |
| **Workflow** | Fixed steps in a fixed order; steps can run side by side or repeat. | The steps are always the same. The invoice desk of the [tour](tour.md) is a workflow. |
| **Team** | An **orchestrator** receives the request, hands parts to **members** and writes the answer. | The orchestrator must decide what happens next, and members help. |
| **Network** | A lead puts tasks on a shared **task board**; teammates take the tasks they can do, at the same time. | The work splits into parts that do not depend on each other. |

When in doubt, start with a workflow or a team. They are the easiest to read and to test.

In the web app, the page **Describe** helps you choose: **Suggest patterns** proposes up to three structures for
your description, and **Test the proposals** runs the same eval cases through each
([The web app](web-app.md#describe)).

## Workflow: steps in order

A workflow runs its steps in a fixed order. A step is one of three things:

- one agent;
- several agents at the same time (`parallel`);
- one agent that repeats until a condition holds (`loop`).

<!-- guide:do cd . -->
<!-- guide:file review-desk/blueprint.yaml -->
```yaml
name: review-desk
description: Drafts a reply, has two reviewers check it at the same time and polishes it.
agents:
  - name: drafter
    description: Drafts the reply.
  - name: legal_reviewer
    description: Checks the draft for legal problems.
  - name: compliance_reviewer
    description: Checks the draft against company rules.
  - name: editor
    description: Improves the draft until it is approved.
workflow:
  sequential:
    - drafter
    - parallel: [legal_reviewer, compliance_reviewer]
    - loop: editor
      until_contains: APPROVED
      max_iterations: 3
```

The drafter goes first. Both reviewers then read the draft at the same time. The editor repeats until its answer
contains `APPROVED`, at most three times. An agent without `instructions` follows its description.

Check the file with `awa validate`. `awa show --mermaid` draws the workflow as a diagram that many wikis and editors
can display:

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa validate review-desk/blueprint.yaml
review-desk: valid (tool names not checked; no tools.py beside it)
$ awa show review-desk/blueprint.yaml --mermaid
flowchart LR
    input([input])
    output([output])
    n1["drafter"]
    n2["legal_reviewer"]
    n3["compliance_reviewer"]
    n1 --> n2
    n1 --> n3
    n4["editor"]
    n4 -.->|until 'APPROVED', max 3| n4
    n2 --> n4
    n3 --> n4
    input --> n1
    n4 --> output
```

Less common steps:

- A `map:` step runs one agent over every item of a list ([Workflows](../develop/workflows.md#a-list-of-items)).
- A judge decides whether a worker's draft may go on
  ([Roles in a blueprint](../develop/teams.md#roles-in-a-blueprint)).
- Output checks send an answer that breaks a rule back to the model
  ([Agents](../develop/agents.md#structured-output-and-output-checks)).

## Team: an orchestrator and members

In a team, one agent leads: the **orchestrator**. It hands a task to a member and reads the result; this is a
**delegation**. A member can ask a **peer** a question directly. An agent can also pass the whole conversation on
(**handoff**), so the next agent answers the person directly.

The example `01_market_brief` in the awa folder is a team of four: an orchestrator, a researcher who reads web pages, an
analyst who checks the findings, and a writer. Copy `examples/benchmarks/core/01_market_brief` to your work folder as
`market-brief`, then look at it:

<!-- guide:do copy awa:examples/benchmarks/core/01_market_brief market-brief -->
<!-- guide:do cd market-brief -->
<!-- guide:run model=bench:01_market_brief -->
```console
$ awa show blueprint.yaml
market-brief 1.0.0
Researches a short list of products on the web and delivers a sourced brief.
entrypoint: team

agent       model    tools                  skills  description
brief_lead  default  -                      -       Runs the brief from the question to the structured, sourc...
researcher  default  web_search, fetch_url  -       Finds public pages about the requested items and reads them.
analyst     default  -                      -       Checks research findings for gaps and contradictions.
writer      default  -                      -       Writes the executive summary of a brief.

team market-brief: orchestrator brief_lead
  delegates: brief_lead -> researcher, analyst, writer
  peers: analyst -> researcher
  shared: none
```

Run it with `--stream` to see every step. `=>` marks a delegation or a question to a peer. The indentation shows who
asked whom. The output below comes from a scripted model and a stand-in for the internet, and its lines are cut short:

<!-- guide:run model=bench:01_market_brief -->
```console
$ awa run blueprint.yaml "Brief on Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora: year of the first release." --stream
> market-brief started
  > brief_lead started
    brief_lead -> delegate_task({"agent": "researcher", "task": "Research: Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora."})
    brief_lead => researcher (delegate): Research: Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora.
    > researcher started
      researcher -> web_search({"query": "Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, first release"})
...
    < researcher finished (310 ms)
...
    brief_lead => analyst (delegate): Check: ...
    > analyst started
      analyst -> consult_peer({"peer": "researcher", "question": "Confirm the year for Fedora."})
      analyst => researcher (consult): Confirm the year for Fedora.
...
    < analyst finished (150 ms)
...
    brief_lead => writer (delegate): Findings: ...
...
< market-brief finished (900 ms)
{
  "topic": "Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora",
  "executive_summary": "Debian first appeared in 1993. Ubuntu first appeared in 2004. Fedora first appeared in 2003.",
...
```

Limits keep a team in bounds. You set them under `team: limits:`:

<!-- guide:contains blueprint.yaml -->
```yaml
team:
  orchestrator: brief_lead
  members: [researcher, analyst, writer]
  peers: {analyst: [researcher]}
  messaging: false
  limits:
    max_delegation_depth: 2
    max_calls_per_member: 3
    delegation_timeout: 180
```

Here a member may be called at most three times, and delegation goes at most two levels deep. A member that takes
longer than 180 seconds is given up. When a limit refuses a delegation, the agent is told, so it can adapt.

A limit you do not set keeps its default:

| Team limit | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `max_calls_per_member` | 20 |
| `max_delegation_depth` | 4 |
| `max_parallel_delegations` | 8 |
| `delegation_timeout` (seconds) | 300 |
| `max_handoffs` | 5 |

## Network: teammates on a task board

In a network, a lead writes tasks on a shared **task board**. Each teammate takes the tasks that fit its
`capabilities`, at the same time as the others.

The example `05_agent_network` writes a supplier risk memo. Two analysts work in parallel, and a writer waits for
both:

<!-- guide:do cd . -->
<!-- guide:do copy awa:examples/benchmarks/core/05_agent_network supplier-network -->
<!-- guide:do cd supplier-network -->
<!-- guide:run model=bench:05_agent_network -->
```console
$ awa show blueprint.yaml --mermaid
flowchart TD
    a0(["risk_lead"])
    a1["spend_analyst"]
    a2["logistics_analyst"]
    a3["risk_writer"]
    a0 -->|tasks| a1
    a0 -->|tasks| a2
    a0 -->|tasks| a3
    a1 <-.-> a2
    a1 <-.-> a3
    a2 <-.-> a3
$ awa run blueprint.yaml "Supplier risk memo for Q3."
Highest spend: Nordwind GmbH with 48230.50 EUR. Slowest delivery: Alpha Logistik with 6.33 days late on average. Risk: a key supplier and a late one need different levers. Next step: review delivery terms of the slowest supplier.

[risk_lead] 13 model call(s), 12339 tokens (12100 in, 239 out), 1400 ms
```

The solid arrows are the tasks the lead hands out. The dashed lines show that teammates can talk to each other.

- The order in which teammates finish varies from run to run; the answer does not.
- A teammate without `capabilities` only takes tasks given to it by name. `awa validate` warns about it.

## How agents talk to each other

| What | Meaning | In the stream |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Delegation | The orchestrator gives a member a task and waits for the result. | `orchestrator => member (delegate): ...` |
| Consult | A member asks a peer a question and waits. | `analyst => researcher (consult): ...` |
| Handoff | An agent passes the whole conversation on. | `triage >> refunds: ...` in `awa chat` |
| Blackboard | Agents write to and read from shared, versioned entries. | `write_shared`, `read_shared` |
| Task board | Tasks with owners and dependencies. | `create_tasks`, `... completed` |

Everything one agent tells another reaches it as information, never as an order. Instructions come only from the
blueprint. [How awa works](../start/how-awa-works.md#how-agents-talk-to-each-other) shows the tools behind each way.

## Write good instructions

- **One job.** The `description` says in one sentence what the agent is for. The orchestrator reads it to decide whom
  to ask.
- **Steps and rules.** `instructions` list the steps and the rules in plain words, with numbers: "never guess a
  missing value", "at most three searches".
- **Name the delegations.** Tell the orchestrator which member gets which part, in which order.
- **Calculated rules are code.** Thresholds go into an approval condition or a rule in `tools.py`
  ([Describe a process](describe.md#many-conditions-and-special-cases)).

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Too many agents for a small job | A slow, costly run that gains nothing | Merge agents with the same skill. |
| Two agents with the same task | The orchestrator picks one by chance | Give each a different, specific description. |
| A step that must happen in a fixed order is left to a team | The orchestrator sometimes skips it | Use a workflow. |
| `delegation refused` or `max_calls_per_member` | A limit stopped the run | Raise the limit if the process needs it; otherwise sharpen the orchestrator's instructions. |
| `awa validate` reports an unknown agent | A name in `workflow`, `team` or `network` differs from the agent's `name` | Use the same spelling. |

!!! example "In code"

    The same structures are Python objects: `Agent`, `Sequential`, `Parallel`, `Loop`, `Team` and `AgentNetwork`
    ([Teams](../develop/teams.md), [Workflows](../develop/workflows.md)). This workflow runs offline with scripted
    models:

    <!-- guide:python -->
    ```python
    from awa import Agent, Sequential
    from awa.testing import FakeChatModel

    drafter = Agent("drafter", instructions="Draft a short reply.", model=FakeChatModel(["Thank you, your order ships today."]))
    editor = Agent("editor", instructions="Polish the draft.", model=FakeChatModel(["Thank you! Your order ships today."]))
    reply = Sequential("reply", [drafter, editor])
    print(reply.run_sync("Customer asks when order 1001 ships.").output)
    ```

    <!-- guide:expect -->
    ```text
    Thank you! Your order ships today.
    ```

<!-- source: guide/approvals.md -->

# Approvals

An [approval](../reference/glossary.md#approval) makes a tool call wait for a person's decision before it runs. Use
it for every step that changes data, sends something or cannot be undone. awa enforces it in code, so a model cannot
talk its way past a gated call.

To add one, list the tool under `approvals:` in `blueprint.yaml`, with a `when` condition if only some calls should
wait:

```yaml
approvals:
  - tool: connector:tickets.create_issue      # every call
  - tool: book_payment
    when: "amount >= 10000"                    # only from 10,000 on
  - tool: connector:mail.send_email
    when: "not endswith(to, '@example.com')"   # only mail leaving the company
```

The run stops before the call. The person sees which agent wants to do what, with which values. In the web app this
is the card **Please check before this happens** (step 8 of the [tour](tour.md)). It shows what will happen, the
values (amounts with their currency, dates written out) and why you are asked, for example *because the amount
is 5,000 EUR or more*:

![The Try it page: the example requests, the steps of the system in plain words, the card that asks for your OK with the values and the reason, and the buttons Approve and Say no](../assets/screenshots/guide/a08-try-approval.png)

--8<-- "docs/assets/screenshots/guide/a08-try-approval.legend.txt"

The person answers in one of three ways:

| Answer | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Approve** | The call runs. |
| **Say no**, with a note | The call does not run. The agent reads the note (**Tell the agent why**) and can explain or try another way. |
| **Approve with changes** | The call runs with the values you corrected, for example a lower amount. In the web app: **Change the values before approving (for experts)**, which takes a JSON object; in a terminal: `awa runs decide RUN_ID --approve --edit-args "@values.json"`. |

A double click cannot send the answer twice. A waiting run holds no resources. With the runs kept in the project
folder (`.awa`), the decision can come days later from any program on this computer, and the run continues where it
stopped. A decision from another computer needs the runs in PostgreSQL
([Keep it running](operate.md#when-many-people-depend-on-it)).

## What asks first without you doing anything

- Every connector operation that changes something: creating a ticket, sending an email, posting a message, changing
  a record. `requires_approval: false` on a connector switches this off, and `awa validate` then warns.
- Built-in tools that act outside: sending email, posting to a webhook, writing, moving or deleting files, changing a
  database.
- In a system from `awa build`: every step that changes data or sends something, and every decision your description
  leaves to a person.
- A function of your own in `tools.py` waits only when it is listed under `approvals:` or marked by its developer.
  `awa show` lists every tool that waits.

## The condition

`tool` is the name exactly as in the agents' `tools`. An approval on `connector:tickets` covers every operation of
that system. Without `when`, every call waits; with `when`, only the calls where the condition is true. A condition
uses the inputs of the tool (`awa show` and `awa connectors show NAME` list them):

| You write | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `amount >= 5000`, `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>` | Compare numbers or text. |
| `and`, `or`, `not` | Combine conditions. |
| `country in ['DE', 'AT']`, `not in` | One of a list. |
| `amount * quantity > 1000` | Arithmetic with `+ - * /`. |
| `contains(recipient, '@partner.example')`, `startswith(...)`, `endswith(...)` | Text tests. |
| `lower(...)`, `upper(...)`, `len(...)`, `number(...)`, `empty(...)`, `abs(...)`, `round(...)`, `min(...)`, `max(...)` | Helpers. |

A condition that cannot be worked out, for example because a value is missing, **asks**. A condition that is false
does not ask, so test both sides of every limit.

### Change the amount, and let the tests catch it

Say your head of finance decides from 10,000 EUR, not 5,000. Copy `invoice-desk` of the tour to `desk-10k` and
change the condition:

<!-- guide:do cd . -->
<!-- guide:do copy invoice-desk desk-10k -->
<!-- guide:do cd desk-10k -->
<!-- guide:do replace desk-10k/blueprint.yaml "amount_eur >= 5000" "amount_eur >= 10000" -->
<!-- guide:contains blueprint.yaml -->
```yaml
approvals:
- tool: finance_approval
  when: amount_eur >= 10000
```

<!-- guide:run exit=1 -->
```console
$ awa eval blueprint.yaml evals/cases.yaml
Evaluation: invoice_desk
========================

System invoice_desk on dataset invoice_desk: 3 case(s) x 1 repetition(s).

- Pass rate: 66.7% (2/3 runs)
- Errors: 0
...
Cases
-----

  case           passed  scores                                                                                      ms  tokens
  small-invoice  1/1     tool:invoice_ledger_query 1.00, no_approval:finance_approval 1.00, contains:INV-2041 1.00  387    1121
  large-invoice  0/1     approval_requested:finance_approval 0.00 (failed), contains:INV-2042 1.00                  385    1121
  paid-invoice   1/1     no_approval:finance_approval 1.00, contains:paid 1.00                                      289     793

Failures
--------

- large-invoice (repetition 1): approval_requested:finance_approval: approval for finance_approval requested 0 time(s), wanted 1..n (requests: none) (decisions applied: none; 1 never asked for)
evaluation failed: pass rate 66.7% (minimum 100.0%)
```

The case of the 7,450 EUR invoice expects an approval that no longer comes. It fails, and `awa eval` ends with exit
code 1. Now you decide. If the new rule is right, change the case too (its invoice must be above 10,000 EUR). If it
was a mistake, change the rule back.

A misspelled name in a condition is an error before anything runs, with the names that exist:

<!-- guide:do replace desk-10k/blueprint.yaml "amount_eur >= 10000" "amout_eur >= 10000" -->
<!-- guide:run exit=1 -->
```console
$ awa validate blueprint.yaml
error: approvals[0].when: condition 'amout_eur >= 10000' reads amout_eur, which the arguments of 'finance_approval' do not have (arguments: amount_eur, invoice_id)
invoice_desk: 1 error(s), 0 warning(s)
```

<!-- guide:do replace desk-10k/blueprint.yaml "amout_eur >= 10000" "amount_eur >= 5000" -->

Tiers, blocked suppliers and other special cases are in
[Describe a process](describe.md#many-conditions-and-special-cases).

## Rules for kinds of tools: policies

`policies:` apply to every tool call of all agents, or of the agents you name:

<!-- guide:file blueprint.yaml append -->
```yaml
policies:
  - deny: [delete_file]
    reason: This desk never deletes files.
  - ask: [external_action]
```

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa validate blueprint.yaml
invoice_desk: valid
```

`deny` refuses a tool and tells the agent the reason. `ask` makes every tool of one kind wait for a person:

- `external_action`: sends, books or changes something.
- `private_data`: reads personal or confidential data.
- `untrusted_input`: reads text from outside, such as web pages and emails.

`agents: [payments]` limits a policy to those agents.

## Where people answer

| Where | How |
| --- | --- |
| The web app, **Try it** | The card **Please check before this happens** with **Approve** and **Say no**. |
| The web app, **Use it** and **Approvals** | Runs that a trigger started and that wait, with the same card. |
| `awa chat` | `approve? [y/N]`; anything but `y` says no and asks for a note. |
| `awa run` | `Approve? [y/N]` with the full request. Without a terminal the run ends paused with exit code 2. |
| `awa runs decide RUN --approve` or `--reject` | Automated runs (`awa worker`, `awa serve`) that wait with the status `waiting`. `--edit-args "@changed.json"` approves with changes. |
| A served system | Your application lists the pending approvals and sends the decision over HTTP; `--approver-role` limits who may decide ([Serving](../develop/serving.md)). |
| Eval cases | Each case lists the decisions a person would make ([Test and improve](test.md)). |

A run can wait for several approvals. They are answered one at a time, and the run goes on when all are answered.

## See an approval in Langfuse

With [Langfuse](langfuse.md), every pause and every decision is part of the run's trace. The pictures show the
invoice desk of the [tour](tour.md#step-10-answer-the-approval-and-finish-the-run) for invoice INV-2042, with a
scripted model. A tool call that waits for a person is marked as a warning, next to the approval request with the
tool and its arguments:

![Langfuse: the approval request of the run for invoice INV-2042, with the tool finance_approval and its arguments, the amount 7450 and the invoice number](../assets/screenshots/tracing-approval.png)

*The approval pause: the exact values the person is asked about.*

When the person decides, the run continues as a second trace of the same thread, with the decision and who
made it:

![Langfuse: the resumed run of invoice INV-2042 with the decision approve, the reviewer head-of-finance and the release that followed](../assets/screenshots/tracing-approved.png)

*The decision, who made it, and the release that followed.*

## Before real use

- [ ] Every action that cannot be undone asks for approval, and the right people answer.
- [ ] Thresholds are in approval conditions or rules, not in instructions.
- [ ] The eval cases cover both sides of every threshold.
- [ ] Waiting runs are kept in a durable store, so a decision can come later.
- [ ] Open approvals escalate when nobody answers (`sla: approval_within`, see
      [Keep it running](operate.md#retries-deadlines-and-notifications)).

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The threshold is only in the instructions | The model sometimes forgets it | Put it in `approvals:` with `when`. |
| The tool name in `approvals:` differs from the agent's `tools` | The approval never asks | Copy the name from `awa show`. |
| `error: approvals[0].when` | The condition names an input the tool does not have | Use a name from the list the message gives. |
| Only one side of a limit is tested | A rule change slips through | One case just below, one just above. |
| `awa run` ends with exit code 2 | Nobody could answer: there is no terminal | Run it in a terminal, or use the worker and `awa runs decide`. |
| A run stays `waiting` | It waits for a person | Look at **Approvals** or `awa runs list --status waiting`. |

<!-- guide:do cd . -->
<!-- guide:do cd invoice-desk -->

!!! example "In code"

    `awa.load` builds the project folder with its `tools.py`, as the commands do. A system with approvals needs a
    **checkpointer**, the place where a paused run is kept. `run` returns a paused result with the exact values that
    wait, and `resume` continues the same thread with the decision (`{"action": "reject", "note": "..."}` says no,
    `{"action": "edit", "args": {...}}` approves with changes). See [Safety: approvals](../develop/safety.md#approvals).
    Run it in the folder `invoice-desk` of the [tour](tour.md) with your provider's key; the output below comes from
    the guide's scripted model, so your answer is worded differently.

    <!-- guide:python -->
    ```python
    import asyncio

    import awa
    from awa.persistence import StateInMemorySaver

    async def main() -> None:
        desk = awa.load(".", checkpointer=StateInMemorySaver())
        paused = await desk.run("Please release invoice INV-2042 for payment.", thread_id="inv-2042")
        print(paused.is_interrupted, paused.interrupts[0]["value"]["tool"], paused.interrupts[0]["value"]["args"])
        done = await desk.resume("inv-2042", {"action": "approve"})
        print(done.output)

    asyncio.run(main())
    ```

    <!-- guide:expect -->
    ```text
    True finance_approval {'invoice_id': 'INV-2042', 'amount_eur': 7450.0}
    Invoice INV-2042 from Alpen Maschinenbau AG (7,450.00 EUR) is released for payment.
    ```

<!-- source: guide/test.md -->

# Test and improve

Tests tell you, with numbers, whether your process still does the right thing. You need them before real work and
after every change to an instruction, a tool, a model or a rule. A test is a list of
[**eval cases**](../reference/glossary.md#eval-case): example requests and the checks their result must pass.

```yaml
- id: large-invoice
  input: Please release invoice INV-2042 for payment.
  scorers:
  - approval_requested:finance_approval
  - contains:INV-2042
  decisions:
  - action: approve
    tool: finance_approval
```

The shortest path:

1. `awa build` already wrote the first cases to `evals/cases.yaml`.
2. Run them: `awa eval blueprint.yaml evals/cases.yaml`, or **Run all tests** on the page **Test** of the web app.
3. Add cases from your own data, and run them again after every change.

Each case calls the model and costs a little, so run the tests when something changes, not all the time. The
[tour](tour.md#step-7-run-the-tests) runs them once.

## Write an eval case

Copy the folder `invoice-desk` of the tour to `desk-tests`. Add a fourth case for when the head of finance says no:

<!-- guide:do cd . -->
<!-- guide:do copy invoice-desk desk-tests -->
<!-- guide:do cd desk-tests -->
<!-- guide:file evals/cases.yaml -->
```yaml
name: invoice_desk
cases:
- id: small-invoice
  input: Please release invoice INV-2041 for payment.
  scorers:
  - tool:invoice_ledger_query
  - no_approval:finance_approval
  - contains:INV-2041
- id: large-invoice
  input: Please release invoice INV-2042 for payment.
  scorers:
  - approval_requested:finance_approval
  - contains:INV-2042
  decisions:
  - action: approve
    tool: finance_approval
- id: paid-invoice
  input: Please pay invoice INV-2043.
  scorers:
  - no_approval:finance_approval
  - contains:paid
- id: large-invoice-rejected
  input: Please release invoice INV-2042 for payment.
  tags: [safety]
  decisions:
  - action: reject
    note: Wait for the delivery note.
    tool: finance_approval
  scorers:
  - approval_requested:finance_approval
  - approval_rejected:finance_approval
  - contains:hold
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | A short name that does not change; reports and comparisons match cases by it. |
| `input` | The request, as a person would write it. |
| `scorers` | The checks of this case. |
| `decisions` | The answers to the approvals the case runs into (below). |
| `tags` | Labels, to run a group with `--tag`. |
| `expected` | The expected answer, for the checks that need one. |

Write the cases a new colleague would need: everyday requests, odd ones (an unknown invoice), the exceptions that go
wrong today, and the ones where the system **must not** act alone.

### The checks

| Check | Passes when |
| --- | --- |
| `contains:<text>` | The answer contains the text, in any case. |
| `exact` | The answer is exactly `expected`. |
| `regex:<pattern>` | The answer matches a text pattern. |
| `tool:<name>`, `no_tool:<name>` | The tool was used, or never used. |
| `delegated:<agent>`, `handoff:<agent>` | Work was handed to this agent. |
| `approval_requested:<tool>`, `no_approval:<tool>` | A person was asked about this tool, or never. |
| `approval_granted:<tool>`, `approval_rejected:<tool>` | A decision approved, or rejected, this tool. |
| `approval:<tool>` | The run ended waiting for approval of this tool. |
| `max_latency:<ms>`, `max_tokens:<n>` | The run stayed under a time or a size. |
| `json_fields` | A structured answer has the values in `expected`. |
| `judge:<criteria>` | A model grades the answer against your words. |

Checks on tools, delegations, handoffs and approvals look at *how* the answer came about. A correct answer that
skipped the approval fails. A `judge:` check is itself a model and can vary, so prefer the other checks.

### Decisions in a process with several approvals

A case answers its approvals like a reviewer would, in the order they are asked:

```yaml
- id: large-invoice
  input: Book invoice INV-7 (6,200 EUR) and tell the supplier.
  decisions:
    - approve                                        # the booking
    - {action: reject, note: Wrong contact person.}  # the email to the supplier
  scorers:
    - approval_granted:book_invoice
    - approval_rejected:notify_supplier
```

A decision is `approve`, `reject`, `{action: reject, note: ...}` or `{action: edit, args: {...}}`. Add `tool:` when
approvals can come in any order, and `repeat: true` with `tool:` when one tool asks many times. With fewer decisions
than approvals, the run ends waiting at the first unanswered one, which `approval:<tool>` checks.

## Run the tests

In the web app, **Run all tests** on the page **Test** runs every case and shows each result:

![The Test page: the button Run all tests, the result 3 of 3 eval cases passed with the meter full, and the card of an eval case with what it sends, its files and its result](../assets/screenshots/guide/a07-test.png)

--8<-- "docs/assets/screenshots/guide/a07-test.legend.txt"

In a terminal, run only the new case, three times, to see how steady it is:

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa eval blueprint.yaml evals/cases.yaml --repetitions 3 --tag safety
Evaluation: invoice_desk
========================

System invoice_desk on dataset invoice_desk: 1 case(s) x 3 repetition(s).

- Pass rate: 100.0% (3/3 runs)
- Errors: 0
- Usage: 12 model call(s), 3537 tokens (3267 in, 270 out), 6 tool call(s)
- Duration: 0.3 s

Reliability
-----------

  measure                                 value
  pass@1 (one run passes)                 100.0%
  pass@3 (at least one of 3 runs passes)  100.0%
  pass^3 (all 3 runs of a case pass)      100.0%
  latency p50 / p95                       121 ms / 123 ms
  cost                                    not computed (no prices given)
  cache hit rate                          0.0%

Caching
-------

  measure                               value
  model calls answered by the provider  12
  model calls replayed (no cost)        0
  model call p50 / p95                  6 ms / 20 ms
  tool results reused / stored          0 / 3
  prompt prefix of invoice_checker      6c23893e5dbddce8 (stable)
  prompt prefix of payment_clerk        b6fbbf4322da619c (stable)

Scorers
-------

  scorer                               mean  pass rate  passed  failed
  approval_requested:finance_approval  1.00     100.0%       3       0
  approval_rejected:finance_approval   1.00     100.0%       3       0
  contains:hold                        1.00     100.0%       3       0

Cases
-----

  case                    passed  scores                                                                                                  ms  tokens
  large-invoice-rejected  3/3     approval_requested:finance_approval 1.00, approval_rejected:finance_approval 1.00, contains:hold 1.00  121    1179
```

| Part | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| Pass rate | The share of runs that passed every check. |
| `pass@1` | How often one run is right. |
| `pass@3` | Whether each case worked at least once in three runs: what the system can do at best. |
| `pass^3` | Whether each case worked **every time** in three runs. When nobody checks each answer, watch this one. |
| `latency p50 / p95` | The typical run, and the one slower than 19 in 20 runs. |
| Scorers and Cases | Which kind of check fails most, and each case with its scores. |
| Failures | Which case failed which check, and why; only when something fails. |

`awa eval` ends with exit code 1 when fewer cases pass than `--min-pass-rate` (default: all). With `--repetitions 3
--min-pass-hat-k 0.9` it also fails unless 90 percent of the cases passed every time. `--case ID` runs one case and
`--concurrency N` runs several at once. Every case works on a fresh copy of the project's files, so cases never
affect each other.

## Before and after a change

A change that fixes one case can break another. Save a baseline first:

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa eval blueprint.yaml evals/cases.yaml --json baseline.json
Evaluation: invoice_desk
========================
...
wrote baseline.json
```

Make the change (an instruction, a rule, a tool, the model), then compare:

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa eval blueprint.yaml evals/cases.yaml --baseline baseline.json --markdown report.md
Evaluation: invoice_desk
========================
...
Comparison with invoice_desk
----------------------------

Pass rate 100.0% -> 100.0% (0 regression(s), 0 improvement(s))
...
```

awa lists every case and check that got worse, and ends with exit code 1 if anything did. `--markdown` also saves
the report as a file. With `--prices prices.yaml` ([Count the cost](operate.md#count-the-cost)) the report shows what
the tests cost, and `--cost-budget AMOUNT` fails an evaluation that costs too much.

## Cases from real runs

Every finished run is a ready-made eval case. `awa runs export-cases` turns runs into cases. In the project of the
tour, the run of step 10 finished:

<!-- guide:do cd invoice-desk -->
<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa runs export-cases RUN_ID --out evals/from_runs.yaml --no-judge
wrote 1 case(s) to evals/from_runs.yaml; run them with `awa eval <blueprint> evals/from_runs.yaml`
```

<!-- guide:contains evals/from_runs.yaml -->
```yaml
  scorers:
  - tool:invoice_ledger_query
  - tool:finance_approval
  decisions:
  - action: approve
    tool: finance_approval
```

The case has the run's input, the decision of the head of finance, a check for every tool the run used, and the
answer as `expected`. Tighten it before you keep it: add `contains:7,450.00` for the figure that must be right, and
remove a `tool:` the process may skip. Secrets are masked, but the file holds real input and answers, so keep it
where you keep your run records.

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa eval blueprint.yaml evals/from_runs.yaml
Evaluation: invoice_desk
========================
...
- Pass rate: 100.0% (1/1 runs)
...
```

## See the test runs in Langfuse

With [Langfuse](langfuse.md) set up, every evaluation run is a trace of its own, and `awa build` also sends its
design and tests. Open the run of a failed case and read its steps as in [Read a trace](operate.md#read-a-trace).
`metadata.blueprint` in the search bar finds the runs of one build.

## Improve the system

| What you see | What to change |
| --- | --- |
| The answer lacks something the process needs | Add it to the agent's instructions, or to the description and build again. |
| The wrong agent did the work, or none | Make each agent's description clearly different. |
| A tool was not used, or the wrong one | Check that the agent has the tool, and say when to use it. |
| A rule was applied wrongly | Put the rule in an approval condition or a rule in `tools.py`, not in the instructions. |
| An approval was not asked for | Add it under `approvals:` ([Approvals](approvals.md)). |
| The run stopped at a limit | Check whether the process needs more steps, then raise the limit. |
| The expected value is wrong | Fix the case: cases describe your process and are not always right the first time. |

### Refinement after a build

When `awa build` reaches its target, it reads the test runs of each agent for waste: a tool called twice with the
same arguments, failed tool calls, flaky cases, picked tools never used. One call of the fast model then writes at
most three lines per agent, each based on one finding. The cases run twice more. The lines stay only when results are
at least as good and input tokens per run are no higher; they appear under the agent's `refinements:` with their
evidence. With nothing to refine, the build prints `Refinement: none`.

### Texts and model settings of an agent

An agent can read its instructions from a file, give its tools its own descriptions, and set fields of its chat model
and LangChain middleware:

```yaml
agents:
- name: analyst
  model: strong
  describe:
    instructions_file: prompts/analyst.md     # instead of instructions:
    tool_docs: {ledger_query: Reads booked invoices by number.}
  refine:
    model_kwargs: {max_tokens: 4000}          # fields of the chat model, every attempt
    middleware:
    - ModelCallLimitMiddleware: {run_limit: 20}
```

| Field | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `describe.instructions_file` | The agent's instructions, read from this file next to the blueprint. |
| `describe.tool_docs` | Per tool name, the description the model reads instead of the tool's own. |
| `refine.model_kwargs` | Fields of the chat model for every attempt. |
| `refine.anthropic`, `refine.openai`, `refine.google` | Fields of that provider's chat model class; each applies only when the attempt uses that provider, so a fallback to another provider never carries them. |
| `refine.middleware` | LangChain agent middleware by class name, with its arguments. |

Every key is checked against the LangChain class when the blueprint loads, so a typo fails before the first run. For
code, put hooks (`@refine_model`, `@refine_agent` from `awa.refine`) in a `refine.py` next to the blueprint. They take
and return plain LangChain objects; `awa run` and `awa eval` load the file.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tests written after the design only fit what it does | Everything passes, nothing is found | Write cases from your process: the exceptions, the limits, the "must not". |
| Expected values from sample data used on real data | Cases fail after you connect a system | Change `expected` to your real values. |
| One run per case | A case passes today and fails tomorrow | Use `--repetitions 3` and watch `pass^3`. |
| A `judge:` as the only check | Results that vary | Add a check that does not vary. |
| `Errors: 1` or **Could not run** | The run could not finish: a key, a limit, a connection | The message names it. |
| `unknown scorer` | A check is misspelled | Compare it with the table above. |

!!! example "In code"

    `awa.evals.evaluate` (or `evaluate_sync` outside async code) is `awa eval` from Python, and `awa.testing` has
    scripted models, so a test needs no key ([Testing](../develop/testing.md)):

    <!-- guide:python -->
    ```python
    from awa import Agent
    from awa.evals import EvalCase, evaluate_sync
    from awa.testing import FakeChatModel

    greeter = Agent("greeter", instructions="Greet the user by name.", model=FakeChatModel(["Hello, Anna!"]))
    report = evaluate_sync(greeter, [EvalCase(id="anna", input="My name is Anna.")], ["contains:Anna"])
    print(report.pass_rate, report.cases[0].case_id, report.cases[0].status)
    ```

    <!-- guide:expect -->
    ```text
    1.0 anna passed
    ```

<!-- source: guide/run.md -->

# Run automatically

Once your process passes its eval cases, let it work without you. A [trigger](../reference/glossary.md#trigger)
starts a run on a schedule, an email, a file or a web request, and other programs can call the process over HTTP or
MCP. The shortest path: add a trigger to the blueprint, try it with `--dry-run`, then start `awa worker`.

```yaml
triggers:
  - name: new-invoice
    file_drop: {directory: inbox, pattern: "*.pdf"}
    input: "Check the invoice in {payload.name} and release it for payment. The invoice says: {payload.text}"
```

| Way | Command | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Talk to it | `awa chat blueprint.yaml` | Trying it out; the page **Try it** of the web app does the same. |
| Give it one task | `awa run blueprint.yaml "..."` | One job from a terminal or a script. |
| Start it on an event | `triggers:` in the blueprint, then `awa worker` or `awa serve` | Work that starts with a schedule, an email, a file, a queue message or a web request. |
| Offer it to other programs | `awa serve`, `awa mcp serve` | Your own applications, desktop assistants and code editors. |

Run every command in the project folder, so awa finds `blueprint.yaml`, `.env` and the `tools.py` next to the
blueprint.

!!! info "Preview"
    Triggers, `awa worker`, `awa serve`, `awa trigger` and `awa mcp serve` work and are tested, but their options may still change in a minor release ([Stability](../about/stability.md)).

## By hand: `awa chat` and `awa run`

`awa chat` is a conversation in the terminal. Short lines show what happens:

- `orchestrator => member`: a delegation.
- `agent -> tool({...})`: a tool call.
- `approval needed:`: a step that waits for you. `y` approves; anything else says no and asks for a note.

`/reset` starts over, `/usage` shows model calls and tokens, `/exit` ends it. A workflow keeps no thread, so each
message is a new task.

`awa run` gives the system one task. `--stream` prints each step, `--json` prints the result for a script, and
`--trace FILE` records what the run did ([Read a trace](operate.md#read-a-trace)). The exit code is `0` when done, `1`
on an error, and `2` when the run waits for an approval nobody could answer.

## The five kinds of trigger

| In `blueprint.yaml` | `awa add trigger --kind` | Starts a run when ... | What the run receives (`payload`) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `schedule` | `schedule` | a point in time comes (`cron`, or `every: 15m`) | `date`, the time of the tick |
| `mailbox` | `mail` | an unread email arrives in an IMAP folder | `from`, `to`, `subject`, `date`, `text`, `attachments` (saved, with their text) |
| `file_drop` | `file-drop` | a file appears in a folder and stops changing | `name`, `path`, `text` of PDF, Word, Excel and CSV files |
| `webhook` | `webhook` | another system sends a signed web request | the JSON the sender posted |
| `queue` | `queue` | a message arrives on a queue | the message |

Each start is a **run** with an id (`proc_...`), a status and a history. The blueprint never holds secrets, only the
names of the settings that hold them (`*_env`).

## Add triggers

`awa add trigger` writes a valid entry and prints how to start and try it. Copy `invoice-desk` of the tour to
`desk-triggers` and add a schedule and a mailbox:

<!-- guide:do cd . -->
<!-- guide:do copy invoice-desk desk-triggers -->
<!-- guide:do cd desk-triggers -->
<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa add trigger blueprint.yaml --kind schedule --name morning-check --cron "0 7 * * MON-FRI" --timezone Europe/Berlin --input "Check all open invoices of {payload.date}."
added trigger 'morning-check' to blueprint.yaml:
  - name: morning-check
    schedule:
      cron: 0 7 * * MON-FRI
      timezone: Europe/Berlin
    input: Check all open invoices of {payload.date}.

Start it:
  awa worker blueprint.yaml
  (It runs until you stop it with Ctrl+C. Runs that need an approval wait; answer them with `awa runs decide` or on the Approvals page of `awa ui`.)

morning-check: runs by itself:
  0 7 * * MON-FRI (Europe/Berlin)
  (Nothing to send; the worker fires it.)

Try morning-check without waiting for a real event:
  awa trigger run blueprint.yaml morning-check --payload "@morning-check.json" --dry-run
  (First save a sample event as morning-check.json in this folder, for example {"date": "..."}. Shows the task the system would get; leave out --dry-run to run it once.)
```

The `cron` text has five fields: minute, hour, day of the month, month, day of the week. `0 7 * * MON-FRI` is 7:00 on
every weekday. A schedule fires once per tick, even when several workers run. After downtime it runs the latest
missed tick (`catch_up: latest`; the alternatives are `all` and `skip`).

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa add trigger blueprint.yaml --kind mail --name ap-inbox --host imap.example.com --input "New email from {payload.from}: {payload.subject}"
added trigger 'ap-inbox' to blueprint.yaml:
  - name: ap-inbox
    mailbox:
      host: imap.example.com
      username_env: AWA_IMAP_USER
      password_env: AWA_IMAP_PASSWORD
    input: 'New email from {payload.from}: {payload.subject}'

Start it:
  awa worker blueprint.yaml
  (It runs until you stop it with Ctrl+C. Runs that need an approval wait; answer them with `awa runs decide` or on the Approvals page of `awa ui`.)

ap-inbox: send an email to the mailbox INBOX on:
  imap.example.com
  (Set AWA_IMAP_USER and AWA_IMAP_PASSWORD in .env.)

Try ap-inbox without waiting for a real event:
  awa trigger run blueprint.yaml ap-inbox --payload "@ap-inbox.json" --dry-run
  (First save a sample event as ap-inbox.json in this folder, for example {"from": "...", "subject": "..."}. Shows the task the system would get; leave out --dry-run to run it once.)
```

Put the values of `AWA_IMAP_USER` and `AWA_IMAP_PASSWORD` into `.env`. In the web app, the page **Use it** has the
same choice as a form under **Add another trigger** ([tour, step 9](tour.md#step-9-let-a-trigger-start-it)):

![The Use it page, the form Add a trigger: the kind file-drop, the folder inbox, the pattern *.pdf, the task text and the Add this trigger button](../assets/screenshots/guide/a09-trigger-form.png)

--8<-- "docs/assets/screenshots/guide/a09-trigger-form.legend.txt"

For Microsoft 365 mail use the `outlook` connector instead ([Microsoft 365](microsoft-365.md)).

## Try a trigger first

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa trigger list blueprint.yaml
NAME           KIND       DETAILS
new-invoice    file_drop  directory=C:\awa-guide-work\desk-triggers\inbox, pattern=*.pdf
morning-check  schedule   cron=0 7 * * MON-FRI, timezone=Europe/Berlin, catch_up=latest
ap-inbox       mailbox    host=imap.example.com, folder=INBOX
$ awa validate blueprint.yaml
warning: triggers.ap-inbox: environment variable AWA_IMAP_USER is not set
warning: triggers.ap-inbox: environment variable AWA_IMAP_PASSWORD is not set
invoice_desk: valid with 2 warning(s)
```

`awa validate` names every setting that is not set yet; a template that cannot work is an error. To see what an event
becomes, without running anything or setting anything, save two sample events, `morning-check.json`:

<!-- guide:file morning-check.json -->
```json
{"date": "2026-10-05"}
```

and `ap-inbox.json`:

<!-- guide:file ap-inbox.json -->
```json
{"from": "anna@example.com", "subject": "Invoice INV-2041"}
```

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa trigger run blueprint.yaml morning-check --payload "@morning-check.json" --dry-run
input:     Check all open invoices of 2026-10-05.
thread_id: (one per run)
dedup_key: morning-check@2026-10-05T00:00:00Z
$ awa trigger run blueprint.yaml ap-inbox --payload "@ap-inbox.json" --dry-run
input:     New email from anna@example.com: Invoice INV-2041
thread_id: (one per run)
dedup_key: (none)
```

The events come from files because Windows PowerShell 5.1 removes double quotes inside an argument; `"@file.json"`
works in every terminal. Without `--dry-run`, the trigger fires once and the process runs in your terminal, asking
for approvals there.

## From an event to a task

| Text | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `input` | What the system is asked to do. | `"Release invoice {payload.invoice_no}."` |
| `thread_id` | Runs with the same thread continue one conversation. | `"inv-{payload.invoice_no\|slug}"` |
| `dedup` | A business key: a second event with the same key starts no second run. | `"{payload.invoice_no}"` |

Put them on a trigger, or under `automation:` for all triggers. In the text:

- `{payload.subject}` is a field of the event, `{payload}` the whole event as JSON.
- `{today}` and `{now}` are the date and time.
- A filter after a bar changes the value: `|slug` makes it safe for an id; also `|lower`, `|upper`, `|trim`.
- `{payload.priority|"normal"}` gives a fallback.

A name that is not in the event, without a fallback, is an error, so a typo never starts runs with an empty key.

## A web request that starts a run

A webhook is an address another system calls. awa accepts a request only when it proves it comes from the sender.
The `scheme` says how: `timestamped` (the default, a signature of time and body), `body` (a `sha256=` signature) or
`token` (the secret itself in the header `X-Awa-Token`). Copy `invoice-desk` to `desk-hook` and add one:

<!-- guide:do cd . -->
<!-- guide:do copy invoice-desk desk-hook -->
<!-- guide:do cd desk-hook -->
<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa add trigger blueprint.yaml --kind webhook --name supplier-invoice --input "Release invoice {payload.invoice_no}." --scheme token
added trigger 'supplier-invoice' to blueprint.yaml:
  - name: supplier-invoice
    webhook:
      secret_env: SUPPLIER_INVOICE_SECRET
      scheme: token
    input: Release invoice {payload.invoice_no}.

Start it (receives the web requests and runs everything):
  awa serve blueprint.yaml
  (It runs until you stop it with Ctrl+C. Runs that need an approval wait; answer them with `awa runs decide` or on the Approvals page of `awa ui`.)

supplier-invoice: send a POST request to:
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/automations/invoice_desk/webhooks/supplier-invoice
  (Headers: X-Awa-Token: the secret in SUPPLIER_INVOICE_SECRET itself. Set SUPPLIER_INVOICE_SECRET in .env.)

Try supplier-invoice without waiting for a real event:
  awa trigger run blueprint.yaml supplier-invoice --payload "@supplier-invoice.json" --dry-run
  (First save a sample event as supplier-invoice.json in this folder, for example {"invoice_no": "..."}. Shows the task the system would get; leave out --dry-run to run it once.)
```

With `SUPPLIER_INVOICE_SECRET=a-long-secret-text` in `.env` and `awa serve blueprint.yaml` running, send the body
`{"invoice_no": "INV-2041"}` saved as `invoice.json`, first with a wrong secret, then with the right one (`curl.exe`
comes with Windows 10 and 11; elsewhere type `curl`):

```console
curl.exe -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/automations/invoice_desk/webhooks/supplier-invoice -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Awa-Token: wrong" --data "@invoice.json"
curl.exe -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/automations/invoice_desk/webhooks/supplier-invoice -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Awa-Token: a-long-secret-text" --data "@invoice.json"
```

The same two requests against the same server, checked on every test run of this page:

<!-- guide:python -->
```python
import os
import time

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from awa.server import build_blueprint_app

os.environ["SUPPLIER_INVOICE_SECRET"] = "a-long-secret-text"   # in real life: in .env
url = "/v1/automations/invoice_desk/webhooks/supplier-invoice"

with TestClient(build_blueprint_app("blueprint.yaml")) as client:
    refused = client.post(url, json={"invoice_no": "INV-2041"}, headers={"X-Awa-Token": "wrong"})
    print(refused.status_code, refused.json()["error"]["message"])

    sent = client.post(url, json={"invoice_no": "INV-2041"}, headers={"X-Awa-Token": "a-long-secret-text"})
    print(sent.status_code, sent.json()["status"])

    run_id = sent.json()["id"]
    for _ in range(100):  # the server executes the run in the background
        run = client.get(f"/v1/process-runs/{run_id}").json()
        if run["status"] not in ("queued", "running"):
            break
        time.sleep(0.1)
    print(run["status"], "|", run["input"])
    print(run["output"])
```

<!-- guide:expect -->
```text
Webhook invoice_desk/supplier-invoice refused: Webhook token does not match
401 Webhook verification failed
202 queued
succeeded | Release invoice INV-2041.
Invoice INV-2041 from Nordwind Office GmbH (1,180.00 EUR) is released for payment.
```

The first line is the server's own log. The caller only sees `401 Webhook verification failed`, the same answer for
every refused request, so it learns nothing. The accepted request gets `202 queued` at once, and the server runs it in
the background. A copy of a signed request within the replay window (five minutes) starts no second run; still add a
`dedup` key such as the invoice number. Requests larger than 1 MiB are refused (`413`).

## Keep the triggers running: `awa worker` or `awa serve`

| | `awa worker` | `awa serve` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runs the triggers (schedule, folder, mailbox, queue) | yes | yes; with a PostgreSQL database it leaves them to `awa worker` |
| Receives web requests (webhooks, the API) | no | yes |
| Use it for | Folders, email and schedules | Webhooks, the HTTP API, or both |

Run one of the two per project folder. The one that runs the triggers holds a lock, and a second one refuses to
start. An extra `awa worker --no-triggers` may run next to it; it only executes queued runs. `--once` handles what is
ready and stops, for a scheduled task or a test. Ctrl+C stops gracefully: running work gets up to 30 seconds, the rest
goes back to the queue. [Keep it running](operate.md) covers what happens to the runs.

| Where it goes | |
| --- | --- |
| Handled files of a file drop | `processed/` next to the watched folder; a refused one goes to `failed/`. Nothing is overwritten. |
| Attachments of emails | `attachments/` next to the blueprint; one larger than 25 MiB is listed but not saved. |
| Every run, and every waiting approval | `.awa/awa.db` and `.awa/checkpoints.db` in the project folder. |

## Offer it to other programs

**As a web API.** `awa serve blueprint.yaml --api-key-env AWA_API_KEY` answers on `http://127.0.0.1:8000`; callers
send the key of the setting `AWA_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer ...`. A request that reaches an approval stops,
and a person answers through the same door:

| Request | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /v1/systems/NAME/runs` | Run one request. Body: `{"input": "...", "thread_id": "..."}`. |
| `POST /v1/systems/NAME/runs/stream` | The same, as a stream of events. |
| `GET /v1/systems/NAME/threads/ID/interrupts` | The approvals a thread waits for. |
| `POST /v1/systems/NAME/threads/ID/resume` | Answer them. Body: `{"decision": {"action": "approve"}}`. |

`--approver-role` limits who may answer approvals. `--rate-limit` and `--max-concurrency` keep the server in bounds.
`--api-keys-file` gives each application its own key. Keep the server on this computer, or behind a proxy your IT
team runs. Every option: [Serving](../develop/serving.md).

**Over MCP**, a desktop assistant or code editor uses the system as a tool and asks its user for approvals. The client
starts the server itself. Give it the command, with absolute paths and the model's settings in `env`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "invoice-desk": {
      "command": "awa",
      "args": ["mcp", "serve", "C:\\awa-guide-work\\invoice-desk\\blueprint.yaml"],
      "env": {"AWA_DEFAULT_MODEL": "<provider>:<model>", "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY": "your-key-here"}
    }
  }
}
```

The client then lists the tool `run_invoice_desk` and, because the desk has approvals, `resume_invoice_desk`. Keep
that configuration file private. [MCP](../develop/mcp.md) has the HTTP transport and the details.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A secret written into the blueprint | You can read it in the file | Use `secret_env` and put the value in `.env`. |
| No `limits:` on a trigger that runs at night | `awa add trigger` and `awa validate` warn | Add `limits:` ([Keep it running](operate.md#limits-and-costs)). |
| Two workers on one folder | `Another awa process ... already runs the triggers` | Run one, or `awa worker --no-triggers` for the second. |
| The same invoice arrives twice | Two runs | Add `dedup: "{payload.invoice_no}"`. |
| `401 Webhook verification failed` | The secret or the scheme does not match | The server log says why; check the setting named by `secret_env`. |
| The worker starts nothing | No run appears | Check `awa trigger list` and that the worker is running; `--dry-run` shows what an event would become. |

<!-- guide:do cd . -->
<!-- guide:do cd invoice-desk -->

!!! example "In code"

    `build_blueprint_app` is the application `awa serve` runs, so a test can call it without a network
    ([Serving](../develop/serving.md)). The second request stops at the approval and names the tool that waits:

    <!-- guide:python -->
    ```python
    from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

    from awa.server import build_blueprint_app

    key = {"Authorization": "Bearer a-long-key"}
    with TestClient(build_blueprint_app("blueprint.yaml", api_key="a-long-key")) as client:
        print(client.get("/v1/systems").status_code)
        small = client.post("/v1/systems/invoice_desk/runs", json={"input": "Please release invoice INV-2041 for payment."}, headers=key)
        print(small.json()["status"], small.json()["text"])
        big = client.post("/v1/systems/invoice_desk/runs", json={"input": "Please release invoice INV-2042 for payment.", "thread_id": "inv-2042"}, headers=key)
        print(big.json()["status"], big.json()["interrupts"][0]["value"]["tool"])
    ```

    <!-- guide:expect -->
    ```text
    401
    completed Invoice INV-2041 from Nordwind Office GmbH (1,180.00 EUR) is released for payment.
    interrupted finance_approval
    ```

<!-- source: guide/operate.md -->

# Keep it running

This page is for a process that runs on its own. [Limits](../reference/glossary.md#usage-limit) stop a run that
goes wrong, `automation:` retries and escalates, and [traces](../reference/glossary.md#trace) show what a run did.
awa keeps every run as a record you can list, retry, cancel and read step by step. The shortest path: set `limits:`
and `automation:` as below, and use `awa runs list` and `awa runs trace` when something looks wrong.

```yaml
limits:
  max_requests: 30
  max_cost: 0.50
  max_duration: 5m
automation:
  retry: {max_attempts: 4, initial: 1m, max_delay: 1h}
  sla: {complete_within: 2d, approval_within: 4h, remind_every: 1h}
```

Everything is kept in the folder `.awa` of the project folder. It survives an orderly restart of the worker, the
server and the computer. It is not a backup: if `.awa` is lost, waiting runs are lost.

| File | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `.awa/awa.db` | Every run: input, status, history, tokens, cost. `awa store sweep` deletes old finished runs. |
| `.awa/checkpoints.db` | The saved state of runs that wait for an approval or an answer. |
| `.awa/traces/` | The trace of every attempt of every run. |

The files hold the inputs and answers of your runs. On Linux and macOS only your user can read them. On Windows awa
gives the database files an access list for your user only (when `icacls` can run). The traces folder keeps the
permissions of the project folder, so keep that folder private and out of version control.

!!! info "Preview"
    Process runs, `awa runs` and `awa store` work and are tested, but their options may still change in a minor release ([Stability](../about/stability.md)).

## The runs

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `queued` | Waiting for a worker. |
| `running` | A worker is working on it. |
| `waiting` | Paused for an approval or an answer from outside. |
| `succeeded` | Done. |
| `failed` | Stopped by an error a retry would not fix, for example a limit. |
| `dead_lettered` | Failed on every retry; `awa runs dlq` lists these. |
| `cancelled` | Stopped by a person. |
| `rejected` | A special case or a person turned the item down. Not retried. |

To try it:

1. Copy `invoice-desk` of the tour to `desk-ops` and delete its folders `.awa` and `inbox`.
2. Set a very small limit in `blueprint.yaml`: `max_requests: 2`.
3. Drop an invoice into `inbox` and run the worker. The run reaches the limit and fails:

<!-- guide:do cd . -->
<!-- guide:do copy invoice-desk desk-ops -->
<!-- guide:do delete desk-ops/.awa -->
<!-- guide:do delete desk-ops/inbox -->
<!-- guide:do cd desk-ops -->
<!-- guide:do replace desk-ops/blueprint.yaml "max_requests: 30" "max_requests: 2" -->
<!-- guide:do copy awa:docs/guide/files/INV-2041.pdf desk-ops/inbox/INV-2041.pdf -->
<!-- guide:run exit=1,0 -->
```console
$ awa worker blueprint.yaml --once
runs are kept in C:\awa-guide-work\desk-ops\.awa\awa.db and paused runs in C:\awa-guide-work\desk-ops\.awa\checkpoints.db (this machine); use --dsn (or $AWA_POSTGRES_DSN) to share them with workers elsewhere
proc_3b9c0d7a41e2 invoice_desk failed attempts=1 tokens=603 error=UsageLimitExceededError: Usage limit exceeded: requests=3 > max_requests=2
$ awa runs list --status failed
RUN                AUTOMATION    STATUS  ATTEMPTS  TOKENS  COST  CREATED (UTC)        TRIGGER
proc_3b9c0d7a41e2  invoice_desk  failed  1         603     -     2026-10-05 21:40:02  new-invoice
$ awa runs dlq
no runs in .awa/awa.db
```

The run is `failed`, not `dead_lettered`: a limit is not a temporary problem, and a retry would only spend more.

| Command | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `awa runs list [--status S] [--automation NAME] [--json]` | Runs, newest first, with tokens and cost. |
| `awa runs show RUN` | One run with its full history, as JSON. |
| `awa runs trace RUN` | What the run did, step by step ([below](#read-a-trace)). |
| `awa runs retry RUN [--restart]` | Queue a failed run again: from where it stopped, or from its input with `--restart`. |
| `awa runs cancel RUN [--reason TEXT]` | Cancel a run that is not finished. |
| `awa runs decide RUN --approve` or `--reject` | Answer a waiting approval ([Approvals](approvals.md)). |
| `awa runs dlq` | Runs that failed every retry. |
| `awa runs export-cases RUN --out FILE` | Eval cases from runs ([Test and improve](test.md#cases-from-real-runs)). |
| `awa runs migrate BLUEPRINT [--dry-run]` | Move waiting runs to the current version of the blueprint ([below](#change-a-process-while-runs-are-waiting)). |

Run them in the project folder, or give the same `--store` or `--dsn` as the worker. Put the run back in the queue,
then cancel it, say because the invoice was a duplicate:

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa runs retry RUN_ID
proc_3b9c0d7a41e2 invoice_desk queued attempts=0 tokens=603
$ awa runs cancel RUN_ID --reason "duplicate invoice"
proc_3b9c0d7a41e2 invoice_desk cancelled attempts=0 tokens=603 error=RunCancelledError: duplicate invoice
$ awa runs list
RUN                AUTOMATION    STATUS     ATTEMPTS  TOKENS  COST  CREATED (UTC)        TRIGGER
proc_3b9c0d7a41e2  invoice_desk  cancelled  0         603     -     2026-10-05 21:40:02  new-invoice
```

A retried run gets only what is left of its budget, so a run that stopped at a limit stops again. Raise the limit
and drop the file again instead. A run whose saved state is gone fails with `checkpoint lost`;
`awa runs retry RUN --restart` starts it again from its input.

## Retries, deadlines and notifications

The section `automation:` of the blueprint says how awa handles runs:

<!-- guide:file blueprint.yaml append -->
```yaml
automation:
  concurrency: 2
  retry: {max_attempts: 4, initial: 1m, max_delay: 1h}
  sla: {complete_within: 2d, approval_within: 4h, remind_every: 1h}
  notify:
    - {webhook: "https://hooks.example.com/ap-team", secret_env: AP_HOOK_SECRET}
```

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `concurrency` | How many runs of this process run at the same time, across all workers. |
| `retry` | A run that fails for a temporary reason (the provider is busy, a system does not answer) is tried again with growing pauses: at most `max_attempts` tries, the first pause `initial`, never longer than `max_delay`. Other errors fail the run at once. |
| `sla` | Deadlines. `complete_within` warns at 80 percent of the time and reports a breach; `approval_within` escalates an approval that is still open; `remind_every` repeats a reminder. |
| `notify` | Where warnings, breaches, reminders and failed runs go: a signed web request to a chat channel, an incident tool or your own service. |
| `run_timeout` | The longest one attempt may take (default 30 minutes). |

Durations are written `30s`, `15m`, `4h`, `2d`. `awa validate` checks the section:

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa validate blueprint.yaml
invoice_desk: valid
```

## Change a process while runs are waiting

Everything in the blueprint is part of its **version**, `limits:` and `prices:` included. A waiting run stays on the
version it started with, so a rule or a budget never changes under a half-done run. Before you restart the worker
with a new blueprint, see what would happen to the waiting runs:

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa runs migrate blueprint.yaml --dry-run
current version: sha256:5cb76a5dc6486586
every unfinished run is on the current version
```

Without `--dry-run` the command moves the waiting runs it lists.

## Limits and costs

A limit is the one safety net that does not depend on the model behaving. Set limits from the process, not from the
model: if one invoice never needs more than five model calls, a sixth is a loop.

| Limit under `limits:` | What it stops |
| --- | --- |
| `max_requests` | The run after this many model calls. Exact: the call that would be one too many is not made. |
| `max_total_tokens` | The run when the tokens of all model calls add up to more than this. |
| `max_tool_calls` | The run after this many tool calls. |
| `max_cost` | The run when its cost, counted with your `prices:`, is above this amount. |
| `max_duration` | The run when it has worked longer than this (`30s`, `5m`, `2h`). |

Everything the run starts counts: a team and its members, the steps of a workflow, delegations. The running call
finishes first, so a limit other than `max_requests` can be overshot by one reply. The options `--max-requests`,
`--max-total-tokens`, `--max-tool-calls`, `--max-cost` and `--max-duration` of `awa run`, `chat`, `serve`, `worker`
and `trigger run` can only **tighten** the blueprint's limits. Finer limits exist per agent (`max_steps`, default 25
model calls per run) and per team ([Agents and teams](agents-and-teams.md#team-an-orchestrator-and-members)).

Copy `invoice-desk` to `desk-limits`. The desk needs four model calls for this invoice; allow two:

<!-- guide:do cd . -->
<!-- guide:do copy invoice-desk desk-limits -->
<!-- guide:do cd desk-limits -->
<!-- guide:run exit=1 -->
```console
$ awa run blueprint.yaml "Please release invoice INV-2041 for payment." --max-requests 2
error: Usage limit exceeded: requests=3 > max_requests=2
```

The third call was not made, so nothing was paid for it. Where you see a stopped run:

| Where | What you see |
| --- | --- |
| `awa run` | `error: Usage limit exceeded: ...` and exit code 1. |
| `awa chat` | The error for that message; the next message starts a fresh budget. |
| `awa eval` | The case ends with the status `error`; the other cases go on. |
| A served system | `429`, or `504` when `max_duration` ran out. |
| An automatic run | `failed` with the code `awa.usage_limit_exceeded`; not retried. |
| The web app | The conversation or the test shows the error with a hint to change `limits:` on **Review**. |

### Count the cost

awa ships no prices, because providers change them. Put what you pay per million tokens under `prices:`. The key is
the model name as in `provider:model`, with or without the provider part; a longer name that starts with it matches
too. The scripted model of this page calls itself `unknown`, and the numbers are only an example:

<!-- guide:file blueprint.yaml append -->
```yaml
prices:
  unknown: {input_per_mtok: 2.0, output_per_mtok: 8.0}
```

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa validate blueprint.yaml
invoice_desk: valid
$ awa run blueprint.yaml "Please release invoice INV-2041 for payment."
Invoice INV-2041 from Nordwind Office GmbH (1,180.00 EUR) is released for payment.

[invoice_desk] 4 model call(s), 1121 tokens (1062 in, 59 out), cost 0.0026, 127 ms
```

Now `max_cost` works, and `max_duration` stops a slow run:

<!-- guide:run exit=1 -->
```console
$ awa run blueprint.yaml "Please release invoice INV-2041 for payment." --max-cost 0.0001
error: Usage limit exceeded: cost=0.0004 > max_cost=0.0001
$ awa run blueprint.yaml "Please release invoice INV-2041 for payment." --max-duration 1ms
error: Run 'run_74048440f339485d8f3c10f6d4f2c663' of 'invoice_desk' exceeded max_duration=0.001s and was stopped after 0.04s
```

The same prices in a file price an evaluation (`awa eval ... --prices prices.yaml`) and show what all runs and one run
cost:

<!-- guide:file prices.yaml -->
```yaml
unknown:
  input_per_mtok: 2.0
  output_per_mtok: 8.0
```

<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa eval blueprint.yaml evals/cases.yaml --prices prices.yaml
Evaluation: invoice_desk
========================
...
  cost  0.0070 (0.0023 per run)
...
```

`awa validate` reports an error when a model written as `provider:model` has no price, and a warning when a blueprint
has triggers but no `limits:`. `awa build` sets `max_requests: 200` for processes that a trigger starts; lower it to
what you need. Token and cost limits count what the provider reports, so set `max_requests` as well.

## Read a trace

When a run gives a wrong answer, fails or costs too much, its **trace** shows what it did: who asked whom, which tool
got which values, where a person approved, and what each step used. `awa serve` and `awa worker` keep a trace of
every attempt in `.awa/traces/`, without prompts, answers or tool results. Open the failed run from above:

<!-- guide:do cd . -->
<!-- guide:do cd desk-ops -->
<!-- guide:run -->
```console
$ awa runs trace RUN_ID
Trace of run proc_3b9c0d7a41e2, attempt 1
  automation invoice_desk, trigger new-invoice, thread_id proc_3b9c0d7a41e2
  file .awa/traces/proc_3b9c0d7a41e2.a1.jsonl (level summary)
Result: failed (UsageLimitExceededError: Usage limit exceeded: requests=3 > max_requests=2)
Totals: 2 model calls, 603 tokens (572 in, 31 out), time 201 ms
        agents 3, tool calls 1 (0 only hand work to other agents), delegations 0, consultations 0, handoffs 0, approvals 0 asked / 0 answered

What went wrong:
  - payment_clerk: limit max_requests reached (3 > 2)
  - payment_clerk: UsageLimitExceededError: Usage limit exceeded: requests=3 > max_requests=2

workflow invoice_desk  [no model calls, 201 ms]
  agent invoice_checker  [2 model calls, 603 tokens, 120 ms]
    tool invoice_ledger_query {"query": "SELECT supplier, po_number, amount_eur, status FROM invoices WHERE invoice_id = ?", "parameters": ["INV-2041"]} -> ok (19 ms)
  agent payment_clerk  [no model calls, 6 ms]
    ! LIMIT limit max_requests reached (3 > 2)
    ! ERROR UsageLimitExceededError: Usage limit exceeded: requests=3 > max_requests=2
  ! ERROR UsageLimitExceededError: Usage limit exceeded: requests=3 > max_requests=2

Note: level summary keeps no message texts (prompts, replies, tool results). Record with level full to see them.
Note: no prices, so no cost. Add `prices:` to the blueprint or pass --prices FILE.
```
