- **Identity.** With `--api-key-env` every client is one caller. `serve_as_mcp(..., authenticator=...)`
  identifies each request's principal: approver roles apply, a session answers only the principal
  that opened it, and every thread is recorded with its owner, so a caller reaches only threads of
  its own tenant. Give it the same `thread_index` as the HTTP server when both share a checkpointer.

`serve_as_mcp({"support": support_team})` does the same from Python (stdio), and
`serve_as_mcp(support_team, transport="http", api_key=...)` over streamable HTTP at `/mcp`.

### The protocol revision

The server speaks MCP revision **2025-11-25**, over stdio and streamable HTTP, verified with the
official `mcp` SDK. A client that asks for an older revision gets the one it asked for; a client that
asks for a newer one gets 2025-11-25. Only tools are served; resources, prompts and sampling are not.
A new SDK release can raise the revision; a test fails then, and this page is updated with it.

## What can go wrong

| You see | Why | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MCPError: ... Connection closed` | The server program did not start: another Python than the one with the `mcp` package, a wrong path, or a crash | Use `command=sys.executable` or a full path; run the command by hand to see its error |
| `MCPError` about an `include` name, a collision or `max_tools` | A listed tool does not exist, two tools get the same name, or the server offers too many | Fix the name, set `tool_prefix`, or narrow the selection |
| `MCPError` naming an unset variable | `${NAME}` without a default and no such variable | Set it, or write `${NAME:-default}` |
| `MCPToolDriftError` | The server's tools changed since `awa mcp lock` | Review with `awa mcp list`; lock again if it is fine |
| The model sees `The MCP session with server 'crm' is closed` | A tool was called after the `async with` block ended | Keep the block open while the agent runs, or use `load_mcp_tools` |
| A client does not list `resume_<name>` | The blueprint has no approvals | Add `approvals:` |
| A client that starts `awa mcp serve` finds no model | The client does not pass its environment on | Put the model settings in the client's `env` block |

Example: `examples/09_mcp_tools.py`.

<!-- source: develop/extend.md -->

# Extend

You can add your own parts to awa without changing awa: tools, skills, connectors, models, agents,
parsers and storage backends. Each is a plain Python object or file that you hand in with one call.
You can also switch built-in parts off or replace them with your own.

This page lists the extension points, shows how a project folder or a package ships parts as
plugins, and builds the two backends you need most often when your data does not fit: a parser for
a file layout and a store backend for a database. Tools, skills, connectors and MCP have their own
pages.

| You want to add | Extension point | Page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A tool for your code or API | a function with `@tool`, a `Toolbox` | [Tools](tools.md) |
| Know-how | a `SKILL.md` folder | [Skills](skills.md) |
| An external system | a `ConnectorSpec`, `register_connector`, `openapi_connector` | [Connectors](connectors.md) |
| The tools of an MCP server | `MCPServer` and `load_mcp_tools`, or `mcp:<server>` in a blueprint | [MCP](mcp.md) |
| A model or provider | a `provider:model` string, a chat model, a profile in a `ModelRegistry`, `register("models", ...)` | [Models](models.md), [below](#plugins) |
| An agent or a team of agents | an `Agent`, a `Team`, or any object with `name`, `card` and `run` (`AgentLike`) | [Agents](agents.md), [Teams](teams.md) |
| LangChain tools, LangGraph graphs, prompt files | `from_langchain`, `from_langgraph`, `import_skills` | [below](#langchain-tools-langgraph-graphs-and-prompts) |
| Parts for a project or for everyone who installs a package | `plugins.py` in the project folder, entry points `awa.<kind>` | [below](#plugins) |
| A built-in part switched off | `components:` in the blueprint, `awa plugins switch` | [below](#plugins) |
| Rules for tool calls at run time | a tool policy | [Tools](tools.md#tool-policies-at-run-time) |
| A safety check | an object with `name` and `check(candidate)` | [Safety](safety.md#guardrails) |
| An observer | a hook, or a global subscriber | [Observability](observability.md) |
| A reader for a file layout | a parser | [below](#write-a-parser) |
| Storage, queues, audit sinks, uploads | a backend of a backend protocol, held to its contract suite | [below](#backend-protocols) |

## Scaffold your own parts

The fastest start is a generated file. These commands write working code with a passing test:

| Command | Writes or does |
| --- | --- |
| `awa new tool <name> [--async] [--approval] [--dir D]` | `<name>.py`, a typed tool with a `Deps` dataclass, and `tests/test_<name>.py` with `ToolContract` |
| `awa new toolbox <name> [--dir D]` | A `Toolbox` with a read tool and an approval-gated write tool, and its test |
| `awa new skill <name> [--category C] [--dir skills]` | `<name>/SKILL.md` and `references/guide.md` |
| `awa tools list <module or file> [--json]` | Each tool's name, risk flags, approval and description |
| `awa tools call <module or file> <tool> --args JSON [--deps ...] [--approve]` | Runs one tool locally; a call that needs approval is refused (exit code 2) without `--approve` |

Point the generated files at your data and keep the tests green.

## Plugins

A plugin is a tool, connector, skill, model, parser or erasure handler that awa finds by name. awa
looks in three places, in this order: the project folder, the installed packages, its built-in
parts. `register(kind, name, obj)` adds one in Python:

```python title="own_model.py"
from awa import Agent
from awa.plugins import register
from awa.testing import FakeChatModel

register("models", "scripted", lambda: FakeChatModel(["Hello from the scripted model."]))
print(Agent("greeter", model="scripted").run_sync("Hi").output)
```

```text title="own_model.out"
Hello from the scripted model.
```

### In a project folder

awa reads `tools.py` and `tools/*.py`, `connectors/*.py`, `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, and `plugins.py`
for `register(...)` calls like the one above. So `model: scripted` then works in the project's
blueprint.

### In a package

A package ships its parts to everyone who installs it, through one entry-point group per kind. The
entry name is the part's name:

```toml
[project.entry-points."awa.tools"]
lookup_order = "acme_awa.tools:lookup_order"   # a tool, a list of tools or a documented function

[project.entry-points."awa.connectors"]
tickets = "acme_awa.connectors:TICKETS"        # a ConnectorSpec

[project.entry-points."awa.skills"]
acme = "acme_awa.skills"                       # a package of skill folders

[project.entry-points."awa.models"]
scripted = "acme_awa.models:scripted"          # a chat model factory without arguments

[project.entry-points."awa.parsers"]
text = "acme_awa.parsers:read_note"            # a parser; the entry name is the file kind

[project.entry-points."awa.erasure"]
tickets = "acme_awa.erasure:TicketErasure"     # an object with erase(request)
```

- A blueprint names an installed package's tools as `plugin:<dist>/<name>`, or `plugin:<dist>` for
  all of them. They are risk-annotated, and approval stays the blueprint's decision.
- A project or a package takes the name of a built-in part only when it says so (`replace=True`, or
  `__awa_replace__ = True` on the object).
- Two installed packages with one name are an error that names both.

### See and switch parts

- `awa plugins list` shows every plugin with its source and status, without importing installed
  plugins. (The project folder's Python files are imported, as when the project runs.)
- `awa plugins show KIND.NAME` shows one.
- `awa plugins check KIND.NAME --target module:Object` runs the contract test of a replacement
  parser, connector, tool or SQL guard.

Built-in parts, including the guards, caches and tracers that are only switches, are switched in the
blueprint:

```yaml
components:
  parser:
    pdf: off
  guard:
    sql_guard: off
```

`awa plugins switch parser.pdf off` writes that entry for you, and `awa.plugins.switches.override`
switches parts for a `with` block in Python. Switching a guard off is reported as a governance
finding.

## LangChain tools, LangGraph graphs and prompts

The importers bring parts you already have into awa and make them first-class. They are preview:
they work and are tested, and their names may still change in a minor release.

### LangChain tools

```python title="import_tools.py"
from langchain_core.tools import BaseTool, BaseToolkit, tool

from awa.tools.importing import import_langchain_tools

@tool
def create_issue(title: str) -> str:
    """Create an issue in the tracker."""
    return f"created {title}"

@tool
def get_issue(number: int) -> str:
    """Return one issue."""
    return f"issue {number}"

class TrackerToolkit(BaseToolkit):  # stands for any LangChain toolkit you already use
    def get_tools(self) -> list[BaseTool]:
        return [create_issue, get_issue]

report = import_langchain_tools(TrackerToolkit(), prefix="gh_")
print(report.render())
```

```text title="import_tools.out"
gh_create_issue  [toolkit TrackerToolkit]
  risk: external_action (name)
  approval: required (inferred: external action (name))
  note: calls pause for a human decision; the agent needs a checkpointer
gh_get_issue  [toolkit TrackerToolkit]
  risk: none
  approval: not required (no external action inferred)
```

`from_langchain(...)` returns the tools themselves. It takes a tool, a toolkit, a function, a
`Runnable`, a list, or an import path such as `"package.module:Attribute"`. The package's code runs,
so import only what you trust.

Every tool keeps its name, description and schema. On the way in, its risk is annotated: an explicit
`risk=` wins over the tool's own annotation, which wins over the name and description. A tool that
acts outside is wrapped with an approval. `requires_approval=True` gates every tool, `False` none.

### LangGraph graphs

A compiled LangGraph graph with a messages channel, `create_agent` graphs included, becomes a member
of a team, a workflow step or a tool:

```python title="import_graph.py"
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain_core.tools import tool

from awa import Agent, Team
from awa.agents.graph_agent import from_langgraph
from awa.persistence import StateInMemorySaver
from awa.testing import FakeChatModel, tool_call

@tool
def issue_refund(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Issue a refund for an order."""
    return f"refunded {order_id}"

billing_graph = create_agent(  # a LangGraph agent you already have; its model is scripted here
    FakeChatModel([tool_call("issue_refund", {"order_id": "A-7"}), "Refunded the second charge of order A-7."]),
    tools=[issue_refund],
    system_prompt="You answer billing questions and issue refunds.",
    name="billing",
)
billing = from_langgraph(billing_graph, name="billing", description="Answers billing questions and issues refunds.")
lead = Agent(
    "lead",
    description="Routes questions to the right agent.",
    model=FakeChatModel(
        [tool_call("delegate_task", {"agent": "billing", "task": "Why was order A-7 charged twice?"}), "We refunded the second charge."]
    ),
)
team = Team("desk", orchestrator=lead, members=[billing], checkpointer=StateInMemorySaver())
result = team.run_sync("Why was I charged twice?")
print(billing.card.tools, "|", result.output)
```

```text title="import_graph.out"
('issue_refund',) | We refunded the second charge.
```

The `GraphAgent` reads its tools from the graph's tool node. It tracks usage, limits, cancellation
and events through LangChain callbacks, passes `thread_id` to the graph's own checkpointer, and
pauses the team when the graph is interrupted.

### Prompt files

`import_skills("team-prompts/", into="skills/")` turns `SKILL.md` folders and Markdown prompt files
into validated skills. A name or description it had to derive is flagged for review. Nothing
imported is executed.

### On the command line

`awa add tool`, `awa add graph` and `awa add skills` do the same and write the result into the
blueprint. The inferred risk becomes `tool_risks:` and a needed approval an entry of `approvals:`,
so `awa validate` sees exactly what will run. `--dry-run` only prints the change.

```console
awa add tool my_tools:make_crm_tools --blueprint support.yaml --agent researcher
awa add graph billing.graph:graph --name billing --blueprint support.yaml
awa add skills ./prompts --into ./skills
```

## Write a parser

awa reads each file with the parser registered for its kind (`csv`, `xlsx`, `pdf`, `docx`, `mail`,
`json`, `sqlite`, `text`). The kind is decided from the bytes. When the shipped parser cannot see a
layout, replace the parser of that kind.

The example is a bank statement that arrives as plain text:

```text title="statements/2026-09.txt"
BANK STATEMENT 2026-09
2026-09-01  Rent                      -1.200,00
2026-09-03  Salary                     3.100,00
2026-09-07  Coffee machine               -89,90

printed on 2026-10-01 by branch 14
2026-09-12  Refund                       15,00
```

```text title="statements/notes.txt"
Remember to ask the bank for the October file.
```

A parser gets the path and a `ParseContext`, adds what it learns to `ctx.profile` and returns it:

```python title="statement_parser.py"
"""A parser for the bank's plain-text statements."""

import re
from pathlib import Path

from awa.data import FileProfile, ParseContext, TableProfile, infer_column

LINE = re.compile(r"^(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})\s+(.+?)\s+(-?[\d.]*\d,\d{2})$")
NAMES = ["Date", "Text", "Amount"]

def profile_statement(path: Path, ctx: ParseContext) -> FileProfile:
    lines = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").splitlines()
    if not lines or not lines[0].startswith("BANK STATEMENT"):
        return ctx.fail(
            "DF-E-PARSE-FAILED", "not a bank statement: the first line must start with BANK STATEMENT"
        )
    rows: list[list[str]] = []
    for number, line in enumerate(lines[1:], start=2):
        ctx.check_deadline()  # stop when the time limit of this file is used up
        if not line.strip():
            continue
        match = LINE.match(line)
        if match is None:
            ctx.flag("DF-W-STATEMENT-LINE", f"line {number} is not a transaction and was skipped")
            continue
        rows.append([cell[: ctx.limits.max_chars_per_cell] for cell in match.groups()])
    columns = [infer_column([row[i] for row in rows], name=NAMES[i], index=i) for i in range(3)]
    ctx.profile.tables.append(
        TableProfile(
            id=ctx.table_id(1),
            header_row=0,  # the file has no header row: the names above are ours
            data_start_row=2,
            rows=len(rows),
            columns=columns,
            sample_rows=rows[:3],
        )
    )
    return ctx.profile
```

- `ctx.fail(code, message)` marks the whole file `error` and returns the profile. `ctx.flag(code,
  message)` adds a warning and goes on. Write the message for the person who reads it.
- `infer_column(values, name=..., index=...)` is the inference awa uses for CSV: it decides the type
  and number and date formats, and flags ambiguity instead of guessing.
- `ctx.check_deadline()` raises when the file has used its time limit. Call it in every long loop.

`parsers_override` replaces a parser for the length of a `with` block:

```python title="try_parser.py"
from awa.data import parsers_override, profile
from statement_parser import profile_statement

with parsers_override({"text": profile_statement}):
    result = profile("statements")

for file in result.files:
    flags = ", ".join(flag.code for flag in file.flags) or "none"
    print(f"{file.path}: {file.status}, flags: {flags}")
    for table in file.tables:
        print(f"  {table.rows} rows")
        for column in table.columns:
            print(f"  {column.name}: {column.type} {column.date_format or ''}".rstrip())
print(result.summary)
```

```text title="try_parser.out"
2026-09.txt: ok, flags: DF-W-STATEMENT-LINE
  4 rows
  Date: date YYYY-MM-DD
  Text: text
  Amount: decimal
notes.txt: error, flags: DF-E-PARSE-FAILED
files=2 tables=1 rows=4 warnings=1 errors=1
```

The line "printed on ..." is reported, not dropped. The note is an error with a reason, and the
other file goes on. A test holds the parser to the rules every parser follows:

```python title="test_statement_parser.py"
from pathlib import Path

from awa.data import parsers_override, profile
from statement_parser import profile_statement

def read(tmp_path: Path, name: str, text: str):
    (tmp_path / name).write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
    with parsers_override({"text": profile_statement}):
        return profile(tmp_path).files[0]

def test_a_statement_becomes_a_table_with_typed_columns(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    file = read(tmp_path, "s.txt", "BANK STATEMENT\n2026-09-01  Rent  -1.200,00\n")

    (table,) = file.tables
    amount = table.columns[2]
    assert (table.rows, amount.type, amount.format.decimal) == (1, "decimal", ",")  # type: ignore[union-attr]

def test_bad_content_is_a_flag_not_an_exception(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    file = read(tmp_path, "s.txt", "BANK STATEMENT\nthis is no transaction\n2026-13-45  Rent  abc\n")

    assert file.status == "ok" and [f.code for f in file.flags] == ["DF-W-STATEMENT-LINE"] * 2

def test_a_file_that_is_no_statement_is_an_error_with_a_reason(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    file = read(tmp_path, "s.txt", "hello\n")

    assert file.status == "error" and "BANK STATEMENT" in file.flags[0].message

def test_the_same_file_gives_the_same_profile_and_is_only_read(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    path = tmp_path / "s.txt"
    path.write_text("BANK STATEMENT\n2026-09-01  Rent  -1,00\n", encoding="utf-8")
    before = path.read_bytes()
    with parsers_override({"text": profile_statement}):
        first, second = profile(tmp_path), profile(tmp_path)

    assert first.files == second.files and path.read_bytes() == before
```

For a server or worker, register the parser once at start-up:
`register_parser("text", profile_statement, replace=True)`.

- A parser replaces the reader of a kind that exists. A new kind (a `.xls` file, a binary vendor
  format) is not detected yet, so it never reaches a parser.
- Parsers run in a thread of the calling process. Only the PDF parser runs in a child process with a
  time and memory limit.

## Backend protocols

awa keeps every technology behind a small interface owned by the code that needs it: the **backend
protocol**. The code that does the work with a real technology is a **backend**. awa's logic never
imports a backend; the command line, the server or your code chooses one.

So you can replace a technology without touching awa, tests need no network or database, and every
backend is held to the same promise by a contract suite.

| Backend protocol | Import | Backends that ship | Contract suite |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Parser` | `awa.data` | CSV, Excel, PDF, Word, mail, JSON, SQLite, text | the rules [above](#write-a-parser) |
| `UploadScanner` | `awa.data` | none: you bring a virus scanner | none |
| `ArtifactRepository` | `awa.persistence` | memory, folder, PostgreSQL | `ArtifactRepositoryContract` |
| `RunStore`, `EventQueue` | `awa.automation` | memory, SQLite (runs only), PostgreSQL | `RunStoreContract`, `EventQueueContract` |
| `AuditLogSink` | `awa.observability` | memory, JSON Lines file | `AuditSinkContract` |
| `Notifier` | `awa.automation` | `WebhookNotifier` | `NotifierContract` |
| `Transport` | `awa.connectors` | the hardened HTTP client, `MockTransport` | [Connectors](connectors.md#write-a-connector) |
| `UploadStore`, `BuildStore`, `BuildEngine`, `SystemFactory` | `awa.server.ports` | folders on disk | none |
| `MessageBus`, `BaseBlackboard`, `BaseTaskBoard` | `awa.messaging`, `awa.tasks` | memory | none |
| `Authenticator`, `BaseRateLimiter`, `BaseThreadIndex`, `BaseIdempotencyCache` | `awa.server` | API key, bearer token, token bucket, memory, PostgreSQL | none |
| `Clock`, `IdSource` | `awa.runtime` | `SystemClock`, `UuidIds`; `FakeClock`, `FixedIds` in `awa.testing` | none |

The contract suites are in `awa.testing.contracts` (preview, extra `testing`). A backend protocol
changes by addition only, which the public API snapshot checks.

Time and ids are backend protocols too, so code that waits or numbers things never sleeps or patches
in a test:

```python title="waiting.py"
import asyncio

from awa.runtime import Clock, as_clock
from awa.testing import FakeClock, FixedIds

async def wait_for_approval(ask, *, clock: Clock | None = None, timeout: float = 3600) -> str:
    clock = as_clock(clock)  # None means the system clock
    started = clock.monotonic()
    while not ask():
        if clock.monotonic() - started >= timeout:
            return "expired"
        await clock.sleep(60)
    return "approved"

clock = FakeClock()
print(asyncio.run(wait_for_approval(lambda: False, clock=clock)), clock.monotonic())

ids = FixedIds()
print(ids.new_id("run"), ids.new_id("run"), ids.new_id("evt"))
```

```text title="waiting.out"
expired 3600.0
run_000000000001 run_000000000002 evt_000000000001
```

An hour of waiting took no time, and the ids are predictable.

## Write a store backend

The `ArtifactRepository` protocol (in `awa.persistence`) stores any JSON value under a text key:

- `put` replaces. A value that is not JSON raises `TypeError`; NaN raises `ValueError`.
- `get` returns the value as stored, or raises `KeyError`.
- `exists` says whether a key is there; `delete` returns whether it was there.
- `list_refs(prefix)` returns sorted keys.

A backend on SQLite:

```python title="sqlite_artifacts.py"
"""Artifacts as JSON text in one SQLite table: a backend for `ArtifactRepository`."""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import json
import sqlite3
from collections.abc import Iterator
from contextlib import closing, contextmanager
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from awa.persistence import ArtifactRepository

class SqliteArtifactRepository(ArtifactRepository):
    def __init__(self, path: str | Path) -> None:
        self._path = str(path)
        with self._connect() as db:
            db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS artifact (ref TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value TEXT NOT NULL)")

    @contextmanager
    def _connect(self) -> Iterator[sqlite3.Connection]:
        with closing(sqlite3.connect(self._path, timeout=30)) as db, db:  # closes; commits or rolls back
            yield db

    async def put(self, ref: str, value: Any) -> None:
        text = json.dumps(value, allow_nan=False)  # TypeError and ValueError, as the backend protocol says
        await asyncio.to_thread(self._write, ref, text)

    def _write(self, ref: str, text: str) -> None:
        with self._connect() as db:
            db.execute("INSERT OR REPLACE INTO artifact (ref, value) VALUES (?, ?)", (ref, text))

    async def get(self, ref: str) -> Any:
        text = await asyncio.to_thread(self._read, ref)
        if text is None:
            raise KeyError(ref)
        return json.loads(text)

    def _read(self, ref: str) -> str | None:
        with self._connect() as db:
            row = db.execute("SELECT value FROM artifact WHERE ref = ?", (ref,)).fetchone()
        return None if row is None else str(row[0])

    async def exists(self, ref: str) -> bool:
        return await asyncio.to_thread(self._read, ref) is not None

    async def delete(self, ref: str) -> bool:
        return await asyncio.to_thread(self._delete, ref)

    def _delete(self, ref: str) -> bool:
        with self._connect() as db:
            return db.execute("DELETE FROM artifact WHERE ref = ?", (ref,)).rowcount > 0

    async def list_refs(self, prefix: str = "") -> list[str]:
        return await asyncio.to_thread(self._list, prefix)

    def _list(self, prefix: str) -> list[str]:
        with self._connect() as db:
            rows = db.execute("SELECT ref FROM artifact ORDER BY ref").fetchall()
        return [ref for (ref,) in rows if ref.startswith(prefix)]
```

Run the contract suite against it:

1. Subclass the suite.
2. Set `adapter` and `capabilities`.
3. Say how to open the backend on a `place`: a fresh folder and name per test. Opening twice on the
   same place is a restart.

```python title="test_sqlite_artifacts.py"
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from awa.testing.contracts import (
    ArtifactRepositoryCapabilities,
    ArtifactRepositoryContract,
    Place,
)
from sqlite_artifacts import SqliteArtifactRepository

class TestSqliteArtifactRepository(ArtifactRepositoryContract):
    adapter = SqliteArtifactRepository
    capabilities = ArtifactRepositoryCapabilities(survives_restart=True, refs_with_nul=True)

    @asynccontextmanager
    async def opened(self, place: Place):
        yield SqliteArtifactRepository(place.path / "artifacts.db")
```

The suites are async tests, so pytest needs `asyncio_mode = auto`:

```ini title="pytest.ini"
[pytest]
asyncio_mode = auto
```

`python -m pytest` runs every promise of the protocol against the backend. Take `allow_nan=False` out
of `put` and run it again: `test_values_json_cannot_hold_are_refused` fails, because the backend
stored a value JSON cannot hold. Behavior a backend may lack is a capability flag, and its test is
skipped rather than failed.

The backend then goes wherever awa takes an `ArtifactRepository`:

```python title="use_backend.py"
import asyncio

from sqlite_artifacts import SqliteArtifactRepository

async def main() -> None:
    artifacts = SqliteArtifactRepository("artifacts.db")
    await artifacts.put("contract:C-17", {"text": "Net 30 days", "pages": [1, 2]})
    print(await artifacts.get("contract:C-17"))
    await artifacts.put("export:C-17:2026", {"rows": 3})
    print(await artifacts.list_refs())

asyncio.run(main())
```

```text title="use_backend.out"
{'text': 'Net 30 days', 'pages': [1, 2]}
['contract:C-17', 'export:C-17:2026']
```

A backend contributed to awa itself follows the rules on [Architecture](architecture.md#rules-for-a-change):
drivers imported only in backend modules and, when optional, inside the function; backends never
import each other; defaults are safe; time and ids are injected.

## What can go wrong

| You see | Why | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AdapterError: Cannot import ...: no module ...` | The package behind an import path is not installed | Install it, or pass the tool object |
| `AdapterError: from_langgraph needs a compiled LangGraph graph` | A `StateGraph` that is not compiled | Call `.compile()` first, or pass the result of `create_agent(...)` |
| An imported tool stops the run | It was inferred to act outside and waits for approval | Give the agent a checkpointer, or pass `requires_approval=False` and gate it in the blueprint |
| Every plain text file is now an `error` | The parser replaced the reader of the whole kind `text` | Return `ctx.fail(...)` only for files that are surely not yours, or keep the override in a `with` block |
| `ValueError: a parser for 'text' is already registered` | `register_parser` refuses to replace by accident | Pass `replace=True` on purpose |
| `async def functions are not natively supported` | pytest does not know the tests are async | `asyncio_mode = auto` and `pytest-asyncio` |
| Your backend passes your tests but the suite fails | Your tests describe your idea of the protocol, the suite its promise | Fix the backend; a protocol changes by addition only |

<!-- source: develop/export.md -->

# Export to plain LangChain and LangGraph

`awa export` turns a project with one agent into a standalone LangChain and LangGraph project that
runs without awa installed. Use it when the agent should live on as plain LangGraph code.

The export is a one-way exit. You edit the new folder with LangChain and LangGraph only, and
nothing is synced back. Staying an awa project remains the default, and no feature of awa is
reduced to make the export possible. The export of a single agent is part of the
[stable core](../about/stability.md).

## Export a project

The project is a blueprint with one agent and its `tools.py`:

```yaml title="refund-desk/blueprint.yaml"
format_version: awa/v1
name: refund-desk
agents:
  - name: clerk
    instructions: Answer refund questions. Refund only after approval.
    tools: [issue_refund]
approvals:
  - tool: issue_refund
    when: "amount > 50"
limits:
  max_requests: 20
```

```python title="refund-desk/tools.py"
from langchain_core.tools import tool

__all__ = ["issue_refund"]

@tool
def issue_refund(order_id: str, amount: float) -> str:
    """Refund an order."""
    return f"refunded {amount:.2f} EUR for {order_id}"
```

```python title="export_it.py"
from pathlib import Path

from awa.exporter import export

export("refund-desk", "refund-desk-graph")  # raises ExportUnsupportedError for a blueprint it refuses
out = Path("refund-desk-graph")
for name in ("langgraph.json", "run.py", "src/refund_desk/graph.py", "src/refund_desk/approvals.py", "tests/test_graph.py"):
    print(name, (out / name).is_file())
code = "\n".join(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") for path in out.rglob("*.py"))
print("imports awa:", "import awa" in code or "from awa" in code)
```

```text title="export_it.out"
langgraph.json True
run.py True
src/refund_desk/graph.py True
src/refund_desk/approvals.py True
tests/test_graph.py True
imports awa: False
```

On the command line:

```console
awa export refund-desk --out refund-desk-graph          # write the folder
awa export refund-desk --check                          # render it and import the graph; write nothing
awa export refund-desk --out refund-desk-graph --force  # replace an earlier export (only an export)
awa export refund-desk --out refund-desk-graph --json   # the result as JSON
```

The destination must not exist or must be empty. `--force` replaces a folder only when it holds
the `NOTICE.md` of an earlier export. The folder is written all at once or not at all.

The export holds:

| In the export | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `pyproject.toml`, `requirements.txt` | dependency ranges, and the exact versions awa ran with |
| `langgraph.json` | LangGraph Studio and `langgraph dev` |
| `README.md`, `NOTICE.md`, `SHA256SUMS` | how to run, test and extend; where it came from; the copied files |
| `run.py` | one run from the terminal, approvals asked on the terminal |
| `src/<package>/graph.py` | `create_agent(...)`: `build_graph(model, checkpointer)` and `graph` |
| `src/<package>/settings.py`, `prompts/<agent>.md` | the model, its settings and the limits; the system prompt as awa rendered it |
| `src/<package>/tools.py`, `discover.py` | your `tools.py`, copied unchanged, and how its tools are found |
| `approvals.py`, `conditions.py`, `limits.py`, `skills/`, `schemas.py` | approval conditions, run limits, skills and the output schema, when the blueprint uses them |
| `tests/` | offline tests that drive the real graph with a scripted chat model |

Importing `graph.py` needs no credentials: the chat model is created on first use through
`init_chat_model`.

The export is a code generator, separate from the engine a run uses. It reads the validated
blueprint and writes LangGraph source; it does not run through the
[engine port](architecture.md#the-engine-port).

## How a blueprint maps

| Blueprint | In the export |
| --- | --- |
| one agent, its instructions, `skills:` | the rendered system prompt in `prompts/<agent>.md` |
| `defaults.model`, `model_settings` | `init_chat_model("provider:model", **settings)`; a profile is resolved at export, and the variable `MODEL` overrides it |
| `max_steps`, `limits.max_requests` | `ModelCallLimitMiddleware` with the smaller of the two |
| `limits.max_tool_calls` | `ToolCallLimitMiddleware` |
| `limits.max_total_tokens`, `limits.max_duration` | `RunLimits` in `limits.py` |
| `approvals:`, with or without `when:` | `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware` (approve, edit or reject), the condition evaluated by the safe parser of `conditions.py`; a call it cannot decide asks |
| `policies: deny:` | the tool is left out |
| `output_schema` | a pydantic model in `schemas.py`, as `response_format` |
| `compaction` | `SummarizationMiddleware` |

**What stays the same.** In the tests, the same scripted model answers drive the awa agent and
the exported graph. Both call the same tools in the same order, pause on the same call, handle a
rejection the same way and return the same structured output. A fresh environment with only the
export's `requirements.txt` cannot import awa and still passes the exported tests.

**What is not reproduced.** awa's own extras: tool timeouts, retries, idempotency and output
framing, caches, run records, redaction and guardrails.

## What is refused

A blueprint that uses any of these is refused as a whole. The command prints one line per
feature, `export.unsupported <blueprint>: <feature> - <what to do>`, writes nothing and exits with
code 4. In Python, `export` raises `ExportUnsupportedError`.

| Feature | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| `team`, `workflow`, `process`, `network`, more than one agent, roles | Export a blueprint with exactly one agent. |
| `connectors`, `builtin:*`, `mcp:*`, `plugin:*` tools, import references | Write the calls as tools in `tools.py`. |
| `data`, `documents`, `special_cases`, `components`, `memory`, `refine` | awa only; move the logic into a tool or the prompt. |
| `auto` | Write the matched skills and tools into the blueprint first and set `auto: false`. |
| `limits.max_cost` | Use a token limit. |
| `policies` with `ask` or `use`, an approval `when` that is an import reference | Use `approvals` with an expression. |
| Model settings `effort`, `retry`, `fallbacks`, `circuit_breaker` | Configure the provider client in the exported code. |
| A `tools.py` that imports anything but the standard library, LangChain, LangGraph or pydantic | Keep the tools free of awa and local modules; the finding names the line. |

Every shipped example is exported or refused with exactly the findings in
`tests/export/expected_refusals.json`.

## Extend the export

| To change | Edit |
| --- | --- |
| the prompt | `prompts/<agent>.md` |
| the model and the limits | `settings.py` |
| anything else: tools, middleware, your own `StateGraph` instead of `create_agent` | `graph.py` |

For persistence, pass a LangGraph checkpointer to `build_graph`; `langgraph dev` supplies its own.
To start again from the blueprint, export into a new folder.

<!-- source: develop/architecture.md -->

# Architecture

awa builds on LangChain and LangGraph. Agents, teams, workflows, tools, limits and approvals are
plain data and Python. They run through one small engine port, and its only adapter is LangGraph.

Read this page when you change awa itself. It shows the layers, where each concept lives, how a run
flows through the packages, the engine port, how to upgrade LangGraph, and the rules a change
follows. To add your own parts without changing awa, see [Extend](extend.md).

## The layers

awa has six layers. Each may import the layers below it, never the ones above:

| Layer | Responsibility | Packages, from the top |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interfaces | Running and serving systems for people and machines | `cli`, `checks`, `testing`, `ui`, `project_setup`, `server`, `automation`, `people` |
| Compiler | A process described as data, and its quality | `exporter`, `ext`, `blueprints`, `quick`, `refine`, `evals` |
| Integrations | Company systems, files and ready-made tools | `connectors`, `data`, `toolkits`, `mcp` |
| Orchestration | Several agents working together | `team`, `workflows`, `tasks`, `messaging`, `directory` |
| Runtime | One agent and what it uses while it runs | `agents`, `guardrails`, `memory`, `skills`, `tools`, `persistence`, `observability`, `models`, `runtime`, `plugins` |
| Foundation | Settings, errors, the shared data contracts and the upstream seam | `config`, `core`, `contracts`, `_compat`, `_internal`, `errors`, `kernel` |

A package sits in the layer its imports put it in, which is not always the role its name
suggests. The Interfaces layer also holds the parts that build on the compiler: `automation`
(triggers and process runs) and `people` (the people directory). `ext` is the import surface for
extension authors; it sits next to the compiler because it re-exports helpers from the layers
below, not because it compiles anything.

Inside a layer the order counts too. The block below lists the packages from the top (may import
everything below) to the bottom (imports nothing above); packages joined by `|` are independent of
each other, packages joined by `:` may import each other. It is the order of `.importlinter`, and a
test keeps them equal:

<!-- layers:start -->
```text
cli : checks : __main__
testing
ui | project_setup
server
automation | people
exporter | ext
blueprints : quick
refine
evals
connectors | data
toolkits | mcp
team
workflows
tasks | messaging
directory
agents : guardrails
memory | skills
tools
persistence
observability
models
runtime
plugins
config : core
contracts
_compat : _internal
errors
kernel
```
<!-- layers:end -->

Imports inside a function count; imports under `if TYPE_CHECKING:` do not. A module whose name starts
with `_` is imported only from inside its package. No core module imports an outer part, a part that
builds on the core (`automation`, `people`, `server`, `ui`, the builder modules of `blueprints`, the
agent network, the connectors and checks for Microsoft 365); this boundary is about dependencies,
not stability ([preview parts](../about/stability.md#preview-parts)). `lint-imports` and
`tests/architecture/test_import_contracts.py` check the contracts; the imports that break a rule today
are listed under `ignore_imports` in `.importlinter`.

`awa` itself exports 37 everyday names, grouped by concept in `awa.__all__`, and loads each on
first use, so `import awa` loads neither LangChain nor LangGraph
(`tests/unit/test_import_cost.py`). Everything else is imported from its package
(`from awa.evals import evaluate`); a package exports its public names in `__init__.py` and keeps
its internals in modules whose names start with `_`. A name that is not on `awa` raises an
`AttributeError` that prints the import line to use.

## Where things live

| You think about | Package |
| --- | --- |
| One agent | `awa.agents`, with `awa.tools`, `awa.toolkits`, `awa.skills`, `awa.memory`, `awa.guardrails` |
| Several agents | `awa.team`, `awa.workflows`, `awa.messaging`, `awa.tasks`, `awa.directory` |
| Systems outside | `awa.connectors`, `awa.mcp` |
| Your files | `awa.data` |
| A process as data | `awa.blueprints`, `awa.quick`, `awa.evals` |
| Running and serving | `awa.automation`, `awa.server`, `awa.cli`, `awa.ui`, `awa.observability` |
| Testing | `awa.testing` |
| Plumbing | `awa.core`, `awa.contracts`, `awa.runtime`, `awa.models`, `awa.persistence`, `awa.errors` |
| Export to plain LangGraph code | `awa.exporter` ([Export](export.md)) |

| Package | Responsibility | Start from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `awa.contracts` | The data every package shares: cards, messages, events, results, usage and limits, `AgentLike` | `RunEvent`, `RunResult`, `Usage`, `UsageLimits` |
| `awa.runtime` | The state of a running run tree: run context, cancellation and deadlines, event streaming, clock and ids | `RunContext`, `cancel`, `subscribe_globally` |
| `awa.models` | Chat model resolution, profiles, resilience, provider errors, the request switch | `resolve_model`, `ModelRegistry`, `ModelSettings` |
| `awa.persistence` | Checkpointers, stores, artifacts, the data store, erasure and retention | `open_checkpointer`, `open_store`, `erase_subject` |
| `awa.agents` | The `Agent` and the middleware that connects its graph to the run context | `Agent`, `AgentHooks` |
| `awa.tools` | The tool contract: approval, hardening, idempotency, risk, policies, toolboxes | `tool`, `Toolbox`, `harden_tool` |
| `awa.team` | `Team` and `AgentNetwork` with their limits | `Team`, `TeamLimits`, `AgentNetwork` |
| `awa.workflows` | `Sequential`, `Parallel`, `Loop`, `Map`, `Checked`, `ProcessWorkflow` | `Sequential`, `ProcessWorkflow` |
| `awa.blueprints` | The blueprint schema; checking, building and explaining it; designing a project from a description and files | `Blueprint`, `load`, `aload` |
| `awa.evals` | Datasets, scorers, the model judge, the runner, reports and baselines | `evaluate`, `Dataset`, `EvalReport` |
| `awa.server` | The HTTP API, its router, data endpoints, jobs and the MCP server | `create_app`, `create_router`, `ServedSystem` |
| `awa.automation` | Triggers, durable process runs and the worker | `Automation`, `Worker` |
| `awa.observability` | Subscribers, OpenTelemetry and Langfuse, run traces, the audit trail, redaction | `OpenTelemetrySubscriber`, `AuditLog` |

The [API reference](../reference/index.md) has every public name. Preview parts work and are tested
but carry no stability promise yet: a preview module declares `__stability__ = "preview"`, and the
public API snapshot keeps its names, backend protocols and commands apart from the stable ones.
[Stability](../about/stability.md) lists them.

### Where a change goes

| You add | It goes in |
| --- | --- |
| A built-in tool | a module of `src/awa/toolkits` and its entry in `src/awa/toolkits/_catalog.py` |
| A SaaS connector | a `ConnectorSpec` (data only) in `src/awa/connectors/_saas.py` |
| A built-in skill | a folder with `SKILL.md` in `src/awa/skills/builtin` |
| An event type | `src/awa/contracts/events.py` and the `RunEvent` union |
| An exception | `src/awa/errors.py`, below `AwaError` |
| A setting | `src/awa/core/settings.py` (an `AWA_*` variable) |
| A blueprint field | `src/awa/blueprints/_schema_agent.py`, `src/awa/blueprints/_schema_structure.py` or `src/awa/blueprints/_schema_policy.py`; checked in `src/awa/blueprints/_check.py`, built in `src/awa/blueprints/_build.py` |
| A scorer | `src/awa/evals/scorers.py`, with its short form in `src/awa/evals/specs.py` |
| A trigger | a class on `src/awa/automation/_trigger_base.py`, exported from `src/awa/automation/triggers.py` |
| A command | a `_<group>.py` module of `src/awa/cli` with `add_<command>`, listed in `awa.cli.COMMANDS` |
| An upstream API | the matching module of `src/awa/_internal/upstream` |

## How a run flows

`awa run support.yaml "Order 1001 arrived broken."` crosses every layer once:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant OP as cli, ui, server, worker
    participant BP as blueprints
    participant TM as Team
    participant AG as Agent, tools
    participant RT as runtime, models, persistence
    participant UP as LangChain / LangGraph
    OP->>BP: load(blueprint, tools)
    BP->>BP: check, resolve tools, skills and models, wrap approvals
    BP-->>OP: Team (agents, topology, limits)
    OP->>TM: run(input)
    TM->>RT: new RunContext (limits, deps, events)
    TM->>AG: agent turn
    AG->>UP: create_agent graph with awa middleware
    UP->>RT: model call (profile, retries, fallbacks)
    AG->>AG: tool call (policy, approval, timeout)
    AG->>TM: delegate_task / transfer_to_billing
    RT-->>OP: events (stream, logs, traces, SSE)
    TM-->>OP: RunResult (output, usage per agent, interrupts)
```

1. A command, the web app, an HTTP request, a trigger or your own code receives the request.
2. `Blueprint.check` validates the schema, every reference, the topology and the risk of each
   agent's tools, without side effects; `build` resolves tools (your functions, `builtin:`,
   `connector:`, `mcp:`, import references), skills, models and approvals and constructs the agents
   and the team, workflow or network. Code that builds systems directly skips this step.
3. The run gets a `RunContext` (run id, limits, deadline, deps, event emitter). The team's graph runs
   the agent holding control for one turn at a time.
4. The agent runs its `create_agent` graph through awa's middleware. Models come from a profile with
   retries, fallbacks and a circuit breaker; tool calls go through policy, approval, timeout and
   output limits.
5. A delegation, consultation, handoff, agent used as a tool or workflow step starts a child run
   that shares the parent's usage, limits and event stream. A gated tool raises a LangGraph
   interrupt; the outermost checkpointed graph saves the state and the run returns with
   `result.interrupts`.
6. Events reach every subscriber of the run tree: `stream()`, hooks, logs, spans, Server-Sent
   Events, the evaluation trace.

### Inside an agent

`Agent` builds one `create_agent` graph on its first run and wraps model and tool calls in
middleware, outermost first:

| Middleware | Does |
| --- | --- |
| Control | Renders the system prompt (instructions, skills, memory note), enforces `max_steps`, repairs invalid structured output, keeps parallel approval pauses in tool-call order |
| Tool policy | Decides every tool call: run, ask a person, change the arguments, refuse |
| Yours | `middleware=[...]`; a team adds the middleware that delivers notes and handbacks before each model call |
| Compaction | Summarizes older turns over a token budget |
| Resilience | Retries, fallbacks and the circuit breaker |
| Run tracking | Blocks real requests when disabled, records usage per call, emits model and tool events, checks `UsageLimits` |

Input guardrails run before the graph and output guardrails on the final answer; `output_type`
becomes `create_agent`'s `response_format`.

### The run tree

Every run started inside another run gets a child `RunContext` that shares the parent's usage
accumulator, limits and event emitter. `UsageLimits` apply to the whole tree and
`result.usage.by_agent` breaks the total down; one stream sees every event of the tree, and
`root_run_id`, `run_id`, `parent_run_id` and `depth` rebuild it; `cancel(run_id)` or a deadline stops
the whole tree. A `Team` compiles to a LangGraph graph with one node that runs the agent holding
control; an `AgentNetwork` runs a coordinator loop over a task board; workflows compile to a graph
with one node per step. All of them are `AgentLike` (`name`, `card`, `run`), so any of them can be a
team member, a workflow step, a served system or an evaluation target.

## Rules for a change

Every module of `src/awa` has one role, written down in `tests/architecture/roles.toml`:

| Role | What it is | May import |
| --- | --- | --- |
| domain | Run semantics and logic: agents, teams, workflows, tools, memory, tasks | backend protocols, other domain code, `core`, `contracts`, the upstream seam |
| backend protocol | An interface the domain needs: a `Protocol`, or a one-method callable | `core`, `contracts` |
| backend | The only code that touches a driver (PostgreSQL, SQLite, SMTP, HTTP, a process) | backend protocols, `core`, its driver |
| root | Chooses and wires backends: command line, server, web app, blueprint builder, the `open_*` factories | everything except test support |
| testing | `awa.testing`: doubles and contract suites | public names of awa |
| seam | `awa._internal.upstream` and `awa._compat`: the only importers of LangChain, LangGraph and the MCP SDK besides `awa.kernel`, which imports no other awa module | upstream |

- Dependencies point inward: domain code imports backend protocols, never a backend or a root.
- Drivers (`psycopg`, `sqlite3`, `smtplib`, `urllib.request`, ...) are imported only in backend
  and root modules, optional ones inside the function, and their absence raises
  `OptionalDependencyError` with the extra to install (ruff rule `TID251`, `src/ruff.toml`).
- Every driven backend protocol has one contract suite, and every backend passes it
  ([Extend](extend.md#backend-protocols)). A protocol changes by addition only.
- Production code never knows that tests exist: no import of `awa.testing` or `pytest`, no test
  switch. Defaults are safe; a relaxation is an explicit argument. Time and ids are injected.
- A public name, a stored format or an exception class changes only on purpose:
  `tests/unit/test_public_api_snapshot.py` compares `tests/fixtures/public_api.json` ([Stability](../about/stability.md#what-a-version-number-promises)).

```console
python -m pytest tests/architecture
python -m pytest tests/contracts
python -m ruff check src
```

How the guards count their findings against a baseline is in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

## The engine port

awa holds agents, prompts, tools, skills, limits, approvals and run records as plain data and
Python functions; the execution engine underneath only builds and runs graphs. Agents, teams
and workflows reach it through one port, `awa.runtime.engine.Engine`, never through LangGraph
directly:

| Operation | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `build_agent(AgentSpec)` | Builds a tool-calling agent from its model, tools, middleware, output type and checkpointer |
| `run(handle, input, RunOptions)` | Runs new input, a `Resume` or the continuation of a stopped thread; returns the final state and the pending `Pause`s |
| `state(handle, thread_id)` | Reads a saved thread: its values, pending pauses and whether it stopped mid-run |
| `pause(value)`, `has_decision()` | Stops a node or tool until a decision arrives (approvals, `wait_for_event`, escalations); tells whether a resume brought one |
| `pauses(error)`, `control_flow`, `is_step_limit(error)` | Tell a pause or a handoff from a failure, and a used-up step budget from other errors |
| `in_thread()`, `detached()`, `outside_run()` | Whether a pause can be saved, and how background tasks and networks leave the enclosing run |

The port works per run, not per step, so it costs one context-variable lookup per run.
Limits, approvals, events and usage stay in awa: the engine receives a step bound, a
durability flag and the middleware list, and nothing else decides. `current_engine()` returns
the LangGraph engine (`awa.runtime._langgraph`) unless `use_engine(engine)` set another one for
the block. The engine tests (`tests/unit/test_runtime_engine.py`) run the same agents, tool
calls, pauses and resumes on the LangGraph engine and on a small engine without LangGraph. A
guard test rejects LangGraph's build, pause and step-limit primitives anywhere outside the
adapter, the seam, the exporter, the kernel and LangGraph-specific modules (`from_langgraph`,
checkpointer and store backends, their contract suites).

What stays LangChain-specific on purpose: messages, tools and chat models are the interchange
format for providers and MCP, the middleware classes are the hook mechanism the port passes
through, checkpointers and stores keep LangGraph's types, and teams and workflows still compile
their graphs with LangGraph's `StateGraph` before they run through the port. `awa export` is a
code generator, not an engine: it writes LangGraph source from the validated blueprint
([Export](export.md)).

## Upgrading LangGraph

A new LangChain or LangGraph release affects only the upstream seam and the engine adapter, and
both are tested continuously. The seam `awa._internal.upstream` imports LangChain and LangGraph,
one module per area, and the engine adapter `awa.runtime._langgraph` builds on it; `awa._compat`
holds the MCP SDK, and `awa.kernel`, which imports no other awa module, is the only other direct
importer. Ruff's banned-import rule (`src/ruff.toml`) refuses an upstream import in any other
module, except in the files the exporter copies into an exported project. The ranges in
`pyproject.toml` stay open within the major version (`langchain>=1.4.3,<2`,
`langgraph>=1.2.14,<2`), and their floors guarantee every name the seam uses.

1. Install the new release inside the range: `pip install -U langchain langgraph`.
2. Run `python -m pytest tests/upstream tests/unit/test_runtime_engine.py`. The upstream tests hold
   one test for every upstream behavior awa relies on and name the awa module behind each broken
   contract; the engine tests run agents, tool calls, pauses, resumes, step limits and run options
   through the adapter.
3. Fix the seam or the adapter, never their callers, and run the full suite.

A new major version is outside the range until an awa release widens it. Scheduled CI jobs run the
same tests against the lowest and the newest allowed releases
([Upstream versions](../about/stability.md#python-langchain-and-langgraph)). In your own code, import LangChain
and LangGraph from their public locations.

## Design principles

- **Models decide within limits; code enforces them.** Steps, tokens, cost, delegation depth,
  parallelism, handoffs and timeouts are counters in Python, never requests in a prompt.
- **Typed contracts at every boundary.** Structured output is validated; results, events, cards and
  messages are pydantic models; `AgentLike` lets every runnable stand in for every other.
- **Content from other agents is data.** Delegated results, notes, task text and tool output reach a
  model as labeled blocks, never as instructions.
- **One run tree.** Delegations, consultations, handoffs and nested systems share one usage total,
  one set of limits and one event stream.
- **Explicit topology.** Each agent gets exactly the delegation and messaging tools its declared
  edges allow.
- **Failures inside collaboration are results.** A failing member returns an error result to its
  caller; only limits, cancellation and approval pauses cross run boundaries.
- **Offline first.** Every system can be tested without a network, and real model requests can be
  blocked for the whole process.
- **Fast to import.** Names load on first use; `import awa` and `awa --help` load neither LangChain
  nor a feature package.

<!-- source: develop/benchmarks.md -->

# Benchmark

The core benchmark measures awa on eight scenarios, from company processes to automation and MCP.
Run it before and after a change: offline with scripted models, or live with your model. It needs
the `files`, `server` and `mcp` extras, and a model for live runs.

```console
python examples/benchmarks/core/run.py --offline --runs 1          # scripted models, no network
python examples/benchmarks/core/run.py --live --runs 3             # the model of the settings
python examples/benchmarks/core/run.py --live --only 2 4 --max-calls 120
```

| # | Scenario | What it measures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Market brief from the web | keyless `web_search` and `fetch_url`, delegation, a peer consult, quotes that really stand on fetched pages |
| 2 | Supplier orders against a REST API | the `rest` connector with a public API, a CSV in Windows-1252, exact totals, approvals decided in the case |
| 3 | GraphQL lookup joined with JSON | the `graphql` connector with a public API, a JSON file, exact ids and sums |
| 4 | Document intake | PDF, Word and Excel, a scan without a text layer, validation rules, a conditional approval approved and rejected |
| 5 | Agent network | a task board with dependent tasks, the blackboard, handbacks, a synthesis |
| 6 | Automation end to end | webhook, file drop and schedule, an approval across a restart, `awa runs decide` |
| 7 | Template to application | `awa build` from a description; the written project validated and run |
| 8 | MCP client | `awa mcp serve` as a separate process, called by the official MCP client over stdio and HTTP |

## How a case is judged

Every case runs several times (`--runs`, default 3). A run passes when every scorer passes, and the
table shows the runs passed and whether all runs of a case passed (pass^k), because a model that is
right two times in three is not reliable. Scorers are deterministic first: exact fields and numbers,
the tools called, delegations, approvals asked and decided, run states and files, and code for what a
spec cannot say (a quote stands on the fetched page, tasks finish in dependency order). A model judge
grades only what is left, such as the wording of a reason. Cases with approvals carry `decisions`, so
a process is measured from the request to its end.

`--offline` replaces the model with a script per scenario and the keyless endpoints with canned
answers; it runs anywhere and is part of the test suite (`tests/examples/test_benchmarks_core.py`).
`--live` uses `AWA_DEFAULT_MODEL` and the real keyless endpoints (search result pages, a holiday API
and a countries API). The runner writes the results per case and scorer (runs passed, model calls,
tokens, latency p50 and p95) to `results/` as JSON and a table, and stops at `--max-calls` (default
400; live runs count across invocations unless `--fresh-ledger`). The exit code is 0 when everything
passed, 1 when an offline run failed and 2 when the call cap stopped the run.

`tests/proof/core` proves the core agent system on its own with scripted models: delegation, handoff,
peer consult, approval pause and resume after a rebuilt checkpointer, every limit, tool errors,
structured output, the event trace, nested teams and cancellation. Each test asserts numbers (model
calls per agent, tool runs, events, usage) and that nothing continues after a limit.

## Add or change a scenario

A scenario is a folder of `examples/benchmarks/core` with `blueprint.yaml`, `cases.yaml`,
`README.md`, a `tools.py` only for real custom logic, and `data/` files that `data_gen.py` recreates
byte for byte. It needs an entry in `harness.SCENARIOS` and a scripted model in `offline.py`; the
offline test then runs it end to end. When a live run fails, fix the cause (a prompt, a tool
description, a default or a bug), add an offline regression test, and run the benchmark again.

| You see | Cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| `--live` ends at once with a message about the provider package or key | The default model cannot be called: install its package, set its key, or set `AWA_DEFAULT_MODEL`. |
| `stopped: the ledger reached --max-calls` and exit code 2 | Raise `--max-calls`, or start over with `--fresh-ledger`. |
| Scenario 8 fails with an import error | Install the `mcp` extra. |
| A live case of scenarios 1 to 3 fails once | A keyless endpoint was slow or down. Run it again with `--only N --cases ID`; a failure that repeats is a finding. |

<!-- source: develop/blueprints.md -->

# Blueprints

A **blueprint** is one YAML (or JSON) file that describes your whole process: the agents that do
the work, their tools and skills, how they work together, and which actions wait for a person.
awa checks the file without running anything and builds it into a running system with one call.

Use a blueprint when you want the process as a file that people who know the work can read and
review. This page is for Python developers who know the [Quickstart](quickstart.md). To write
blueprints without code, see [Describe a process](../guide/describe.md); every command is in the
[CLI reference](../reference/cli.md).

## Write and run a blueprint

Four agents check an invoice and book it. Every booking waits for a person:

```yaml
# invoice_desk.yaml
name: invoice-desk
description: Checks incoming invoices against purchase orders and books them.
version: 1.0.0

defaults:
  model: default          # a profile name or provider:model
  max_steps: 12

agents:
  - name: intake
    description: Receives invoices, coordinates the checks and reports the outcome.
    instructions: |
      1. Delegate field extraction to extractor.
      2. Delegate the purchase-order match to matcher.
      3. If the invoice matches, delegate booking to bookkeeper; otherwise explain the mismatch.
    skills: [orchestration-planning, delegation-briefs]

  - name: extractor
    description: Extracts vendor, amount, currency and due date from an invoice.
    instructions: Extract the fields exactly as written on the invoice.
    tools: [read_invoice]
    output_schema:
      type: object
      properties:
        vendor: {type: string}
        amount: {type: number, minimum: 0}
        currency: {enum: [EUR, USD]}
        due_date: {type: string}
      required: [vendor, amount, currency]

  - name: matcher
    description: Compares an invoice with its purchase order.
    instructions: Report every difference in vendor, amount or quantity.
    tools: [find_purchase_order]
    capabilities: [procurement]

  - name: bookkeeper
    description: Books matched invoices for payment.
    instructions: Book the payment with book_payment and return the booking reference.
    tools: [book_payment]
    skills: [safe-tool-execution]

team:
  orchestrator: intake
  members: [extractor, matcher, bookkeeper]
  peers:
    bookkeeper: [matcher]
  limits:
    max_calls_per_member: 4
    delegation_timeout: 120

approvals:
  - tool: book_payment          # every booking waits for a human
```

Load it, run it, and answer the approval:

```python
from awa import load
from awa.persistence import StateInMemorySaver

desk = load("invoice_desk.yaml",
            tools=[read_invoice, find_purchase_order, book_payment],
            checkpointer=StateInMemorySaver())       # required because of the approval
result = await desk.run("Process invoice INV-1042.")
if result.is_interrupted:
    print(result.interrupts[0]["value"])        # the pending book_payment call
    result = await desk.resume(result.thread_id, {"action": "approve"})
print(result.output)
```

`load` checks the file, matches the tool names against `tools=` and builds the team. A run that
waits for a person must be saved somewhere, so approvals need a checkpointer. Given a project folder
or its `blueprint.yaml`, `load` also picks up the `tools.py` and the `skills/` folder next to the
blueprint, as every command does ([The project folder](project-folder.md)).

## Validation

`Blueprint.check(tools=None, skills=None)` finds every problem without building anything. It
checks names and references, the team, workflow references, approvals, output schemas and skills.
It checks tool names too when you pass the tools. Each finding is a `BlueprintIssue` (severity,
path, message). `build` refuses a blueprint with errors and raises `BlueprintError` listing them.

```python
from awa import Blueprint

blueprint = Blueprint.from_yaml("invoice_desk.yaml")
for issue in blueprint.check(tools=[read_invoice, find_purchase_order, book_payment]):
    print(issue)
print(blueprint.to_mermaid())
```

On the command line, `awa validate` does the same and `awa show` explains the blueprint in words.

Blueprints round-trip: `Blueprint.from_dict`, `from_yaml`, `to_dict`, `to_yaml`.
`Blueprint.explain()` returns the auto-matching report (the same as
`awa.blueprints.explain(system)` for a built system).

## Loading tools

`load`, `aload`, `Blueprint.build` and `abuild` take `tools=`: a list or a mapping of names to
tools. You rarely need to pass them yourself: the command line (`validate`, `run`, `chat`, `eval`,
`serve`, `worker`, `trigger run`), `awa.load`, `awa.server.build_blueprint_app` and the web app
load the `tools.py` and the `skills/` folder next to the blueprint by themselves. `--tools` and
`--skills` only add more.

Some tools need no code of yours. The blueprint resolves them itself:

| Written as | Is |
| --- | --- |
| `builtin:read_csv` | a built-in toolkit tool ([Tools](tools.md#builtin-toolkits)) |
| `connector:jira.search_issues` | an operation of a connected system ([Connectors](connectors.md)) |
| `mcp:crm` | the tools of an MCP server ([MCP](mcp.md#in-a-blueprint)) |
| `plugin:<dist>/<name>` | a tool of an installed plugin ([Extend](extend.md#plugins)) |

More ways to load tools:

- `awa.blueprints.load_tools("tools.py")` collects tools the way `--tools` does. It takes dotted
  module names or `.py` files, and returns every LangChain tool they define plus the functions in
  their `__all__` (a `Toolbox` is flattened into its tools). Each file is imported under a module
  name of its own, so two `tools.py` in different folders never collide.
- A tool may be written as `"package.module:attribute"`. Such references are only imported with
  `allow_imports=True`, because importing runs module code. Enable it only for blueprints you trust.
- Code in a tools file (`when:` predicates, loop `until:` conditions, tools) is referenced by path,
  `"./tools.py:needs_approval"`, resolved against the blueprint's folder, or by file stem,
  `"tools:needs_approval"`.

## How the agents work together

A blueprint with one agent runs that agent. With more agents, pick one structure; the
[Teams](teams.md) and [Workflows](workflows.md) pages explain each in depth.

| Section | The agents | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `team` | An orchestrator delegates to members | The model should decide who does what. |
| `workflow` | Steps in a fixed order, in parallel or in a loop | The order is known in advance. |
| `process` | Steps in order, each checked before the next starts | Each result must pass checks or a person ([The process section](process-section.md)). |
| `network` | A lead creates tasks that teammates claim | The work splits into tasks that teammates pick up ([Agent networks](teams.md#agent-networks)). |

- `team` takes `name`, `description`, `orchestrator`, `members`, `delegates`, `peers`,
  `symmetric_peers`, `handoffs`, `handoff_history`, `messaging`, `blackboard`, `task_board` and
  `limits`. Members are agents, or the workflow or network by name.
- A `workflow` step is an agent, team or network name, or `sequential:`, `parallel:`, `loop:` or
  `map:` with nested steps.
- `network` takes `name`, `description`, `lead`, `teammates`, `peers` (a mapping or `all`),
  `teammates_create_tasks`, `blackboard` and `limits` (`max_tasks`, `max_concurrent_teammates`,
  `max_task_attempts`, `max_lead_turns`, `max_message_turns`, `idle_timeout`, `run_timeout`,
  `max_result_chars`).

Short forms keep simple blueprints short. `agents` may map names to tasks
(`checker: Validates the totals.`) or to agent fields. `team: <orchestrator>` makes every other
agent a member, `network: <lead>` every other agent a teammate, and `workflow: [a, b]` is a
sequence:

```yaml
name: invoice_processing
auto: true
agents:
  coordinator: Coordinates the processing of incoming invoices.
  extractor: Reads incoming invoices and extracts the fields.
  checker: Validates the totals against the purchase order.
team: coordinator
```

A workflow with a parallel review and a loop:

```yaml
workflow:
  sequential:
    - intake
    - parallel: [legal_reviewer, compliance_reviewer, style_reviewer]
      fail_fast: false
      name: reviews
    - loop: editor
      until_contains: APPROVED
      max_iterations: 3
  carry: all
```

A `map` step runs one step once per part of a list, concurrently, and checks that every item has
exactly one result ([Workflows](workflows.md#a-list-of-items)):

```yaml
workflow:
  sequential:
    - map: invoice_reader
      part_size: 5        # items per part; more than one is passed as a JSON array
      max_concurrency: 4
    - writer
```

A network (teammates claim the ready tasks matching their `capabilities`):

```yaml
network:
  lead: research_lead
  teammates: [market_researcher, analyst, writer]
  peers: {}
  limits: {max_tasks: 8, max_lead_turns: 10, run_timeout: 1200}
```

Agents may also carry a role (`role`, `sub_agents`, `rubric`, `judges`, `reviews`): an
orchestrator over workers, a judge that gates a worker's output with a typed verdict, and
reviewers that read it once. A role tree needs no `team:` section. See
[Agent roles](teams.md#roles-in-a-blueprint) and `examples/blueprints/market_brief.yaml`.

### Nesting

The team, workflow and network nest by name. A team member or workflow step may name the workflow
or the network (give them a `name`), and a workflow step may name the team.

- Only the entrypoint gets the checkpointer. Nested workflows and teams persist on its thread, so
  an approval anywhere in them pauses the whole run.
- A network pauses for approvals only as the entrypoint. `check` reports approvals inside a nested
  network.
- `build(task_board=..., bus=..., blackboard=...)` hands shared objects of your own (a
  `BaseTaskBoard`, a `MessageBus`) to the network when the blueprint uses one, else to the team.

`Blueprint.build_agent(name, tools=...)` builds one role on its own, with its model, tools
(approval-gated as declared), skills, memory and output schema. Use it to compose roles in code or
to test one role.

## The schema

`name` and `agents` are required. The sections are listed from common to rare.

| Section | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `name`, `description`, `version` | The system. `name` is also the default name of the team, workflow and network. `version` (default `1.0.0`) is yours to bump. |
| `defaults` | Settings every agent inherits: `model`, `model_settings`, `max_steps` (default 25), `skill_mode` (`inline` or `on_demand`). `tool_timeout`: seconds a call of the blueprint's own tools (`tools.py`, import references) may take (default 120, `null`: no limit) unless a tool sets `@tool(timeout=...)`. `cache`: the cache settings ([Models](models.md#prompt-caching-and-result-caches)); `AWA_CACHE_*` variables win. |
| `agents[]` | One entry per agent; `name` is required. The common fields: `description`, `instructions`, `model`, `model_settings`, `tools`, `skills`, `skill_mode`, `output_schema`, `max_steps`. Below the table: the rare ones. |
| `approvals[]` | `tool` and an optional `when` (below). |
| `team`, `workflow`, `process`, `network` | How the agents work together ([above](#how-the-agents-work-together)). Set `process` or `workflow`, not both. |
| `entrypoint` | `team`, `workflow`, `network` or an agent name. Default: the team if declared, else the workflow, else the network, else the only agent. |
| `limits`, `prices` | What one run may use at most (below). |
| `auto` | `true` gives every agent the built-in skills and tools its task calls for (agents override it with their own `auto`). Tools that act outside the agent are only suggested. `Blueprint.explain()` and `awa show` report what was matched and why; see [`awa.quick`](quickstart.md#a-team-from-names-and-tasks). |
| `data[]` | The real files a process works on ([Data from your files](#data-from-your-files)). |
| `connectors`, `toolkits`, `mcp_servers[]`, `tool_risks` | Connected systems ([Connectors](connectors.md)), built-in toolkit settings ([Toolkits](tools.md#builtin-toolkits)), MCP servers ([MCP](mcp.md#in-a-blueprint)) and corrections of the risk check ([Tools](tools.md#untrusted-output-and-risky-combinations)). |
| `triggers[]`, `automation` | What starts runs by itself and how those runs are processed (below). |
| `policies[]` | Run-time tool policies for all agents or those in `agents` (below). |
| `special_cases` | Rule tables that decide on the result of a `process:` step ([Special cases](#special-cases)). |
| `components` | Built-in parts switched on or off by kind and name, written by `awa plugins switch` ([Extend](extend.md#plugins)). |
| `format_version` | The file format, `awa/v1` (the default). An unknown format is refused with a message that names it. Unrelated to `version`. |

`output_schema` is a safe subset of JSON Schema (objects, arrays, scalars, enums, defaults and the
usual constraints), converted into a pydantic model. Anything unsupported is an error, never
silently ignored.

### More agent fields

- **Memory and long conversations:** `memory` (`scope`, `auto_recall`) and `compaction`
  (`max_tokens`, `keep_last_messages`); see [Memory](memory.md).
- **Documents:** `documents` names `data:` entries the agent always has
  ([The process section](process-section.md)).
- **Directory data:** `capabilities`, `tags`.
- **Auto-matching:** `auto` overrides the blueprint's `auto`.
- **Roles:** `role`, `rubric`, `judges`, `reviews`, `max_iterations` (how often a judge may send a
  draft back, default 3), `sub_agents` and `delegation` (`max_depth`, `max_parallel` of the
  sub-agents) place the agent in a role tree ([Roles in a blueprint](teams.md#roles-in-a-blueprint)).
- **The system message from sections:** `goal`, `system`, `escalation` and `acknowledge_ungated`
  ([Agent spec](agent-spec.md)).
- **Texts and model settings:** `describe` (instructions from a file, tool descriptions), `refine`
  (provider fields and middleware) and `refinements` (lines a build added, with their evidence);
  see [Test and improve](../guide/test.md#texts-and-model-settings-of-an-agent).

### Approvals

An entry is a `tool` and an optional `when`. `when` is either:

- a condition over the call arguments, such as `"amount >= 5000"`; `check()` checks it against the
  tool's arguments ([Conditional approvals](safety.md#conditions));
- or a predicate that takes the arguments: `"package.module:function"`, a file path such as
  `"./tools.py:needs_approval"` (relative to the blueprint's folder), or the stem of a loaded tools
  file (`"tools:needs_approval"`).

### Limits and prices

`limits` caps one run: `max_requests`, `max_total_tokens`, `max_tool_calls`, `max_cost`,
`max_duration`. `max_cost` needs `prices` (`<model>: {input_per_mtok, output_per_mtok,
cache_read_per_mtok}`, the shape of `PriceTable.from_mapping`). What each limit stops, and where
a stopped run shows, is in [Keep it running](../guide/operate.md#limits-and-costs).

- `awa run`, `chat`, `eval`, `serve`, `worker` and the web app apply the limits to every run tree.
  Their `--max-*` options can only tighten them (`merge_limits`; in `eval` the larger value
  holds), and a served request asking for more gets the blueprint's limits.
- An automation stores the `usage` and `cost` of each process run. A breach ends the run `failed`
  with `awa.usage_limit_exceeded`, without a retry.
- `check` errors when `max_cost` is set and an agent's model, written as `provider:model`, has no
  price. It warns when the blueprint has triggers but no limits.
- In Python, `Blueprint.usage_limits()` and `price_table()` give the objects for
  `run(usage_limits=...)`. `build()` itself applies nothing.

### Triggers and automation

`triggers[]` starts runs by itself: schedules, webhooks, file drops, mailboxes, queues.
`automation` says how triggered runs are processed: templates, dedup, concurrency, retries, SLAs,
notifications. The guide is [Run automatically](../guide/run.md).

- Webhooks check a signature or token (`scheme`: `timestamped`, `body`, `token`).
- File drops and mail attachments arrive with their text.
- An attempt may take `run_timeout` (default `30m`).
- `check` warns about templates that do not parse and unset secret variables.
- Without a database, `awa serve` (or `awa worker`) runs every trigger and keeps runs and paused
  runs in `.awa/` next to the blueprint. With the same `--dsn`, the server receives webhooks and
  events and `awa worker` processes on many machines run the rest.

In Python, `awa.blueprints.triggers` writes `triggers:` entries (`trigger_entry`, `add_trigger`)
and lists the commands that run them (`trigger_steps`).

### Policies

A policy has `deny` (tool names refused), `ask` (risk flags whose tools pause for a human),
`reason`, and `use` (a `ToolPolicy` function, imported with `allow_imports`). Policies become the
agents' `tool_policy`. `check` counts denied and asked tools as gated.

## Special cases

`special_cases` holds rule tables that decide what happens with the result of a `process:` step.
Each table is named after its step. Someone who knows the process can fill it in like a
worksheet: a list of rows, an `else` and a `when_unclear`.

```yaml
special_cases:
  decide:                                  # the step these cases are for
    cases:                                 # first match wins
      - {if: "supplier in ['Blocked Supplies Ltd']", then: reject, message: Blocked supplier.}
      - {if: [{field: amount_eur, op: ">=", value: 20000}], then: ask, by: board}
      - {if: [{field: amount_eur, op: ">=", value: 5000}], then: ask, by: finance}
      - {if: [{field: status, op: "=", value: paid}], then: go, to: archive}
      - {if: [{field: amount_eur, op: "<", value: 5000}], then: approve}
    else: ask                              # when no row holds; default ask
    when_unclear: ask                      # ask or reject, never approve
    decimal: "."                           # how numbers written as text are read; "." or ","
```

A bare list is the short form of `cases` (`decide: [{if: ..., then: ask}]`); `else` and
`when_unclear` then default to `ask`.

| Part | What it takes |
| --- | --- |
| `if` | A list of `{field, op, value}` conditions that must all hold, or an expression in the language of approval conditions (`"amount_eur >= 20000 or len(lines) > 50"`). |
| `op` | `=`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `one of`, `not one of` (`==`, `in` and `not in` are read as `=`, `one of` and `not one of`). `<` to `>=` need a number, `one of` a list. |
| `then` | `approve` (no person needed for this step), `ask` (a person decides; `by` names the role), `reject`, or `go` with `to: <step>` (also written `go: <step>`). `message` is one sentence for the person or the record. |
| `else` | What happens when every row is false. Required in the model and `ask` by default. `approve` is allowed and gives a warning in `check` and `awa show cases`. |
| `when_unclear` | What happens when a row cannot be decided: `ask` (default) or `reject`. `approve` and `go` are refused when the blueprint loads. |

### How a table decides

1. The rows are tried in order. The first true row decides.
2. A row is true, false or unclear. The first unclear row stops the table, and `when_unclear`
   decides. An unclear row never falls through to a later row or to `else`.
3. `else` decides only when every row is false.

A row is **unclear** when a value it reads:

- is missing or empty;
- is not a finite number (`NaN`, infinity);
- is a list or an object where a `{field, op, value}` row expects one value;
- or is not one clear number where the row compares it with numbers only (`"n/a"`, `true`, and
  `5.000` or `5,000`, which read as 5 or as 5000).

More rules:

- Every row compiles to one expression and is evaluated in strict mode, by the same evaluator as
  approval conditions.
- A row is read from left to right. Once a part is false the row is false, and a value it did not
  reach does not matter: `amount_eur < 5000 and supplier one of [...]` is false for 6,000 even
  without a supplier.
- Text compares exactly, including capital letters: `ACME` is not `Acme`. Numbers written as text
  (`"1,250.50"`) are read as numbers with the table's `decimal`.

### In a run

The table of a step decides on the step's output after its `schema` and `rule` checks passed and
before its `approval` checks:

- `reject` ends the run with status `rejected`.
- `ask` pauses for a person, together with any approval check that applies, in one question.
- `go` continues at a later step.
- `approve` adds no question of its own; an approval check of the step still asks.

`check` refuses a table for a step the process does not have, a `go` to a step that is not later,
and a `go` that jumps over a step with a rule, an approval or special cases. How a run moves
through the steps, with retries and `when`, is in
[The process section](process-section.md#ifelse-retries-and-special-cases).

### Test a table

`awa show cases blueprint.yaml` prints each table in words, its warnings and notes, and the
boundary table (row, probe, input, expected outcome), without a model. `check` reports the
warnings and the rows that never apply.

In Python the table is `awa.workflows.SpecialCases`:

```python
from awa import Blueprint
from awa.workflows import boundary_cases, case_notes

table = Blueprint.from_yaml("blueprint.yaml").special_cases["decide"]
outcome = table.decide({"amount_eur": 6200, "supplier": "Acme Tools"})
outcome.then, outcome.source, outcome.row  # ("ask", "row", 3); source is "row", "else" or "unclear"
```
