```python
table.describe()                           # each row in words: "If amount is 5,000 EUR or more: a person decides (finance)"
boundary_cases(table)                      # test inputs at every edge, each with the outcome the table gives
case_notes(table)                          # rows that never apply, numbers no row decides
```

`boundary_cases` probes every row and records what the table decides, so you can keep each probe
as an eval case:

| The row tests | Probes |
| --- | --- |
| a number limit `c` | just below, exactly, just above `c`: steps of 1 when the field is compared with whole numbers only, else 0.01 or the finest decimal place used |
| `one of`, `not one of` | a value in the list, one outside it, and text in the list in other case |
| a text | exactly that text, another text, the same text in other case |
| `true` or `false` | both |
| every field | missing, and a number that reads two ways (`5.000` with a decimal point, `5,000` with a decimal comma) |

`case_notes` reports a row that never applies because earlier rows already decide every value it
covers, and a row whose conditions contradict each other. For a table that tests one number field
only, it also names the numbers no row decides. Only rows that test a single number field are
analyzed, so no note does not prove that every row can apply.

## Data from your files

A process often starts from files you already have: a bank statement, a folder of invoices. When
you build from your own files (`awa build "<process>" --data <files>`, or
`build_project(..., data=...)`), awa:

1. copies them into the project's `data/files/` folder (the originals are never touched);
2. profiles them without a model ([Data profile](data.md));
3. writes a `data:` section that records which file plays which role and what the process relies
   on in it.

```yaml
connectors:
  files:                       # the agents read the files only through this
    use: workspace
    root: data/files
    include: [read_csv, query_csv]
data:
  - name: bank_lines
    path: data/files/bank.csv  # relative to the blueprint; may be a glob
    role: input                # input | reference | template | output
    description: Bank statement lines to be matched to invoices.
    expect:                    # what the process relies on; every item is optional
      columns: [Buchungstag, Betrag_EUR]
      decimal: ","
      date_format: DD.MM.YYYY
    handling: Match each line to an open invoice by amount and reference.
```

`expect` may also name a key, a sheet, the header row and a minimum number of rows. `mask` and
`digest_tokens` set what the model sees of a document in a process step
([What the mask covers](process-section.md#what-the-mask-covers)).

Agents never open files themselves. A build gives them:

- one read-only `files` connector, with only the read operations that fit the kinds of file found;
- an `output` connector for `data/output/`. Each write waits for a person's approval in the
  generated configuration. You can remove the approval; `check` only warns about it.

### Check the files

`expect` is checked offline against the files as they are now. So a renamed column, a moved header
row or a changed number format is found before a run. `awa validate` and `awa data check` run the
check; from Python, pass a profile to `Blueprint.check`:

```python
from awa import Blueprint
from awa.data import profile

blueprint = Blueprint.from_yaml("blueprint.yaml")
for issue in blueprint.check(data=profile(["data/files/bank.csv"])):
    print(issue)      # prints nothing while the files match
```

With `Betrag` written where the file has `Betrag_EUR`:

```console
$ awa data check blueprint.yaml
error: data[0].expect.columns[1]: column 'Betrag' does not exist in 'data/files/bank.csv' (its columns: 'Buchungstag', 'Betrag_EUR', 'Verwendungszweck'); did you mean 'Betrag_EUR'? [DF-V-003]
blueprint.yaml: 1 error, 0 warnings
```

The exit code is 1 on errors. `awa data run PROJECT --file NAME` (or `--all`) runs the built
process on input files; results go to `data/output/`. Uploads, profiles and builds over HTTP are
on [Data API](data.md#the-data-endpoints).

## Designing and building from a description

`design` asks an architect agent to draft a blueprint from a plain-language description of the
process. It then checks the draft and feeds errors back, for up to `max_repairs` repair rounds.
The result has no error-severity issues; review it before you run it.

```python
from pathlib import Path

from awa.blueprints import design

blueprint = await design(
    "Incoming invoices are checked against purchase orders. Mismatches go to a clerk; "
    "matches above 10,000 EUR need a manager's approval before payment.",
    model="strong",
    tools=[read_invoice, find_purchase_order, book_payment],   # the architect may only use these
)
Path("invoice_desk.yaml").write_text(blueprint.to_yaml())
```

- Without `tools`, the architect names the tools it needs; implement them before building.
- It always sees the built-in tools (`builtin:<name>`, with what each one needs in `toolkits:`) and
  the skills, so it uses them instead of inventing equivalents.
- From synchronous code, call `asyncio.run(design(...))`.

### Build a tested project

`design_project` goes further. It writes the acceptance cases first, then a blueprint wired to a
local workspace of sample data, the process rules as tested tools, the approvals and one
`ConnectionStep` per outside system. `build_project` evaluates that design and repairs it in
bounded rounds:

```python
from awa import UsageLimits
from awa.blueprints import build_project

report = await build_project(
    "Incoming supplier invoices are checked against their purchase order ...",
    out_dir="invoice_desk",
    model="strong",
    usage_limits=UsageLimits(max_requests=150),
    on_progress=lambda step: print(f"[{step.stage}] {step.message}"),
)
print(report.summary())    # what passes, what is connected, what is left to do
```

- `BuildReport` has `passed`, `pass_rate`, `rounds`, `stopped`, `usage`, `eval_report`, `flaky`,
  `design` and `directory`.
- Pass a `ProjectDesign` to `build` to evaluate a design you already have. `environment=` chooses
  the reachable systems (`"auto"` discovers them from the environment and `.env`, names only).
- The test designer (`TEST_DESIGNER_INSTRUCTIONS`) also designs `triggers` (`TriggerDesign`) with a
  `sample_payload`, `assumptions`, and cases that send a `payload` to a `trigger` instead of an
  `input`. The build writes the triggers
  into the blueprint and names them in the README.
- The design briefs include the closest shipped examples, chosen by word overlap without a model
  call.

What this looks like to a user, and the project folder it writes, is in
[Describe a process](../guide/describe.md).

## Projects

`awa init <dir> --template minimal|team|workflow|network|support` writes a runnable starter
project: `blueprint.yaml`, a typed `tools.py`, sample data, `evals/cases.yaml`, `.env.example`,
`README.md`, `pyproject.toml` and offline tests as `test_blueprint.py` in the `tests` folder of the
project (every agent gets a scripted `FakeChatModel` through a `ModelRegistry`).
For real use you need a model key and your own tools. From Python:
`awa.blueprints.scaffold.create_project("my-desk", template="support")`. What each file is for:
[The project folder](project-folder.md).

## What can go wrong

| You see | Cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| `unknown tool 'read_invoice' (known: none)` | The blueprint names a tool you did not pass. Give `tools=[...]` to `load` or `build`; on the command line put a `tools.py` beside the blueprint or add `--tools tools.py`. |
| `declares approvals (used by bookkeeper) ... pass a checkpointer` | A paused run must be saved somewhere. Pass `checkpointer=StateInMemorySaver()` (from `awa.persistence`), or a database-backed one in production. |
| `Step 'x' uses the agent 'y', which does not exist` | A step of `process` names an agent that is not in `agents`; the message suggests the closest name. |
| `team.orchestrator: unknown agent 'c' (known: a, b)` | A name is misspelled. Names in `team`, `workflow` and `network` must match an agent. |
| `Blueprint file not found: '...'` | A one-line string is read as a path. For YAML text use `Blueprint.from_yaml_text`. |
| `column '...' does not exist in '...'` (data) | A file changed under the `data:` section. Fix the name in `expect`, or put the file back; the message offers the closest real name. |

## Related

- [Describe a process](../guide/describe.md): the same YAML explained for non-programmers.
- [CLI](../reference/cli.md): `awa validate`, `show`, `run`, `chat`, `eval`, `serve`, `build`.
- [Testing](testing.md): offline tests and evaluation of blueprints.
- [Data profile](data.md): what `awa data inspect` reports about your files.
- [The process section](process-section.md): steps with documents and checks that run before the next step starts.
- Examples: `examples/blueprints/support_triage.yaml` (a team with peers, handoffs, a task board and an approval), `examples/blueprints/document_review.yaml` (a workflow with a parallel review), `examples/processes/invoice-check/`. Reference: [Blueprints](../reference/api/core.md#awa.blueprints).

<!-- source: develop/project-folder.md -->

# The project folder

A project is one plain folder that holds everything a process needs: the blueprint, your tools,
your files, the tests and the settings. The web app (`awa ui`), `awa build` and `awa init` write it.
Every command, the web app and `awa.load` read it the same way, so you can switch between them at
any step.

Read this page to know what a project consists of, or to work on it from Python or a terminal
instead of the web app. You need awa installed ([Install](../start/install.md)).

## What is in it

| Path | What it holds | Written by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `blueprint.yaml` | The agents, how they work together, the connectors, the approvals and the triggers. The only file a project needs. | all |
| `tools.py` | Your own tools (and the rules and approval steps of a built project). Loaded by itself, next to the blueprint. | all, when needed |
| `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | Your own skills. Loaded by itself, next to the blueprint, in addition to the built-in skills. | `awa new skill`, you |
| `plugins.py`, `tools/*.py`, `connectors/*.py` | More parts of the project: `register(...)` calls for models, parsers and the like, more tool files, connector specs ([Plugins](extend.md#plugins)). | you, when needed |
| `data/` | Your files (`data/files/`), the results (`data/output/`), their profile and the sample data that stands in for external systems not yet connected. | web app, `awa build` |
| `evals/cases.yaml` | The eval cases. | all |
| `tests/` | Offline pytest tests of `tools.py` (and of the blueprint after `awa init`). | all, when needed |
| `CONNECT.md` | How to connect each external system, step by step (read by `awa connect`). | web app, `awa build` |
| `.env.example` | The names of the settings the project reads, without values. | all |
| `.env` | The values: model keys, addresses, passwords. awa writes it readable by you only and never shows a value again. | web app, `awa setup`, `awa connect`, you |
| `.awa/` | Local run data: runs, approvals, uploads, traces. | web app, `awa serve`, `awa worker` |
| `.gitignore` | Keeps `.env`, `.env.bak` and `.awa/` out of version control. | all |

`awa init` also writes a `pyproject.toml` and a `README.md`; `awa build` and the web app write a
`README.md` that sums up the design.

Settings are read from the process environment first, then from the project's `.env`.

!!! warning "Open only projects you trust"
    `tools.py` and `skills/` are code and instructions that run on your computer.

## Use it from Python

`awa.load` takes the folder (or its `blueprint.yaml`) and builds the system with the project's
`tools.py` and `skills/`, exactly as the commands and the web app do. Run it, answer an approval,
and evaluate the cases:

```python
import asyncio

import awa
from awa.evals import Dataset, evaluate
from awa.persistence import StateInMemorySaver

desk = awa.load("invoice-desk", checkpointer=StateInMemorySaver())
result = asyncio.run(desk.run("Check invoice INV-1042."))
if result.is_interrupted:  # a tool call waits for your approval
    result = asyncio.run(desk.resume(result.thread_id, {"action": "approve"}))
print(result.output)

report = asyncio.run(evaluate(desk, Dataset.load("invoice-desk/evals/cases.yaml")))
print(f"{report.pass_rate:.0%} of the cases pass")
```

- Pass `tools=` or `skill_registry=` to use other tools or skills than those of the folder.
- The settings come from the process environment, then from the `.env` of the project folder that
  contains the working directory. To run the script from elsewhere, call
  `awa.config.load_environment("invoice-desk")` first.

## Every step without the web app

Each step of the web app has a command and a Python call:

| Web app | Command line | Python |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Set up: the model key | `awa setup`, `awa env set NAME` | `awa.setup` |
| Start from an example | `awa ui --example ID`, `awa init DIR --template NAME` | `awa.blueprints.scaffold.create_project` |
| Data: your files | `awa data inspect FILES` | `awa.data.profile` |
| Data: external systems | `awa data add-system`, `awa data remove-system` | `awa.blueprints.read_declared_systems` lists them |
| Describe | `awa build "<process>" --data FILES` | `awa.blueprints.build_project`, `awa.blueprints.design_project` |
| Suggest and test patterns | none | `awa.blueprints.suggest_patterns`, `awa.blueprints.try_patterns` |
| Review | `awa validate`, `awa show` | `awa.Blueprint.check`, `awa.Blueprint.explain` |
| Connect | `awa connect DIR` | the values in `.env`, the connector in `blueprint.yaml`, as `CONNECT.md` says |
| Test | `awa eval blueprint.yaml evals/cases.yaml` | `awa.evals.evaluate` |
| Try it | `awa chat blueprint.yaml`, `awa run blueprint.yaml "<task>"` | `awa.load` |
| Use it: triggers | `awa add trigger`, `awa trigger run`, `awa worker`, `awa serve` | `awa.blueprints.triggers.add_trigger`, `awa.automation.build_automation`, `awa.automation.Worker` |
| Use it: runs | `awa runs list`, `awa runs retry` | `awa.automation.SqliteRunStore` |
| Approvals | `awa runs decide` | `awa.automation.Automation.decide` |
| Assistant | `awa brief` | `awa.blueprints.write_brief` |

The web app's download is the folder itself without `.env`, `.awa/` and the databases; in git,
the `.gitignore` keeps `.env` and `.awa/` out. To leave awa, `awa export` and `awa.exporter.export`
turn a one-agent project into a standalone LangGraph project ([Export](export.md)).

Every command is on [Command line](../reference/cli.md); every page of the web app is on
[The web app](../guide/web-app.md).

<!-- source: develop/agent-spec.md -->

# Agent spec

Instead of one block of free-text `instructions`, an agent in a blueprint can describe its job in
sections: a goal, the context, how to work, the rules. awa puts the sections in a fixed order and
adds what the code already knows, such as the step, its documents and the tools that need an
approval. `awa validate` then lints the result.

The fields are optional. A blueprint that leaves them out loads, builds and validates all the same.
The other agent fields are in [Blueprints](blueprints.md).

## An agent with sections

With `goal` or `system` set, the system message is rendered from sections:

```yaml
agents:
  - name: check_invoice
    role: worker
    description: Checks supplier invoices against price list and order. Use for every incoming supplier invoice before payment approval.
    goal: Decide for each invoice line whether price and quantity match the order and the price list.
    system:
      context: Wrong prices cost money only if they reach payment; finance approves or blocks payment on this result.
      how_to_work: |
        1. Match each invoice line to the order line by article number.
        2. Compare the unit price with price_list; a difference above 1% is a deviation.
        3. Compare the quantity with goods_receipt.
      tools_in_step: "Use `read_csv` once per input file and filter by article number."
      rules:
        - Mark an article missing from price_list as missing_reference, because finance decides those manually.
      output: auto
    tools: ["builtin:read_csv"]
    output_schema: {$ref: schemas/invoice_check.json}
    escalation: {to: person, when: ["parse failure after retries", "deviation above 10%"], how: 'status "escalate" with a reason'}
```

## Agent fields

| Field | Type | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `goal` | text, one sentence | What the agent achieves. |
| `system` | mapping | The sections of the system message (below). |
| `tools`, `skills` | list | Tool references and skill names. |
| `escalation` | `{to: person or orchestrator, when: [...], how}` | When and how the agent hands a case on. |
| `acknowledge_ungated` | list of tool references | Hand-written agents only: acting tools that run without an approval on purpose (lint T14 becomes a note). |
| `output_schema` | mapping, or `{$ref: <file>}` | A `$ref` names a JSON or YAML schema file inside the blueprint's folder; it is read when the blueprint is loaded from its file. |

The sections of `system`:

| Section | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `context` | The background of the work. |
| `how_to_work` | The method, for example numbered steps. |
| `tools_in_step` | When to use which of the agent's tools in this step (not a tool manual). |
| `done_when` | What must hold before the agent answers. |
| `rules` | A list; each rule with its reason (`"..., because ..."`). |
| `special_cases` | Extra special-case lines beyond those generated from the process. |
| `output` | What the answer must contain; `auto` renders the fields of `output_schema`. |
| `examples` | 0 to 3 of `{input, output, why}`. |
| `delegation_brief` | Orchestrator only: what every brief to a member states. |

For a judge and a reviewer, `judges:` is set on the judge and `reviews:` on the reviewer. The
judge's verdict schema comes from the role contract and is never written in YAML.

Special cases stay in the top-level `special_cases: {<step>: <table>}`
([Blueprints: special cases](blueprints.md#special-cases)). The renderer turns the table into the
lines of the "Special cases and escalation" section.

## The system message

The sections come in a fixed order, and empty ones are left out:

1. Role and goal
2. Context
3. How to work
4. Tools in this step
5. Done when
6. Rules
7. Special cases and escalation
8. Output
9. Before you answer
10. Example(s)

Then come the judge's or reviewer's rules with the rubric, Delegation for an orchestrator, and four
house rules.

The code fills in:

- the role and the step (`step 2 of 3`);
- the documents of the step input;
- one sentence per gated tool: the system asks for the approval, the agent does not;
- the messages of the step's checks, the special-case table and the retries;
- the output fields;
- "Before you answer": at most three checks generated from the required fields of
  `output_schema`, the step's checks and the gated tools (none for a judge or reviewer).

An agent with free-text `instructions` keeps the text verbatim as its Instructions section. It
still gets Context, How to work, Tools in this step, Done when, and Special cases and escalation
when the spec sets them, so a refinement adds a method without rewriting the text.

The message stays the same for the whole run, so a provider can cache it.

## Lint (`awa validate`)

`awa validate` lints with the `authored` profile, where E01 and the A-rules are warnings.
`--profile generated` makes every rule as strict as the table lists. Free-text `instructions` get a
note and only E06, E10 and E11.

| Code | Severity | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E01 | error | no goal, no output section, or an acting agent with no escalation |
| E02, E03 | error | the text names a tool or skill the agent does not have |
| E04 | error | an unrendered `{placeholder}` |
| E05 | error | the text names a document that is not declared |
| E06 | error | pasted data (more than 15 table lines, or a `<<<DATA` block) |
| E10 | error | more than 8,000 characters |
| E11 | error | something shaped like a key, token or password |
| W13 | warning | an orchestrator without a delegation brief |
| W15 | warning | a system message above 4,000 characters (6,000 for an orchestrator), or more than 10 tools |
| A02 | error | a document named in the text that no step of the agent gets |
| A03 | warning | a later step decides on fields but this step has no `output_schema` |
| A04 | warning | more than three skills |
| T01 | error | a tool name that is not 1-64 letters, digits, `_` or `-` |
| T03 | error, note | description missing or under 40 characters; fewer than three sentences is a note |
| T05 | error, note | input schema root is not an object; without `additionalProperties: false` is a note (awa does not send strict mode) |
| T13 | error | MCP hints contradict each other, or say read-only for a tool awa's risk data says acts |
| T14 | error (generated), warning (hand-written) | an acting tool without an approval; a note when listed in `acknowledge_ungated` |
| T21 | error | a judge or reviewer with an acting tool, also when pinned |
| T22 | error (generated), warning (hand-written) | the text speaks of an approval ("for the manager's approval"), but none of the agent's tools is gated and no step of it has an approval check |

Full examples of a worker, an orchestrator, a judge and a reviewer are in
`tests/fixtures/agentspec/examples/`.

<!-- source: develop/process-section.md -->

# The process section

The `process:` section of a blueprint is a line of steps. Each step has one agent and optional
checks. The checks run after the agent has answered and before the next step starts, so a result
that fails a check stops the run, and the next agent is never called.

Use it when each result must pass rules, or a person, before the process goes on. A step can also
be tried again, be skipped by a condition, or have a rule table of special cases. This page is for
developers who write or review a blueprint and know [Blueprints](blueprints.md). The section is
optional; `format_version` stays `awa/v1`.

## An example

Two steps: read an invoice, then compare it with a price list. Bad values stop the run; a large
deviation asks a person.

```yaml
agents:
  - name: extractor
    description: Reads one supplier invoice and returns its fields.
    tools: [builtin:read_file]
    output_schema:
      type: object
      properties: {supplier: {type: string}, total: {type: number}}
      required: [supplier, total]
  - name: price_checker
    description: Compares the invoice lines with the price list.
    documents: [price_list]            # the agent always has this document
    tools: [builtin:read_file]
    output_schema:
      type: object
      properties: {ok: {type: boolean}, max_deviation_pct: {type: number}}
      required: [ok, max_deviation_pct]
data:
  - name: price_list
    path: data/files/price_list.csv
    role: reference
    expect: {columns: [item, unit_price], decimal: "."}
process:
  carry: previous
  steps:
    - name: extract
      title: Read the invoice
      agent: extractor
      checks:
        - kind: schema                  # the output has the fields of the agent's output_schema
        - kind: rule
          fail_when: "empty(supplier) or total <= 0"
          message: The invoice has no supplier, or a total of zero or less.
    - name: validate
      agent: price_checker
      checks:
        - kind: rule
          fail_when: "max_deviation_pct > 25"
          message: A line is more than 25 percent away from the list price.
        - kind: approval
          when: "max_deviation_pct > 2"
          reason: Invoices that deviate from the price list are decided by a person.
          by: accounts_manager
```

The complete, runnable version is `examples/processes/invoice-check/` (three steps: read the
invoice, compare with a price list document, decide with a person).

## What a step does, in order

1. **`when`.** A step whose `when` is false is `skipped`. If the condition cannot be decided, the
   run stops.
2. **Documents.** The step's documents (and its agent's) must exist and match their `expect:`.
   If not, the step fails before any model is called, with a message that says what to do.
3. **The agent runs.** Its input is the carried text, then a block that lists each document with
   a digest of the file. The block is marked as data: the model is told to treat it as data. That
   lowers the risk of instructions hidden in a document; it does not remove it. Documents come in
   the step input, not in the instructions, so one agent can sit on two steps with different
   documents.
4. **The answer is not empty.** An empty answer fails the step.
5. **`schema` and `rule` checks**, in the order written. A failed check (or an error of the agent)
   is tried again when the step has a `retry`. After the last try, `after_last_try` decides.
6. **Special cases** of the step (`special_cases.<step>`), on the output that passed the checks.
7. **`approval` checks, last.** A person is never asked about a result that already failed a
   check. When several approvals apply, or an approval and a special case that asks, the person is
   asked once, with every reason.

How a run ends when a step does not pass:

- A failed check, or an error of the agent, after the last try (with `after_last_try: stop`)
  stops the run with `StepCheckFailedError` (code `awa.step_check_failed`) or with the agent's
  error. The message names the step and says what to do. Its `steps` attribute lists the status of
  every step.
- A rejection, by a special case or by a person, stops the run with `StepRejectedError` (code
  `awa.step_rejected`, a `StepCheckFailedError`). Automation runs, served runs and jobs then have
  the status `rejected`, and an automation never retries it.
- There is no "accept anyway".

## The checks

- **`schema`**: the output must match a JSON schema. Without `schema:`, the agent's own
  `output_schema` is used. A JSON object in the answer text counts as the output.
- **`rule`**: `fail_when` is an expression over the output fields and `text` (the answer text).
  When it is true, the step fails with `message` and the values the rule read.
- **`approval`**: pauses the run until a person decides. `when` limits it (no `when`: always).
  `reason` is shown to the person; `by` names the role that should decide.

**Rules and approval conditions fail closed.** A rule that cannot be evaluated on the output (a
missing field, text where a number is expected) fails the step instead of passing it. An approval
condition that cannot be evaluated asks.

The expression language is the one of `approvals[].when`: comparisons, `and`, `or`, `not`, `in`,
arithmetic and `contains`, `startswith`, `endswith`, `lower`, `upper`, `len`, `number`, `empty`,
`abs`, `round`, `min`, `max`. There are no loops over list items and no regular expressions:
"every line has a price" needs a `schema` check, another step or a tool.

"Checked" means the checks passed. It does not mean the answer is correct: review results that
matter. A step with no checks of its own still gets the automatic ones (documents, non-empty
answer); `check` warns about it.

## The fields

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `process` | A mapping with `steps` and `carry`, or a bare list of steps. A step may be written as the agent's name. `process` and `workflow` cannot both be set. |
| `process.carry` | `previous` (default): a step receives the previous step's result (the JSON of its structured output, else its text). `all`: it receives the request and every earlier step's result. |
| `steps[].name` | Letters, digits, `_` and `-`, up to 48 characters, unique. Default: the agent's name (`_2`, `_3` for a repeated agent). |
| `steps[].title` | A label for people, up to 80 characters. |
| `steps[].agent` | An entry of `agents` (or the name of a team or network of the blueprint). |
| `steps[].documents` | Names of `data:` entries the agent gets in this step. |
| `steps[].checks` | `schema`, `rule` and `approval` checks ([above](#the-checks)). |
| `steps[].retry` | How often the step is tried: `{max_attempts, initial, backoff, max_delay, jitter, on}` (the shape of `automation.retry`; `attempts` or `tries` and `wait` are accepted too, `retry: 3` is the short form). At most 5 tries; `on` is `[error, check]` by default. Not allowed for an agent that writes or sends. |
| `steps[].after_last_try` | `stop` (default), `ask`, or `go: <later step>` (also `{go: <step>}`). `go` is not allowed for an agent that writes or sends, nor into a step whose agent does. |
| `steps[].when` | The step runs only when this condition is true; otherwise it is `skipped`. |
| `special_cases.<step>` | The rule table of the step (top level of the blueprint, named after the step). See [Blueprints: special cases](blueprints.md#special-cases). |
| `agents[].documents` | Names of `data:` entries the agent always has, in every step it does. They are listed in its instructions and checked and delivered like step documents. |
| `data[].role` | `input`, `reference`, `template` (the agent copies its layout) or `output`. |
| `data[].mask`, `data[].digest_tokens` | How personal data is hidden in the digest the model sees (`none`, `placeholders`, `drop`; default: none, unless the project says otherwise), and its size (200 to 12000 tokens). See [What the mask covers](#what-the-mask-covers). |

## If/else, retries and special cases

```yaml
process:
  - name: extract
    agent: invoice_reader                # reads only: a step that writes or sends may not retry
    retry: {max_attempts: 3, initial: 10s, on: [error, check]}
    after_last_try: ask                  # stop (default) | ask | go: <later step>
    checks:
      - {kind: rule, fail_when: "amount_eur <= 0", message: No amount found.}
  - name: board_review
    agent: board_secretary
    when: "amount_eur >= 50000"          # skipped below 50,000
  - name: decide
    agent: payment_clerk
    checks:
      - {kind: approval, when: "amount_eur >= 20000", reason: Large payments need a person.}
  - name: archive
    agent: archivist
special_cases:
  decide:                                # first match wins
    cases:
      - {if: "supplier in ['Blocked Supplies Ltd']", then: reject, message: Blocked supplier.}
      - {if: [{field: amount_eur, op: ">=", value: 5000}], then: ask, by: finance}
      - {if: [{field: status, op: "=", value: paid}], then: go, to: archive}
      - {if: [{field: amount_eur, op: "<", value: 5000}], then: approve}
    else: ask
    when_unclear: ask                    # ask | reject, never approve
```

### Retry

- Each try is its own step of the run graph. The try number is kept in the run's checkpointed
  state: a run that pauses for a tool approval in try 2 continues in try 2 when the decision
  comes, and try 1 is not run again.
- With `on: check`, the next try gets the message of the failed check in its input.
- The wait before try n+1 is `initial * backoff**(n-1)`, at most `max_delay` (default ten times
  `initial`), spread by `jitter`.
- Never tried again: a reached limit, a cancellation, a run timeout, a guardrail block, a
  permission or configuration error, and programming errors (`ValueError`, `TypeError` ...).
- Every try costs a model run. `limits` bound the whole run, retries included.

### After the last try

- `stop` fails the run.
- `ask` pauses for a person: approve continues with the last result, reject ends the run as
  `rejected`.
- `go: <step>` marks the step `failed` and the steps in between `skipped`. It continues at that
  step with what the step before the failed one handed on; the failed result is never passed on.

### `when`

The condition reads the request's JSON fields, the output fields of every earlier step that passed
(a later step wins), and `text`. It is evaluated like a special case: a value it needs that is
missing or unclear stops the run with a message, instead of guessing. A step skipped by `when`
skips its checks too; `check` warns when the step has a rule, an approval or special cases.

### Special cases

How a table decides is in [Blueprints: special cases](blueprints.md#special-cases). In a run:

- `approve` adds no question of its own. An approval check of the step that applies still asks: in
  the example, 25,000 EUR asks a person although no row asks.
- `ask` pauses for a person. `by` is recorded and shown, not enforced.
- `reject` ends the run with status `rejected`.
- `go` continues at a later step after this step's approval checks; the steps in between are
  `skipped`.

There are no loops back: a `go` must lead to a later step. What else `check` refuses is listed in
[Checks of the blueprint](#checks-of-the-blueprint).

### Try it without a model

The dry run walks the process with stand-in agents that answer the values you give:

1. Put the values in a file, for example `{"supplier": "Acme Tools", "amount_eur": 6200}` in
   `values.json` (a file avoids the quoting rules of each shell). Fields of an agent's output
   schema that you leave out get sample values.
2. Run `awa show dry-run blueprint.yaml --input values.json`.
3. Read the path it prints: each step, each try with the wait a real run would make, each pause
   with the question and how the dry run answered it, and the result.

`--fail extract=2` lets the first two tries fail; `--decide reject` says no at each pause. The dry
run asks no model, calls no tool and reads no document. So it is free and gives the same path every
time; it proves the routing, not what a model would answer. In Python:
`await awa.blueprints.dry_run(blueprint, values, checkpointer=StateInMemorySaver(),
fail={"extract": 2})`.

## Approvals: what is and is not protected

- A step approval needs a checkpointer (`StateInMemorySaver()` in tests, a database-backed one in
  production). `Blueprint.needs_checkpointer()` says whether a blueprint needs one: it covers
  tool approvals, `ask` policies and step approvals. `build`, `awa run`, `awa eval`, `awa serve`
  and the web app use it. Without a checkpointer `build` refuses, and a workflow built in code fails
  at the approval instead of passing it.
- The decision is `{"action": "approve"}` or `{"action": "reject", "note": "..."}`. **Anything
  else, a malformed answer included, counts as a rejection.** A rejection ends the run with the
  note of the person. The step's agent does not run again when the approval is answered.
- **awa does not check who answers.** `by` records the role and shows it. Enforcing roles is up to
  the code that calls `resume` (your API, the approvals inbox of your product).
- The payload the person sees is `{kind: step_approval, tool: "step:<name>", step, title, agent,
  reason, output, args, by}`. The approval card of the web app names the step and the agent.
  `ApprovalRequestedEvent` and `ApprovalDecidedEvent` carry the tool `step:<name>`, so the audit
  log and the traces record who decided.
- Tool approvals (`approvals:`, policies) stay as they are. A step approval gates the result of a
  step; a tool approval gates a call. A step whose agent has a gated tool can pause twice: first
  inside the agent, then at the step approval.

## What the mask covers

`mask: placeholders` or `drop` hides personal data in the **digest** that is put into the step
input. It does not cover what a tool reads from the file itself: a read tool of the agent returns
the original.

So `check` reports an error when a masked document is attached to an agent with a tool that looks
like a file reader (`builtin:read_file`, `connector:files.<op>` and similar names). Remove the
tool, or set the document to show everything and say so in the step. This is judged from the tool
reference alone; a tool with another name is not recognized.

## Events, results and traces

- `StepEvent` (`type: step`) reports `started`, `checking`, `needs_approval`, `checked`,
  `failed`, `retrying`, `skipped` and `rejected` per step, with the checks run so far. Its `agent`
  is the step's agent; `attempt` is the try (for a step with a `retry`), and `case` the id of the
  special case that decided (`<step>.case.<row>`, `<step>.case.else`, or
  `<step>.case.<row>.unclear`). After an approval pause, `started` can appear again for a step
  whose agent paused on a tool approval. See [Events](../reference/api/core.md#awa.contracts).
- The result's `metadata["steps"]` lists every step with `name`, `title`, `agent`, `status`
  (`checked`, `skipped`, or `failed` for a step that continued elsewhere after its last try),
  `checks`, `run_id` and `duration_ms`, plus `attempts` (with a retry), `case` (the special case
  that decided, in words too), `message` and `continued_at` when they apply.
- Traces show one line per step with its try and its special case, and the failed checks;
  `awa runs trace` renders them. OpenTelemetry (and Langfuse) gets an `awa.step` span event on the
  workflow span with `awa.step.attempt` and `awa.step.case` (the message text only with content
  capture).

## Checks of the blueprint

`awa validate` and `Blueprint.check` report these. Errors stop `build`; warnings do not. "Writes
or sends" is judged from the tool's risk (`external_action`), the same judgment as the approval
check of `tool_risks`.

| Finding | Severity |
| --- | --- |
| `process` and `workflow` both set; a process without steps; invalid or duplicate step or check names | error |
| A step without an agent, or with an unknown one (the closest name is suggested) | error |
| A document name that `data:` does not declare (step or agent) | error |
| A `schema` check without any schema; an expression that does not parse or reads a name that is not an output field of the agent; a rule without a `message` | error |
| A masked document attached to an agent with a file-reading tool | error |
| `special_cases.<name>` for a step the process does not have; a `go` to an unknown or earlier step, or one that jumps over a step with a rule, an approval or special cases | error |
| A `retry` or `after_last_try: go` for an agent that writes or sends, or `after_last_try: go` into a step whose agent does | error |
| A `when` on a step with a rule, an approval or special cases (they are skipped with it) | warning |
| A document whose file is missing (when the files are checked), a document attached to an agent that cannot read it, a result file attached as input, a document attached twice | warning |
| A step with only the automatic checks; an agent on no step; no `limits` on a process of two or more steps; more than 12 steps | warning |
| A field the next agent's instructions name in backticks that an earlier step returns but the previous one does not (with `carry: previous`) | warning |

## Commands

- `awa show <blueprint>` prints the steps with their agents, documents and checks in words;
  `awa show --mermaid` draws the chain.
- `awa show cases <blueprint>` prints the special cases with their boundary tests.
- `awa show dry-run <blueprint> --input VALUES` walks the process without a model (exit code 1
  when a step would fail).
- `awa run` and `awa eval` run a process like any workflow. `awa eval` cases may carry
  `metadata: {step: <name>}`, and a `decisions:` entry with `tool: "step:<name>"` answers a step
  approval. A run that stops at a check ends with an error, so a case cannot expect it; test those
  stops in code.

## How it is tested

The flow is proven offline with scripted models: order, checks, documents, the pause and its
resume, the stops, running one step again, retries, `when`, special cases and the dry run. The
tests are `tests/unit/test_workflows_process.py`, `tests/unit/test_workflows_process_retry.py`,
`tests/unit/test_blueprints_process_build.py`, `tests/unit/test_blueprints_process_routing.py`,
`tests/unit/test_cli_show_dry_run.py` and `tests/examples/test_process_invoice_check.py`.

Not proven: how well a real model does a step, and whether a retry helps a real model pass a check
it failed. A live result comes from one model and a small number of runs; read it as that.

## Related

[Blueprints](blueprints.md), [Workflows](workflows.md), [Human in the loop](safety.md#approvals),
[Data from your files](blueprints.md#data-from-your-files), [Events](../reference/api/core.md#awa.contracts).

<!-- source: develop/configuration.md -->

# Configuration

awa reads a few values from the environment: your model key, which models to use and where to keep
state. You set them once, usually in the `.env` file of your project folder. Agents, tools and
limits are not set here: they live in code or in a [blueprint](blueprints.md).

Read this page when a value does not take effect, when you move a project to a server, or when you
configure awa from Python. Install awa first ([Install](../start/install.md)).

## Set a value

Write a value into the project `.env` and check where each value comes from:

```console
awa env set AWA_TRACE_LEVEL=full      # write one into the project .env
awa env list                          # every setting, its value and where it comes from
```

`awa env set` checks a value before it writes it. A secret, such as a model key, takes only the
name (`awa env set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`): awa asks for the value without showing it, and never repeats
a secret in its messages. A setting that decides where requests go or switches a protection (marked
*confirm* in the [Settings reference](../reference/settings.md)) needs `--confirm`. `awa doctor`
shows the same sources and checks the values.

In Python, the values are one `Settings` object:

```python
from awa.core.settings import get_settings

settings = get_settings()            # read on first use, then cached
print(settings.default_model)        # a provider:model string, see Models
print(settings.anthropic_api_key)    # ********** (a SecretStr, see below)
```

## Where values come from

A value is taken from the process environment, else from the project `.env`, else the default.
Every `awa` command and the library use this rule. `awa env list` and `awa doctor` show the source
of each value: `env`, `env (empty)`, `.env:<line>` or `default`.

For `Settings` in code, keyword arguments come first:

1. **Keyword arguments** in code: `Settings(checkpointer_backend="postgres")`.
2. **Environment variables** of the process. A variable that is set but empty counts as set for the
   loader (it is not filled in from `.env`); `Settings` treats it as unset and takes the `.env`
   value.
3. **The project `.env`.**
4. **The defaults** in the [Settings reference](../reference/settings.md).

### The project folder

awa looks for the `.env` in the project folder. It finds that folder like this:

- `--project DIR` (or `AWA_PROJECT_DIR`) names it.
- Otherwise awa starts at the folder of the blueprint a command names, else at the working
  directory. It walks up to the nearest folder that has `blueprint.yaml`, a `pyproject.toml` with
  `[tool.awa]`, or an `.awa/` folder. A `.env` makes only the start folder itself a project.
- The search stops at the home folder (never a project), at a repository root (a folder with
  `.git`) and at the drive root. Without a match, the start folder is the project.

### What reaches `os.environ`

The `awa` command line exports the values of the project `.env` that the process environment
lacks. So provider SDKs that read the environment themselves (LangChain providers, LangSmith) see
them too.

Only names awa knows are exported: the [registry](../reference/settings.md), its aliases, the names
your blueprint declares in `*_env` keys (a trigger's `secret_env`, a mailbox's `username_env`), and
the variable `--api-key-env` names. `PATH`, `PYTHON*`, proxies, `LD_*`, `GIT_*`, `DOCKER_*`, `PIP_*`,
`UV_*`, `BASH_ENV`, `TEMP` and similar names are never exported, whatever declares them.

Library code (`get_settings()`, `awa.config.env_value`) reads the `.env` without changing
`os.environ`. Call `awa.config.load_environment(export=True)` to export as the command line does.

### Unknown names

An `AWA_*` name that no setting has (in the environment or in `.env`), and an unknown
`ANTHROPIC_*`, `OPENAI_*`, `AZURE_OPENAI_*` or `LANGSMITH_*` name in `.env`, gives one warning with
the closest known name:
`warning: AWA_DEFUALT_MODEL is not a known setting (did you mean AWA_DEFAULT_MODEL?)`.
With `AWA_STRICT_SETTINGS=true` the command stops with exit code 78 instead.

### Settings in code

`get_settings()` caches the object for the whole process. It does not see later changes to the
environment until you call `get_settings.cache_clear()`.

To configure something explicitly, create your own `Settings` and pass it to the functions that
take one:

```python
from awa import Settings
from awa.models import ModelRegistry
from awa.persistence import open_checkpointer

settings = Settings(_env_file=None, checkpointer_backend="postgres",
                    postgres_dsn="postgresql://app:secret@db:5432/app")
models = ModelRegistry(settings)
async with open_checkpointer(settings) as checkpointer:
    ...
```

`_env_file` picks another file (`_env_file=".env.staging"`; triggers and the names a blueprint
declares then read that file too), or none at all (`_env_file=None`).

## The settings most projects need

The [Settings reference](../reference/settings.md) lists every variable awa reads, generated from
the code. These are the ones you are most likely to set:

| Variable | What it does (default) |
| --- | --- |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY` | The key of your model provider. Azure OpenAI also needs `AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT`; Entra sign-in is on [Models](models.md#azure-openai). |
| `AWA_DEFAULT_MODEL`, `AWA_FAST_MODEL`, `AWA_STRONG_MODEL` | The models of the `default`, `fast` and `strong` profiles, as `provider:model` (below). |
| `AWA_ENV` | `local`, `test`, `staging` or `production` (`local`): a label for traces only; see [below](#awa_env). |
| `AWA_POSTGRES_DSN` | The PostgreSQL connection string of every `postgres` backend (unset). |
| `AWA_DATA_BACKEND` | Where runs, steps and results are kept: `sqlite` or `postgres` (unset: `postgres` with a DSN). `awa store use` sets it. |
| `AWA_CHECKPOINTER_BACKEND`, `AWA_STORE_BACKEND`, `AWA_ARTIFACT_BACKEND` | The backends of `awa.persistence.open_checkpointer`, `open_store` and `open_artifact_repository` (`memory`). With a `memory` store, long-term memories and remembered decisions are lost when the process stops. |
| `AWA_RUN_MAX_REQUESTS`, `AWA_RUN_MAX_TOOL_CALLS`, `AWA_RUN_MAX_TOKENS`, `AWA_RUN_MAX_SECONDS`, `AWA_RUN_MAX_DEPTH` | The ceilings of every run tree; see [Limits](safety.md#limits). |
| `AWA_TOOL_PROFILE` | `cost` or `quality` (`cost`): how much of a long tool result the model sees. |
| `AWA_TRACE_LEVEL` | `off`, `summary` or `full` (`summary`): how much the traces of automated runs record; see [Run traces](observability.md#run-traces). |
| `AWA_LANGFUSE_TRACING` | `true`: the `awa` commands that run systems send every run to Langfuse (`false`); see [Langfuse](observability.md#langfuse). |
| `AWA_CACHE_ENABLED` | The master switch of every cache; see [Prompt caching and result caches](models.md#prompt-caching-and-result-caches). |
| `AWA_LOG_LEVEL` | A logging level name (`INFO`) for your own logging setup, such as `logging.basicConfig(level=settings.log_level)`; awa does not read it. |

**The model profiles.** When `AWA_DEFAULT_MODEL`, `AWA_FAST_MODEL` and `AWA_STRONG_MODEL` are unset,
the profiles follow the provider whose credentials are complete, in the order Anthropic, OpenAI,
Azure OpenAI, Google, Mistral, Groq, Ollama (see [Set up a project](../guide/setup.md)). You can
register more profiles on a `ModelRegistry`. Agents and blueprints name a profile, so switching providers is a configuration change ([Models](models.md)).

**Provider names.** Fields with an alias read the conventional variable without prefix that the
provider SDKs also use (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`). They also accept `AWA_<FIELD>` as a fallback; the name
without prefix wins when both are set. In code, a field is mostly the variable in lower case
without `AWA_` (`AWA_RUN_MAX_REQUESTS` is `settings.run_max_requests`); the
[`Settings`](../reference/api/core.md) reference lists every field and its alias.

`.env.example` in the repository lists every variable with a comment. It is generated from the
registry (`python scripts/gen_settings.py`), like the reference. The `.env` that `awa init` writes
lists the ones a new project needs.

Some settings sit outside `Settings`:

- The HTTP server takes `--api-key-env`, `--host`, `--port` and `--log-level` on the command line.
  See [Serving](serving.md).
- The CLI takes flags per command. See [CLI](../reference/cli.md).
- Connectors read their own variables (`JIRA_URL`, ...); see [Connectors](connectors.md). The local
  `workspace` connector, which a build from your own files uses, reads `AWA_WORKSPACE_DIR` (the
  folder with the data, default `data`) and `AWA_WORKSPACE_DB` (a SQLite file in it); see
  [Blueprints](blueprints.md#data-from-your-files).

## Secrets

Every credential is a `pydantic.SecretStr`:

- the three provider keys (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY`) and the
  Entra client secret `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`,
- `LANGSMITH_API_KEY`, `LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY` and `LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY`,
- `AWA_POSTGRES_DSN`, because a DSN usually contains a password.

A secret prints as `**********` in `repr`, `str`, `model_dump()`, `model_dump_json()` and pydantic
validation errors. So logging a `Settings` object, or a traceback that shows one, does not leak it.
Only `.get_secret_value()` returns the value. awa calls it at the last possible moment: when it
creates the provider client, or opens the Postgres connection.

```python
settings = Settings(ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-...")
repr(settings)                                   # ... anthropic_api_key=SecretStr('**********') ...
settings.anthropic_api_key.get_secret_value()    # 'sk-ant-...'
```

Handle secrets like this:

- **Keep secrets out of code and blueprints.** Supply them through the environment, or through a
  secret manager that injects environment variables (Kubernetes secrets, Docker secrets, a vault
  agent, CI secrets).
- **Never commit `.env`.** The repository's `.gitignore` excludes it.
- **Use `${VAR}` references for MCP server credentials in blueprints.** Write
  `headers: {Authorization: "Bearer ${TICKETS_TOKEN}"}`. The references are expanded when the server
  is used, and the values are redacted from errors. See [MCP](mcp.md).
- **Errors from model construction are redacted.** They never contain the key that awa passed to
  the provider.

## `AWA_ENV`

`AWA_ENV` labels the deployment: `local`, `test`, `staging` or `production`. Any other value is a
validation error.

It is **metadata only**. awa attaches it to runs as the `env:<env>` trace tag (see
`build_trace_tags`), so you can filter traces by environment. awa never changes behavior because of
it: defaults, security checks and limits are identical in every environment.

Your application may branch on it, for example to refuse an in-memory checkpointer in production:

```python
from awa.core.settings import get_settings
from awa.errors import ConfigurationError

settings = get_settings()
if settings.env == "production" and settings.checkpointer_backend == "memory":
    raise ConfigurationError("production needs AWA_CHECKPOINTER_BACKEND=postgres")
```

## One file per environment

Keep one environment file per deployment and select it at startup:

```python
import os

from awa import Settings

settings = Settings(_env_file=f".env.{os.environ.get('AWA_ENV', 'local')}")
```

In containers, prefer injecting environment variables directly. They take precedence over any
`.env` file.

## Configuration errors

- A value that does not validate fails when `Settings` is created, with a pydantic
  `ValidationError` that names the field. An example is `AWA_CHECKPOINTER_BACKEND=redis`.
- A value that is valid on its own but unusable where it is used raises `ConfigurationError`. An
  example is a `WebhookNotifier` given a URL that is not `https://`.
- `MissingConfigurationError` is a `ConfigurationError` for a value that a selected feature needs,
  such as `AWA_POSTGRES_DSN` for a `postgres` backend.

Both subclass `ValueError` as well as `AwaError`, and carry the stable codes `awa.configuration` and
`awa.missing_configuration`. See [Exceptions](../reference/exceptions.md).

```python
from awa.errors import ConfigurationError
from awa.persistence import open_store

try:
    async with open_store(settings) as store:
        ...
except ConfigurationError as exc:     # also MissingConfigurationError
    raise SystemExit(f"awa is misconfigured: {exc}")
```

## Blueprint files

A blueprint is configuration as code. Loading one follows fixed rules:

- **Format version.** `format_version: awa/v1` records the file format. It is optional when
  reading, and `to_yaml()` / `to_dict()` always write it. A blueprint that names a format this
  version of awa does not know, such as `awa/v2`, is rejected with a clear error. It is never
  misread.
- **Explicit loaders.** `Blueprint.from_yaml_file(path)` reads a file;
  `Blueprint.from_yaml_text(text)` parses a string. `Blueprint.from_yaml(source)` (and `awa.load`)
  decides by a fixed rule: a `Path`, or a one-line string that does not read `key: value` or start
  with `{`, is a file. Anything else is YAML text. So a mistyped path fails with
  `Blueprint file not found: '...'`, not with a confusing schema error.
- **Limits.** Files and texts larger than `MAX_BLUEPRINT_BYTES` (1 MB) are rejected before they are
  parsed. So are structures with more than 100,000 values, where every use of a YAML alias counts,
  and structures nested deeper than 64 levels.
- **Safe YAML only.** Blueprints are read with `yaml.safe_load`, so no YAML tag can construct Python
  objects. Import references (`"package.module:attr"`) are only resolved with `allow_imports=True`.

## What can go wrong

| You see | Cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| `ValidationError` naming a field, for example `checkpointer_backend` | The value is not allowed (`AWA_CHECKPOINTER_BACKEND=redis`). Use one of the values in the [Settings reference](../reference/settings.md). |
| `MissingConfigurationError` for `AWA_POSTGRES_DSN` | A `postgres` backend is selected but no connection string is set. Set it, or choose `memory` or `sqlite`. |
| a value in `.env` has no effect | The environment sets the same name (it wins; `awa doctor` says `env overrides .env for ...`), the `.env` is in another folder than the project (`awa env list` shows the source), or the name is mistyped (a warning names the closest known name). |
| a changed environment variable has no effect | `get_settings()` caches. Restart the process, or call `get_settings.cache_clear()`. |
| `awa doctor` says `invalid settings` | The same `ValidationError`; `awa doctor` names the variable ([Install](../start/install.md)). |

Reference: [`Settings`](../reference/api/core.md), [Settings reference](../reference/settings.md),
[Exceptions](../reference/exceptions.md), [Blueprints](../reference/api/core.md).

<!-- source: develop/project-map.md -->

# Project map

This page is a map of the awa repository: where something lives, what it is for, and where its tests and docs
are. A test keeps it true: every package under `src/awa` is on this page, and every package on this page exists.

## The folders of the repository

| Folder | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `src/` | The library: the Python package `awa`, split into the packages below |
| `tests/` | Every test: `unit/` (offline, no key), `examples/` (the runnable examples and use cases), `proof/` (the core proof with scripted models), `architecture/` (the structure guards and the import contracts), `contracts/` (every backend against its backend protocol), `upstream/` (what awa relies on in LangChain and LangGraph), `integration/` (PostgreSQL and other real services, skipped without them), `property/`, `typing/` (`assert_type` checks of the public API types, run by `mypy tests/typing`), `docs/` (the checks of the documentation, run as their own CI job), `_helpers/` (shared test helpers) and `fixtures/` |
| `docs/` | These pages: `start/`, `guide/` (the walk-through with screenshots), `develop/`, `reference/`, `about/` |
| `examples/` | Small programs numbered `01_` to `11_`, plus `blueprints/`, `recipes/`, `usecases/`, `benchmarks/` and `evals/` |
| `deploy/` | Reference deployment files: the Dockerfile, a Docker Compose setup with PostgreSQL, a TLS edge and Langfuse, placeholder settings ([Production](production.md#reference-setup-with-docker-compose)) |
| `scripts/` | Tools for maintainers and the installers: screenshots, the architecture baseline, the generated schemas |

## The layers

A package may import only the layers below it, and inside a layer only the packages listed after it
(`.importlinter` holds the order; `lint-imports` and a test check every module). The interfaces sit on top,
the foundation at the bottom.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    IF["Interfaces: run and serve it for people and machines"]
    CP["Compiler: describe a process as data, test it"]
    IN["Integrations: company systems, files and ready-made tools"]
    OR["Orchestration: several agents working together"]
    RT["Runtime: one agent and what it uses"]
    FD["Foundation: settings, errors, contracts, the upstream seam"]
    IF -->|imports| CP -->|imports| IN -->|imports| OR -->|imports| RT -->|imports| FD
```

## The packages of `src/awa`

Tests are in `tests/unit/` unless the path says otherwise. Pages: [Architecture](architecture.md) explains the
layers, [API reference](../reference/index.md) has every name.

| Package | What it is for | Layer | Tests | Docs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `awa._compat` | The one door to the MCP client and server SDKs | Foundation | `tests/unit/test_compat_*.py`, `tests/upstream/test_*.py` | [Compatibility](../about/stability.md#python-langchain-and-langgraph) |
| `awa.core` | Settings, logging, ids, redaction, shared plumbing | Foundation | `tests/unit/test_core_*.py` | [Runtime](../reference/api/core.md#awa.runtime), [Exceptions](../reference/exceptions.md) |
| `awa.contracts` | The data every package shares: cards, messages, events, results, limits | Foundation | `tests/unit/test_contracts_*.py` | [Contracts](../reference/api/core.md#awa.contracts) |
| `awa.runtime` | The state of a running system: context, stop button, clock and ids | Runtime | `tests/unit/test_runtime_*.py` | [Runtime](../reference/api/core.md#awa.runtime), [Backend protocols](extend.md#backend-protocols) |
| `awa.models` | Chat model choice, retries, fallbacks | Runtime | `tests/unit/test_models_*.py` | [Models](models.md) |
| `awa.persistence` | Saved state: checkpoints, artifacts, run records | Runtime | `tests/unit/test_persistence_*.py` | [Memory](memory.md), [Persistence](../reference/api/data.md#awa.persistence) |
| `awa.config` | Where settings come from: the one `.env` loader and the settings registry | Foundation | `tests/unit/test_config_loader.py`, `tests/unit/test_settings_registry.py` | [Configuration](configuration.md), [Settings reference](../reference/settings.md) |
| `awa.kernel` | The small rules everything builds on: conditions and redaction; imports no other awa module (preview) | Foundation | `tests/architecture/test_kernel_isolation.py`, `tests/unit/test_core_redaction.py` | [Observability](../reference/api/server.md#awa.observability) |
| `awa._internal` | Private plumbing shared by several packages: the upstream seam to LangChain and LangGraph (`upstream`), retry, serialization, HTTP client, sandbox, ids, logging | Foundation | `tests/unit/test_core_*.py` | [Architecture](architecture.md) |
| `awa.ext` | The import surface for extension authors: redactors, ids, logging and the sync-over-async runner (preview) | Compiler | `tests/unit/test_ext_door.py` | [Architecture](architecture.md) |
| `awa.errors` | Every error awa raises, importable from one place | Foundation | `tests/unit/test_core_exceptions.py` | [Exceptions](../reference/exceptions.md) |
| `awa.agents` | The `Agent`: instructions, tools, skills, memory, run, resume; `graph_agent` runs an existing LangGraph graph as an agent | Runtime | `tests/unit/test_agents_*.py` | [Agents](agents.md) |
| `awa.tools` | Making tools and making tool calls safe (approval, limits, risk); `importing` brings in LangChain tools | Runtime | `tests/unit/test_tools_*.py` | [Tools](tools.md) |
| `awa.toolkits` | The ready-made tools: files, data, SQL, documents, web, mail | Integrations | `tests/unit/test_toolkits_*.py` | [Toolkits](tools.md#builtin-toolkits) |
| `awa.data` | A profile of your files, made without a model; safe intake; the parser backend protocol (preview) | Integrations | `tests/unit/test_data_*.py` | [The data profile](data.md), [Write a parser](extend.md#write-a-parser) |
| `awa.skills` | Reusable know-how loaded from `SKILL.md` files; `importing` brings in skill folders and prompts | Runtime | `tests/unit/test_skills_*.py` | [Skills](skills.md) |
| `awa.memory` | Long-term memory and shortening of long conversations | Runtime | `tests/unit/test_memory_*.py` | [Memory](memory.md) |
| `awa.guardrails` | Deterministic checks of inputs and outputs | Runtime | `tests/unit/test_*guardrail*.py` | [Guardrails and limits](safety.md#limits) |
| `awa.team` | `Team` and `AgentNetwork` (preview): delegation, consulting, handoffs | Orchestration | `tests/unit/test_team_*.py` | [Teams](teams.md), [Agent network](teams.md#agent-networks) |
| `awa.workflows` | Steps in order, in parallel or in a loop | Orchestration | `tests/unit/test_workflows_*.py` | [Workflows](workflows.md) |
| `awa.messaging` | The message bus, who may talk to whom, the blackboard (preview) | Orchestration | `tests/unit/test_messaging_*.py` | [Collaboration](teams.md#shared-state-notes-blackboard-directory-and-task-board) |
| `awa.tasks` | The shared task board and per-agent planning (preview) | Orchestration | `tests/unit/test_tasks_*.py` | [Collaboration](teams.md#shared-state-notes-blackboard-directory-and-task-board) |
| `awa.directory` | Who does what, and whether they are available (preview) | Orchestration | `tests/unit/test_directory_*.py` | [Collaboration](teams.md#shared-state-notes-blackboard-directory-and-task-board) |
| `awa.connectors` | Links to external systems, and the engine behind them | Integrations | `tests/unit/test_connectors_*.py` | [Connectors](connectors.md), [Write a connector](connectors.md#write-a-connector) |
| `awa.mcp` | The tools of MCP servers as agent tools | Integrations | `tests/unit/test_*mcp*.py` | [MCP](mcp.md) |
| `awa.people` | Find colleagues in Entra ID or a local list, pin them to roles, `role:` recipients (preview) | Interfaces | `tests/unit/test_people_*.py`, `tests/contracts/test_people_directory.py` | [Microsoft 365](../guide/microsoft-365.md) |
| `awa.blueprints` | A process as data: schema, check, build, design, build on your files | Compiler | `tests/unit/test_blueprints_*.py` | [Blueprints](blueprints.md) |
| `awa.quick` | A running team from names and tasks in one call | Compiler | `tests/unit/test_blueprints_short_forms.py` | [Blueprints](blueprints.md) |
| `awa.refine` | Refinement hooks of a project's `refine.py`: chat model and middleware in, out | Compiler | `tests/unit/test_blueprints_refine.py` | [Test and improve](../guide/test.md) |
| `awa.exporter` | Eject a project with one agent into a standalone LangChain and LangGraph project | Compiler | `tests/export/`, `tests/unit/test_exporter_*.py` | [Export](export.md) |
| `awa.evals` | Eval cases, scorers, the judge, reports | Compiler | `tests/unit/test_evals_*.py` | [Testing](testing.md) |
| `awa.templates` | The files of `awa init` and `awa new` (data, no code) | Compiler | `tests/unit/test_cli_init.py` | [Command line](../reference/cli.md) |
| `awa.server` | Systems as an HTTP API, jobs and MCP; the data endpoints (preview) | Interfaces | `tests/unit/test_server_*.py` | [Serving](serving.md), [The data API](data.md#the-data-endpoints) |
| `awa.automation` | Triggers, durable process runs, the worker, approvals (preview) | Interfaces | `tests/unit/test_automation_*.py` | [Blueprints](blueprints.md), [Automation](../reference/api/server.md#awa.automation) |
| `awa.observability` | Event subscribers, traces, OpenTelemetry, the audit log | Runtime | `tests/unit/test_observability_*.py` | [Observability](observability.md) |
| `awa.testing` | Offline test doubles; contract suites (`awa.testing.contracts`, preview) | Interfaces | `tests/unit/test_testing_*.py`, `tests/contracts/test_*.py` | [Testing](testing.md), [Write a store backend](extend.md#write-a-store-backend) |
| `awa.checks` | `awa check`: small read-only checks of Microsoft 365 (preview) | Interfaces | `tests/unit/test_checks.py`, `tests/unit/test_connect_microsoft.py` | [Connect Microsoft 365](../guide/microsoft-365.md) |
| `awa.plugins` | One registry of plugins (project folder, installed packages, built-ins) and the part switches; `awa plugins` | Runtime | `tests/unit/plugins/` | [Plugins](extend.md#plugins) |
| `awa.ui` | The local web app behind `awa ui` (preview) | Interfaces | `tests/unit/test_ui_*.py` | [The web app](../guide/web-app.md) |
| `awa.project_setup` | `awa setup` and `awa.setup()`: the model key, database and tracing, and local services in Docker | Interfaces | `tests/unit/test_setup_*.py` | [Set up a project](../guide/setup.md) |
| `awa.cli` | The `awa` command | Interfaces | `tests/unit/test_cli_*.py` | [Command line](../reference/cli.md) |
| `awa.__main__` | `python -m awa` | Interfaces | `tests/unit/test_cli.py` | [Command line](../reference/cli.md) |

## Python API

Generated from the docstrings. Each page starts with a runnable example.

| Page | Packages |
| --- | --- |
| [Core](api/core.md) | `awa.blueprints`, `awa.quick`, `awa.refine`, `awa.runtime`, `awa.contracts`, `awa.models`, `awa.config`, `awa.core.settings`, `awa.project_setup`, `awa.plugins`, `awa.ext` |
